cards.title: jetos: fleet/remote deployment — push generations with proof-gated rollback
cards.body:
deploy-rs/colmena/NixOps parity, first-party. Roadmap already names fleet rollout as future Epoch 7 — this card tracks it. Scope: build closures locally (or on a builder), push to remote hosts over SSH, activate with proof-before-switch (#236) on the remote, health-check window with automatic rollback, multi-host rollout ordering with dependency graph, secrets delivery at deploy time, no daemon/root beyond what activation needs (U28), offline-capable (U29). Reconcile with U15 (fleet parse/capture, done) for the config side.

- D-JOS-FLEETTARGET1=A: Hybrid: host target fields with label defaults and reusable target refs. Each fleet host carries typed target/authority fields beside its system. If omitted, the friendly label can be used as a safe SSH default. Reusable deploy.target refs avoid duplication for bastions/CI. Host key policy, privilege boundary, and identity are proof-visible.
- D-JOS-FLEETROLLOUT1=A: Hybrid: staged proof-gated rollout with plan/stage controls. Default push is staged and proof-gated with rollback-and-stop. Experts can choose batch/canary/dependency order, health timeout, and stage-only/continue flows using the same rollout object. All-at-once is an explicit policy, never the default.

4. Remote activation: run proof-before-switch remotely with minimal privilege, write remote generation ledger, stream structured logs, and never expose raw SSH/QEMU output as the primary diagnostic.
5. Health/rollback: implement ratified staged policy, per-host health checks, automatic rollback, halted rollout state, and resume/replay metadata.
6. Secrets: integrate U13 recipients and deliver secrets at deploy time only to selected host identities.
7. Tests: fake SSH transport tests for build/ship/activate/rollback, bad target diagnostics, unknown host still E1242, and a local loopback smoke where possible.
8. Artifacts/docs: systems/fleets/<name>/proof.json, per-host logs, rollout graph, docs/spec + diagnostics updates.

cards.title: jetos: declarative disks + impermanence (disko parity)
cards.body:
disko and impermanence are the community pieces every serious NixOS deployment bolts on — ship them first-party. Scope: typed disk layout declaration (partitions, filesystems, LVM, LUKS encryption, ZFS/btrfs pools/subvolumes) consumed by the #263 installer instead of imperative partitioning; mount generation from the same truth; opt-in ephemeral root (tmpfs/rollback-snapshot root) with an explicit persist list — safe-by-default semantics: nothing silently lost, activation diff shows exactly what persists.

Owner gates: disk/persist declaration surfaces are new syntax — ballot first. Reconcile with whatever partitioning #263 already implements; extend, don't fork it.
cards.plan:
Plan refreshed 2026-07-07 by codex-main.

Ratified decisions:

cards.title: Sema soundness audit: adversarial review + fuzz corpus expansion
cards.body:
jet-sema (~40k lines) owns all checking (I3); a soundness hole means unsound generated Rust reaches users silently — the worst bug class in the project (I1/I2). #185 (done) swept reachable ICEs and rustc leaks; this card hunts the other two classes: accepts-invalid (sema approves a program it must reject) and miscompiles (approved program computes the wrong thing).

Audit surface, in priority order:
1. Ownership/move/borrow proofs, including the tier-2 view/ref rules (E2-M5) and RAII cleanup (S63).
2. Sendability proofs for tasks/channels (E2-M1) — data-race freedom claims.
3. #Unsafe gate containment (D-LL1): generated `unsafe` appears only inside user-written gates; safe Jet emits none (tests/golden.rs enforces — extend it).
4. Generics + trait resolution: associated types, error conversion for `?`, trait delegation (S62), argument labels/defaults (S61).
5. Comptime/@Pure evaluation boundary (M9.5, E2-M16) — comptime results must agree with runtime semantics.
6. Newer surface: fan-out `f.[…]` (S75), fixed-size lists `[T#N]` (S76), refinements (D-REFINE1 when landed).

Method: adversarial review pass per area → each suspected hole becomes a tests/ui fixture or golden test BEFORE the fix; extend tests/fuzz_sema.rs with generative/mutation strategies over the ratified grammar; use the interpreter-vs-compiled differential battery (I2, jet dev parity) as a miscompile oracle — divergence is always a bug in one side.

Done means: audit notes committed under docs/ (findings, per-area verdict, corpus description); every confirmed hole has a failing test then a fix, all suite green; fuzz corpus + runner wired so #211 CI can execute it in budget; no invariant bent. No owner gates expected — if a finding requires a semantics change visible to users, ballot it before fixing.
cards.plan: Order: (1) read docs/spec/architecture.md R1–R12 + spec.md sections per area; (2) per audit area, spawn adversarial review (opus-tier reasoning) over the relevant sema modules — CheckerCore.rs, CheckerInfer/, CheckerCoreLib.rs, Bundle.rs; (3) write attack programs as tests/ui fixtures — expect reject; write miscompile candidates as differential fixtures — expect byte-identical interpreter/compiled output; (4) extend tests/fuzz_sema.rs: grammar-directed generation from crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs so the fuzzer only speaks ratified syntax; (5) fix confirmed holes smallest-first, full suite between fixes; (6) audit notes + corpus docs; full nix develop -c cargo test green at close.

cards.title: Workspace re-partition: shrink jet-driver, make placeholder crates real or fold them
cards.body:
jet-driver is ~44k lines and has absorbed three products: the compiler driver, Jetpack (Jetpack/CLI.rs ~4.5k, package engine), and JetOS (Jetpack/JetOS.rs ~7.2k). Meanwhile four workspace crates are shells: jet-queries (375 lines), jet-rt (401), jet-net (295), jet-impact (314). Epoch 4 (jetpack) and Epoch 7 (jetos) will grow these surfaces substantially — re-partition before they grow, not after.

Scope:
1. Extract Jetpack and JetOS out of jet-driver into their own crates (jet-pack / jet-os or per ratified naming canon: jetpack engine, jetos). jet-driver keeps only compile-pipeline orchestration + CLI dispatch.
2. For each shell crate decide: become real now, or fold into its owner until needed. jet-queries is the big one — it is the incremental-compilation seam; decide whether the query architecture becomes load-bearing now (retrofitting incrementality into a 268k-line compiler later is strictly worse). Produce a recommendation with the decision reasoning recorded in architecture.md.
3. Update docs/spec/architecture.md: crate map, dependency direction rules, which crate owns which pipeline stage (R1–R12 mapping).
4. Enforce direction: no back-edges (e.g. codegen must not depend on driver). Add a workspace-level check if cheap (cargo tree assertions in a test).

Strictly behavior-preserving: zero user-visible change, golden/snapshot suites byte-identical, full suite green. No owner gates expected (no user-facing syntax); if extraction forces a user-visible rename anywhere, ballot first. Sequencing note: do this card before the monster-file decomposition card touches Jetpack/JetOS/CLI files, so those files move once, not twice.
cards.plan: Order: (1) map current jet-driver module graph + who imports what (rg + cargo tree); (2) write the target crate map as a short architecture.md draft section — get it reviewed in-repo before moving code; (3) extract JetOS first (most self-contained), then Jetpack engine, then CLI dispatch cleanup — one extraction per commit, full suite green between each; (4) shell-crate verdicts: implement or fold, one commit each; (5) jet-queries decision writeup (incrementality now vs later) — this is a design recommendation, not a gate: record in architecture.md; (6) final pass: dependency-direction test, docs updated, full nix develop -c cargo test green.

cards.title: Decompose monster files: CoreLib.rs, Canvas.rs, TIR lower/emit, CheckerCoreLib.rs, JetOS.rs
cards.body:
Largest files today: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib.rs (13.5k lines), Source/Canvas.rs (8.4k), crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/lower.rs (8.3k), crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib.rs (7.5k), crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/JetOS.rs (7.2k), Parser/Items.rs (5.7k), TIR/emit.rs (5.3k), TIR/subset.rs (5.1k), CheckerInfer/calls.rs (4.8k), Jetpack/CLI.rs (4.5k), jet-jit/src/lib.rs (4.5k). These files burn agent context every session and are where merge mistakes concentrate. Style rule already says small modules — enforce it.

Scope: semantics-preserving decomposition of every file above ~3k lines into responsibility-named submodules. Seams follow responsibility, not line count — e.g. CoreLib.rs splits by core module family (files/io/net/…), lower.rs by TIR construct family, CheckerCoreLib.rs mirroring the CoreLib split so sema and codegen stay navigable in parallel. Target ≤ ~1,500 lines per file; judgment allowed where a real unit resists splitting — record why in the commit message.

Rules: pure code motion — no renames of public items, no behavior change, no drive-by refactors. Safety net is the existing suite: golden outputs and UI snapshots must be byte-identical; full suite green after every file's decomposition (one file per commit). Sequencing: JetOS.rs, CLI.rs, and Canvas.rs only AFTER the workspace re-partition card lands, so they move across crates once, not twice; start with CoreLib.rs / lower.rs / CheckerCoreLib.rs / Items.rs, which the re-partition does not touch.

Done means: no source file above the target without a recorded justification; module maps make sense from names alone; zero snapshot diffs; full nix develop -c cargo test green. No owner gates.

cards.title: Canvas frontend redesign — implement ratified family
cards.body: Implement the ratified Canvas frontend redesign as the next E6 Canvas slice. Build the modified hybrid surface: Workbench-style project/file viewer, hybrid code/split/graph editor, context-command model, UE5-style node/pin visual language, hover-only types, compact getter capsules, embedded simple variables, graphite styling, and detail toggles. Source remains the only semantic truth.
cards.plan:
# Plan: Canvas modified hybrid UI

Ratified inputs:
- D-FE-CANVAS1 outcome E with owner modifications.
- Existing E6 Canvas architecture and protocol from #352; do not introduce a graph asset or GUI-owned semantics.

Scope:
- Source/Canvas/html.rs, Source/Canvas/js.rs, Source/Canvas/*.rs protocol helpers, tests/canvas.rs, tests/web_dev.rs, docs/design/frontends/canvas/NOTES.md if behavior notes drift.
- Keep /canvas and /__jet_canvas routes source-backed.

Implementation steps:
1. Replace the old palette-first left surface with a persistent Workbench-style project/file viewer backed by /canvas/project and source ids. It must show workspace/package/file/function graph navigation and source-control/provenance facts where available.
2. Keep hybrid editor modes: Code, Split, Graph. Ensure selection, source-span jump, graph picker, replay/debug overlay, inspector, and project viewer all point at the same source-backed graph state.
3. Move commands out of the palette. Add command entrypoints through right-click, Ctrl+K, and drag-from-pin release menus. Drag-release menus must filter to compatible pin/node actions and show denied actions with exact why/fix where an existing diagnostic applies.
4. Polish node language: consistent shape/color families for exec/control/data/effect/fallible/reference pins; pin label is only the variable/field name; type appears in hover/inspector detail, not default label text.
5. Render variable/const getters as compact pure capsule/bubble nodes. Allow simple variables to embed inside field/value sockets for clean graphs, with an expand action back to a normal node.
6. Add detail toggles for types, diagnostics, effects, debug values, and package metadata so the default graph is streamlined graphite/gray rather than crowded.
7. Preserve keyboard focus, reduced-motion behavior, NO_COLOR/non-visual fallbacks where terminal output is involved, and existing source transaction audit payloads.

Acceptance:
- A real Jet program opened through jet dev --target=web shows the modified hybrid Canvas UI at /canvas.
- Project/file viewer is not a command palette; commands are available through context surfaces and Ctrl+K.
- Getter capsules, embeddable variables, hover-only types, and compatible drag-from-pin menus are visible in browser proof.
- Existing graph/edit/source-control/debug features still work; no stub controls.

Ratified inputs:

2. Build dashboard landing page from real data.json/source/proof facts: hosts, selected host, generation ribbon, service health, alerts, monitoring summary, proof/rollback status, and last run status. Keep copy plain and operational.
3. Build sidebar categories: Dashboard, Settings, Monitoring, Services, Packages, Secrets, Generations, Changeset, Proof/Provenance. Back categories with an internal page registry so future Studio pages register title/id/source/data needs without redesign.
4. Move settings into category pages with ordinary controls. Each setting edit must stage a source transaction and show exact Jet diff before apply.
5. Make Changeset a first-class page: unified diff, impact ledger, generation delta, proof requirements, per-hunk include where supported, Build only, Build and switch, Discard.
6. Keep one apply path. Edits from settings, dashboard alerts, rollback actions, and changeset review all stage into the same changeset/apply gate.
7. Preserve source-backed guarantees: no hidden GUI semantic state, exact config.jet diff, provenance/proof visibility, browser/headless fallback, and deterministic review output.

# Plan: categorized jet ? help palette

Scope:

cards.body: Implement the ratified hybrid jetpack/jetos CLI output as an E4 output substrate slice. # Plan: jetpack/jetos hybrid CLI output

Ratified inputs:
- D-FE-CLI1 outcome D with owner modifications: keep colored + - ~; both -y and --yes; add nh-style dependency chain/graph visualization for long builds/downloads.

Scope:
- crates/jetpack/src/Output.rs, crates/jetpack/src/CLI/*.rs command call sites, crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/commands.rs and generation/proof call sites that already share Theme/Output.
- tests/jetpack.rs, CLI usage tests, fixture stderr/stdout snapshots where output is pinned.

Implementation steps:
1. Extend the shared Theme/Output layer with consequence-scaled rendering: quiet ledger, pinned live region for long work, plan gate for mutations, deterministic plain fallback.
2. Preserve colored +, -, ~ for plan diffs; NO_COLOR replaces color with stable text markers while keeping symbols readable.
3. Normalize confirmation bypass so -y and --yes are accepted everywhere the mutation confirmation gate appears. Non-TTY mutation without yes prints plan and exits without applying.
4. Add dependency-chain progress model for long realization/build phases: downloads, builds, cached/reused nodes, current edge, counts, size/elapsed where known. Render as a pinned graph/chain in TTY; append ledger lines in non-TTY.
5. Wire jetpack add/build/env/gc and jetos plan/build/switch/proof through the same output primitives where they already share command execution paths.
6. Erase live regions before diagnostics; diagnostics remain verbatim.
7. Keep JSON output schemas untouched unless a separate schema version decision is raised.

Acceptance:
- Trivial commands stay quiet.
- Long build/download commands show useful dependency-chain progress in TTY.
- Mutations show a plan with + - ~ and require confirmation unless -y/--yes.
- Non-TTY output is deterministic and non-interactive.

Verification:
- nix develop -c cargo test --test jetpack <focused CLI output tests>

cards.title: JetOS replacement truth gate — import real NixOS and prove installed guest
cards.body: Owner asked whether JetOS can replace an entire NixOS flake/flake-parts/Home Manager config tomorrow. Audit verdict: no. Current JetOS has substantial generation/installer/VM proof plumbing, but no full semantic NixOS/HM importer and no real installed-guest acceptance proof for the owner config. This card owns the decisions and implementation gates to make that claim true.

# Plan: JetOS real NixOS replacement gate

Ratified inputs:
- D-JOS-NIXIMPORT1=C semantic NixOS/flake-parts/Home Manager importer with audited facts-only fallback.
- D-JOS-REALGUEST1=C real installed-guest proof required for replacement claims; fake QEMU only tests plumbing.
- D-JOS-DESKTOPPROOF1=C live desktop/session/app/user-home proof, not file presence.

Implementation slices:
1. Add NixOS import IR and CLI: jet os import <flake-or-dir> --host <name> [--user <name>] [--write] [--facts-only]. Parse/evaluate available Nix facts through structured JSON, not text scraping. Generate JetOS modules for system, users, packages, services, files, secrets, overlays, specialisations, Home Manager; emit exact omissions.
2. Add fixture coverage for flake.nix, flake-parts, nixosModules, home-manager.users, overlays, mkDefault/mkForce, disabledModules, specialisations, secrets, system packages, user packages.

6. Upgrade image variants: no sparse marker says built; raw/sd/qcow only built after real artifact + smoke proof.
7. First boot: generated system launches Studio control center and proves source/proof/rollback/update health path; Canvas opens from source spans only.
8. Update docs/spec/roadmap and tests so replacement claims require import+real guest tier.

Acceptance:
- Owner-style NixOS flake/flake-parts/Home Manager fixture imports to JetOS source with zero silent omissions.
- Generated JetOS config builds offline where fixtures provide packages, and omissions are explicit otherwise.
- Real VM tier command installs, reboots, logs in, opens Studio, proves desktop/services/packages/network/home/rollback from installed disk.

cards.title: Canvas full-language and Core parity truth gate
cards.body: Audit verdict: Canvas is source-backed for shipped graph/edit operations, but it does not fully edit every language feature, does not browse all Core methods, and the Run path is a debug-overlay simulation. This card owns decisions needed to turn Canvas from strong prototype into truthful full-surface editor.
cards.plan:
# Plan: Canvas full-language/Core parity gate

Ratified inputs:
- D-CANVAS-PARITY1=C AST-derived semantic ratchet plus manual UX matrix.
- D-CANVAS-CORECATALOG1=C typed Core action catalog from sema-known Core facts.
- D-CANVAS-ACTIONAUTH1=C intent cards with expert authority drawers.
- D-CANVAS-CODELENS1=C explicit Edit Source mode using source transactions.
- D-CANVAS-PROOFLENS1=C proof/debug rail with stale-proof reasons.

Implementation slices:
1. Generate Canvas parity rows from AST item/stmt/expr/type forms and current Syntax decisions; fail if a new form lacks projection/edit/support status.
2. Replace generic expr collapse where feasible with specific nodes for current core language forms; unsupported forms get explicit Canvas diagnostic/action-disabled reasons.
3. Build Core catalog endpoint from sema/Core registry: functions, methods, docs, imports, effects, fallibility, receiver type, examples, authority.
4. Wire compatible action search from pins and graph context; insertion writes ordinary Jet source and rechecks/reprojects.
5. Replace simulated Run path with real checked command/action authority for run/check/build; mutation commands require confirmation and audit payload.
6. Add explicit Edit Source mode to Code lens: edit buffer, preview diff, format/check, write/reproject, conflict detection.
7. Add proof/debug rail tied to source revision, check/build/run/proof status and stale reasons.
8. Reconcile docs/spec/spec.md, docs/reference/canvas-protocol.md, and parity matrix.

Acceptance:
- Every shipped AST language form has Canvas parity status and tests or unsupported diagnostic.
- Core method browser exposes all current Core modules/methods with typed compatible insertion.
- Split/Edit Source changes text, formats/checks, reprojects graph, and can run real output.
- Canvas Run/Build authority is real, not a toast/simulation.

Verification:
- nix develop -c cargo test --test canvas
- nix develop -c cargo test --test web_dev
- Browser smoke: edit source and graph, insert Core method, run, stale proof rail updates.
- nix develop -c scripts/agent/verify-full.sh before done.

log.text: Done after full verification. Final gate: nix develop -c scripts/agent/verify-full.sh passed. cards.title: Canvas requirement: multiple execution pins IN and OUT on nodes
cards.body: OWNER REQUIREMENT (2026-07-09, verbatim): 'multiple execution pins BOTH in and out SHOULD NOT be impossible, those are requirements for functional parity with blueprint.' Multi-exec-OUT partially exists (branch then/else, pattern arms); must generalize: any control construct with N outgoing paths projects N labeled exec outs (switch arms, loop body/done, early returns). Multi-exec-IN needs design: in Blueprint any node accepts multiple incoming exec wires (execution converges); in source-backed Jet a statement executes wherever control reaches it — N incoming exec wires = N call/reach sites of the same statement span, which today's projection renders as one exec-in accepting only one wire. Design task: projection + wiring transactions letting multiple exec sources target one node (shared continuation = e.g. moving the target into a helper fn Canvas auto-extracts, or a labeled block both paths jump to). If a canonical mechanism needs new syntax or an auto-extract convention, STOP and raise a ballot (I8: one mechanism). Deliverable: design note under docs/plans/epoch-6/ + ballot if gated + implementation with interaction scenarios (wire two exec outs into one node, assert source + execution).

cards.title: R12 parity: comptime/REPL tier-0 missing BigInt (E0956) — audit full builtin surface
cards.body:
Owner hit this live (2026-07-09): `big :: BigInt(100)` in jet repl fails with E0956 "calling BigInt can't run at compile time yet", while examples/features/text/bigint.jet (D-BIGINT1=A, golden) runs fine AOT. The REPL executes through the comptime interpreter (tier-0), so every builtin the AOT backend supports but comptime doesn't is a user-visible parity break — R12 requires JIT/dev/REPL parity through the same executable TIR.

Scope:
1. Implement BigInt construction + arithmetic + to_string in the comptime interpreter (crates/jet-comptime; CtValue may need a BigInt variant — check how AOT lowers it first).
2. Audit: enumerate every builtin/Core call AOT supports vs the comptime whitelist; produce the parity matrix as a test (ui or dedicated tests/parity.rs) so new builtins can't ship AOT-only. E0956 sites are the search key.
3. Each fixed gap needs a repl transcript test; keep E0956 wording for genuinely impossible-at-comptime effects only.

Repro: printf 'big :: BigInt(100)\n:quit\n' | target/debug/jet repl

Scope: corpus-wide lossless check — parse(fmt(src)) token-stream-equal parse(src) for every example and every tests/ui fixture. One test closes the class; new syntax is covered automatically with no per-feature test to remember.

cards.title: durability: maintainer devtools subcommands (W3)
cards.body:

Scope (surface per D-DEVTOOLS1): reduce <file.jet> (delta-debug; oracle = front-end accepts + rustc rejects, or matches a given diagnostic code); ice-report <file.jet> (bundle source + generated Rust + rustc stderr + versions); new-example <topic>/<name>; new-ui <name>; check-fixture-paths (validates path-embedding fixtures against real files); bless wrapper.

1. jet devtools reduce <file.jet> [--code EXXXX]: delta-debug minimizer; oracle = front-end accepts + rustc rejects (I2 repro) or diagnostic code match.
2. jet devtools ice-report <file.jet>: bundle source + generated Rust + rustc stderr + jet/rustc versions into one attachable file.

Scope: doc-comment pass mapping each lowering region to its TIR variant and the R12 parity contract; restructure the four TIR consumers to exhaustive match on the TIR enum so a new variant breaks the build in every consumer; distinguish honest named-unsupported fallthroughs from lazy wildcards.

cards.title: durability: tower enforcement gates (W5)
cards.body:
Plan: docs/plans/agent-durability.md W5. Today any phase jump is legal (store.mjs:224-243, triage-to-done included), decision add validates only the title, ratify outcome is unchecked against option keys, agents can write frozen/owner-lane cards, card delete cascades away ratified decisions, verdicts get mis-filed as log notes.

Scope (strictness per D-TWRGUARD1): card.checklist[] + done-gate; card.gates field required before leaving planning (BALLOT FIRST becomes structural); ballot-ready validation on decision add with --draft escape; tower verdict command minting an owner verdict as a ratified decision + card flip; ratify outcome must match an option key; owner-attribution rules for ratify/activate; non-assignee write guard; frozen/owner-lane write guard; no cascade-delete of ratified decisions; blockedBy accepts decision ids; release of a building card requires --handoff; ratify hook auto-appends syntax-decision chores (Syntax.rs, syntax-decisions.md log, jet devtools grammars, re-bless) to the card checklist.

Exit: each guard has a Tower test proving refusal/acceptance; existing board data migrates clean; skills docs updated to match.
cards.plan:
D-TWRGUARD1=C ratified — agent-hard, owner-soft. Criteria/checklist data model + done-gate + acceptance ballots are OWNED BY #463 (D-TWR-CRIT1=C); this card builds the rest of the guard family on top. All gates apply only when --by ≠ owner; owner writes bypass everything; every bypassing owner-quote is event-logged. Steps:
1. store.mjs guard layer (single chokepoint in mutate path): (a) ballot-ready validation on decision add — gist/story/inWild/options[].code/rec required, --draft flag exempts and keeps it out of the owner queue; (b) ratify/activate rejected for agents unless --quote "owner's words" given (recorded in event log); (c) no agent writes to frozen or owner-lane cards; (d) release of a building card requires --handoff note; (e) card delete refuses to cascade away ratified decisions (they retire to history instead once #461 lands; until then delete is refused outright); (f) ratify outcome must match an option key; (g) blockedBy accepts decision ids.
2. tower verdict '#N' --outcome "..." --by owner — mints an owner verdict as a ratified decision on the card and flips the card, so verdicts stop landing in logs (owner rule).
3. Ratify hook: ratifying a syntax-group decision auto-appends the standard chores (Syntax.rs, syntax-decisions.md log, jet devtools grammars, re-bless) to the card's criteria (#463 model).
4. Errors: E_GATE_* family, each with an actionable message naming the missing thing.
5. Tests: one refusal + one acceptance test per gate; owner-bypass test per gate; migration clean on live-shaped fixture.
6. Docs: Tower/AGENTS.md gate table; tower + tower-ballot skills.
Exit: every gate has paired refusal/acceptance tests; live board migrates clean; skills updated; suite green.

cards.title: Tower: archive finished board history
cards.body: tower.json is 4.2MB; 68% is closed history (496 ratified decisions = 1.7MB, 305 done cards = 1.1MB). Every write rewrites + backs up the full file (backups/ 82MB), streams it to the phone, and lands it in git (356 versions). Ballot D-TWR-ARCHIVE1 decides where finished history lives. Messages data (103KB) already removed with the messaging feature.
cards.plan:
D-TWR-ARCHIVE1=B ratified (auto-retire split live/history) MODIFIED by owner comment: keep a walk-back buffer before anything retires, and done must be strictly tested (that half lands via #463/#458). Steps:
1. store.mjs — .tower/history.json append-only ledger {decisions[], cards[], events[], each with retiredAt}. Written under the same cross-process lock; committed to git.
2. Retire policy WITH BUFFER (owner comment): on every write, retire (a) decisions status=ratified whose ratifiedAt is older than config retireAfterDays (default 3) — inside the window they stay in tower.json, show in the UI 'recently decided' strip, and tower decision reopen works one-step; (b) cards phase=done older than the same buffer AND passing the #463 done-gate rules; their questions ride along; (c) events beyond the newest 500.
3. Walk-back UX: Now view gets a collapsed 'Recently decided (N) — reversible for X days' strip listing buffered ratifications with one-tap Reopen. Reopen pulls it back to open and reverts the card advance.
4. Merged reads: findCard/decision show/card show fall through to history transparently; tower archive restore <id> moves an item back to live (reopen for ratified decisions). Board Done counts read a per-epoch summary; full done lists lazy-load via GET /api/history?epoch=.
5. CLI: tower archive status|show <id>|restore <id>. First write after upgrade migrates the existing 496 ratified decisions + 305 done cards (all outside any buffer) → tower.json ~0.5MB.
6. Tests: buffer respected (nothing retires early), reopen-from-buffer, retire-after-buffer, merged reads, restore, migration on a live-shaped fixture, backups shrink.
7. Docs: Tower README/AGENTS.md + tower-setup skill (retireAfterDays).
Exit: tower.json ≤ ~0.6MB after migration; every retired item still reachable by id; a ratification can be walked back within the buffer from phone UI; suite green.

log.text: verified by orchestrator: suite 79/79 (independent rerun); migration smoke on live-board copy: 4.2M -> 1.8M live + 2.4M history; archive status/show/restore + archived-read fallback + recentlyDecided strip working. Live retire fires on this write. Closing.

decisions.title: Build a jetdoc generator from the compiler semantic graph?
decisions.gist: Jet has doc comments (`///`, S49) and a live doctest mechanism (D-TEST4, implemented). The open question is whether to build `jet doc` — a tool that generates browsable API docs from parsed/type-resolved compiler output. Two sub-questions are entangled: (a) when does it ship relative to the sema index (D-SEMINDEX1/c96), and (b) what structured doc comment syntax does S49 need to add before generated docs are useful beyond a flat text dump? Doctests are already solved; this decision is about the API documentation generation surface only.
decisions.explainer: A semantic-graph doc generator reads the sema index (types, signatures, trait impls, doc comments) and emits HTML/Markdown API docs with tested examples. It is an E3 testing/docs ergonomics exit criterion. It depends on stable compiler seams (the `jet-sema` seam crate and the semantic index API card). Doctests close the loop: example code in `/// ` blocks is extracted and run as tests. Without this, doc quality decays because examples are untested. This card does not cover the LSP or IDE dossier views (those are D-DOSSIER1).
decisions.story: I publish a Jet library. I want `jet doc` to generate browsable API docs from my doc comments the same way `cargo doc` does — and I want any `/// ` example to fail CI if it stops compiling, not just silently rot.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) The inWild and Option A code use a pre-D-TEST4 doctest format; D-TEST4 is ratified — correct format is ```jet blocks with // => trailing comments. (2) Doctest execution (jet test --doctests) is already live via D-TEST4/c51; the open question is API doc generation only. (3) S49 says "plain text v1" — no structured doc section syntax is ratified; jetdoc built on this baseline can only emit a flat text dump. Either ratify S49 sections first or scope jetdoc explicitly to flat text. (4) Options A and C are functionally equivalent in sequencing (both gate on c96); the real decision is whether jetdoc is an E3 exit criterion.

options.name: Phase 1 AST doc now; Phase 2 sema-indexed when D-SEMINDEX1 lands (recommended)
options.detail: Phase 1 (Epoch 3, unblocked): a `jet doc` subcommand reads parsed public items and their raw `///` comments from the AST alone. Emits flat HTML per module: public signatures + doc text. No sema index required. Doctest execution (jet test --doctests) is already live via D-TEST4 — this adds browsable API surface only. Phase 2 (when D-SEMINDEX1/c96 is stable): upgrade to cross-linked, type-resolved, trait-impl-inclusive docs. Prerequisite before either phase: ratify S49 structured doc section syntax (currently "plain text v1") so Phase 1 emits structured sections instead of a raw text dump. Raise that as a follow-on ballot.
options.code:
$ jet doc
Building docs for mylib v0.1.0
  Phase 1 (AST): public symbols + raw doc comments
Wrote: docs/api/index.html
  note: type links and trait impls added in Phase 2 (when sema index lands)

$ jet test --doctests   # already live via D-TEST4
running 3 doctests
test mylib::add ... ok

options.name: Defer `jet doc` to Epoch 6 (after sema index + S49 sections)
options.detail: Do not build jetdoc until D-SEMINDEX1/c96 is stable and S49 structured sections are ratified. Avoids rebuilding Phase 1 when Phase 2 is ready. Doctests (D-TEST4) keep examples honest in the interim. Authors maintain hand-written Markdown. Viable internally but not for a public registry where doc quality is an ecosystem contract.

options.name: Hand-written docs only
options.detail: No generated docs tool. Doctests still run (D-TEST4). No browsable API surface. Keeps toolchain surface smaller. Only viable for small internal libraries; not scalable as the registry grows.
options.code:
// No jet doc. Docs are maintained manually in docs/.
// Examples compiled only when author writes a #Test block by hand.

comparisons.note: Swift DocC builds docs from typed declarations and links symbols across articles and API pages.
comparisons.code: /// Doc comment attached to a symbol

comparisons.note: rustdoc reads HIR/MIR and emits structured HTML. Doc tests (```` ``` ```` blocks in `///` comments) are compiled and run by `cargo test --doc`. This is the gold-standard baseline for jetdoc to match.
DocC compiles doc comments into a structured catalog; examples are verified at build time. Goes further than rustdoc with tutorials and interactive playgrounds.

decisions.bestCurrent: Swift DocC: Swift DocC builds docs from typed declarations and links symbols across articles and API pages.
decisions.recommendation: Phase 1 AST-level `jet doc` now (unblocked); Phase 2 sema-indexed upgrade when D-SEMINDEX1/c96 lands (Option A). Prerequisite: ratify S49 structured doc section syntax before either phase ships.

decisions.title: Add generic modules (ML-functor-style module parameterized by a type or value)?
decisions.gist: Jet has generic types and functions. Generic modules — a module parameterized by a type or value at the module level, instantiated to produce a new module — do not exist. This decides whether to add them or keep the surface at generic types and functions only.
decisions.explainer: ML-style functors let you write `module Map(K: Ord)` and instantiate it as `module IntMap = Map(Int)`. The result is a new module with all members specialized to `K = Int`. In Jet, generic types already handle the common case (`Map[K: Ord, V]`); generic modules go further by allowing module-level abstraction (sharing multiple related types, hiding implementation modules, enforcing interface contracts at the module boundary). Under I8, if generic types already cover the use case, a second mechanism is a strike. The complexity is high: module instantiation affects name resolution, the module graph, and comptime. There is no ratified syntax precedent in Jet for module-level generics.
decisions.story: I'm building a pluggable hash-map where the key comparison strategy is a module (not just a function). I want `module HashMap(K: KeyModule)` where `KeyModule` supplies `hash`, `eq`, and an associated `Error` type — none of which are cleanly expressible as a single generic type parameter.

options.name: Add generic modules (ML-functor style)
options.detail: Ratify module-level parameterization. A module can declare type/value parameters; instantiation produces a new named module. Requires new syntax, new name-resolution rules, and comptime integration. Only justified if a concrete use case cannot be served by generic types alone.

options.name: Keep generic types and functions only (status quo)
options.detail: The existing `Type[T: Trait]` and `fn foo[T: Trait]()` cover the overwhelming majority of parameterization needs. Module-level generics add complexity for a narrow use case. Reject until a concrete case proves generic types are insufficient. I8-clean.

options.name: Defer pending concrete use case
options.detail: Don't reject outright — park the card until a real Jet codebase hits the wall with generic types and functions and needs functor-level abstraction. Then revisit with a concrete motivating example.
options.code:
// deferred: no syntax or implementation
// reopen when a concrete stdlib or user case requires it

comparisons.note: OCaml functors are the canonical ML-functor. `module Map.Make(Ord)` produces a map module specialized to `Ord.t`. Widely used but notoriously hard to read for newcomers.
comparisons.code:
module IntMap = Map.Make(Int)
let m = IntMap.add 1 "one" IntMap.empty

comparisons.note: Rust has no module generics — generic types and traits cover the use case. This is the status-quo model Jet already follows; it has proven sufficient for a production systems language.
comparisons.code:
// No generic modules; use generic structs + traits:
struct HashMap<K: [Hash, Eq], V> { ... }

decisions.title: What exact syntax distinguishes generic-module type parameters, value parameters, and instantiation?
decisions.gist: Before choosing a spelling: resolve the conflict with D-GENMOD1's floor example (paren type params) and D-LINALG1's blessed `<N>` value-in-angles. The current option set contains no choice that is consistent with both prior decisions simultaneously. A new option (annotation-kind in `<...>`, no extra keyword) resolves both. The "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling may also close Options A–C entirely; confirm its scope before proceeding.
decisions.explainer: Owner instruction integrated: Jet generics use `<T>`, so generic modules must not invent `[]` for type parameters. Adversarial pass: mixing type and value parameters can become C++-template soup or force users to guess whether an argument is a type or value. Patch: keep type parameters in `<...>`, keep compile-time value parameters in `(...)`, and require instantiation to mirror declaration. If that still feels too large for E3, choose the Epoch 6 defer option and keep ordinary generic structs/functions as the only generic surface for now.
decisions.story: Priya is writing a fixed-size LRU cache package. The key type controls hashing/equality, while the capacity is a compile-time value. She wants one generic module that exports `Cache`, `put`, and `get`, then instantiates `StringCache32` once for the rest of the package.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Address GENMOD2; integrate the instruction that Jet generics use `<T>`, provide better options, and include an option to defer to Epoch 6.
Agent answer: Corrected. The previous `[]` type-parameter option was wrong for Jet because `[]` already reads as list/indexing while `<T>` is the ratified generic form. Updated options now center `<T>` for type parameters, separate compile-time value parameters with `(...)`, and add an Epoch 6 defer option.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): PRIOR DECISION CONFLICTS (must resolve before any option is adopted): D-GENMOD1's ratified code example uses `module Sorted(T: Ord)` — type param in parens; Option A contradicts this. D-LINALG1 blessed Vec<N> (value-in-<...>) as the substrate spelling; Option A puts values in (...), directly contradicting. The comptime section of syntax-decisions.md says "Rejected: const generics in v1" — module value parameters are const generics and this rejection may apply. PARSER HAZARD (Option A): `Lru<String>(32)` is syntactically identical to D-SERDE6 turbofish `fn<T>(arg)`; parser cannot resolve without name-resolution, violating parse-before-sema. VOCABULARY HAZARD (Option B): `const` is a teaching-error-only keyword (S14); using it inside `<...>` is the first real use. MISSING OPTION E: unified `<K: Hash, capacity: Int>` with annotation-kind as distinguisher — consistent with D-LINALG1, avoids all vocabulary collisions.

options.name: Unified `<...>`: annotation kind distinguishes type vs value params (recommended)
options.detail: Both type and value parameters live in `<...>`. A parameter whose annotation is a bound/trait (`K: Hash`) is a type parameter; one whose annotation is a value type (`capacity: Int`) is a value parameter — no extra keyword, no dual-bracket syntax. Instantiation mirrors declaration: `Lru<String, 32>`. Consistent with D-LINALG1's `Vec<N>` substrate (value-in-angles already blessed). Supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype floor example which used parens — that was explicitly a placeholder "until GENMOD2 decides." Parser: distinguishes a type expression (capital-cased, D-CASING1) from a value expression at instantiation sites in `<...>` — mostly mechanical at the lexer level.

options.name: Defer generic modules to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not add module-level type/value parameters now. Ordinary generic structs and functions (`fn sort<T: Ord>`, `struct Vec<T>`) already cover most use cases. Defer if the "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling in the comptime section applies to module value parameters, or if the D-LINALG1 `Vec<N>` value-parameter surface needs a unified ruling before any single site commits.

options.name: Ordinary generic types/fns only — no module-level parameters
options.detail: Decline generic modules entirely. Priya's LRU cache is a generic struct with a capacity field; the type-level instantiation story is solved by generic types already. Module-level parameters are a second mechanism for the same parametrization job (I8 risk). Only reconsider if a concrete use case cannot be expressed with generic types.

comparisons.note: Rust uses `<T>` for type parameters and also has const generics in `<...>`. Good precedent for Option B, but Jet should avoid forcing values into type syntax unless needed.
C++ templates mix type and value parameters in angle brackets. Powerful, but visually dense and a known complexity sink.
comparisons.code: template<typename K, int N> struct Lru { ... };

comparisons.note: OCaml functors are module-level generics, but parameters are module-shaped. Powerful, less beginner-direct than Jet’s desired package surface.
Zig uses comptime parameters in function-like declarations; clear for values, but Jet already has `<T>` for type generics.
comparisons.code: fn Lru(comptime K: type, comptime capacity: usize) type { ... }

decisions.recommendation: Unified `<K: Hash, capacity: Int>` — annotation kind distinguishes type vs value parameters in `<...>` (Option A). Consistent with D-LINALG1's Vec<N>; supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype floor example. If the "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling applies, choose Option B (defer).

decisions.title: Should Jet define a generic database driver interface with parameterized-queries-only enforcement?
decisions.gist: Jet already has SQLite support in core.db (c50). The question is whether to define a generic Driver trait that any database backend implements, with the interface enforcing parameterized queries only — making string-concatenated SQL structurally impossible. No generic driver interface exists today; this is the next step above the SQLite-specific API.
decisions.explainer: A Driver trait with a parameterized-only API eliminates SQL injection by construction — you cannot build a raw SQL string and execute it through the driver interface. This is a strong safety guarantee consistent with I1 (safe by default). The SQLite implementation (c50) becomes the first impl of Driver; Postgres, MySQL, and others would follow as stdlib or community packages. The interface design needs to cover: connection lifecycle, transactions (#Transact?), async vs sync, and error types. None of those require new syntax — they use existing Jet markers and the T ? E error type. The main risk is locking in a Driver shape before we know what async looks like in Jet; a sync-only v1 Driver is safe to ship now.
decisions.story: I want to write database code that works with SQLite in tests and Postgres in production, and I want the compiler to make it impossible to accidentally run string-interpolated SQL.

options.name: Define Driver trait + parameterized-only API; SQLite as first impl
options.detail: Specify a Driver trait with query(sql: &str, params: []Param) -> Result<Rows, DbError> and no raw-execute surface. SQLite (c50) is refactored to implement it. Safe by construction against SQL injection. Sync-only for now; async variant deferred until Jet's async story is settled.

options.name: Per-database APIs only; no generic Driver trait
options.detail: Keep core.db as the SQLite-specific API. Each new database gets its own module with its own API. No shared interface. Simpler short-term; loses the cross-backend portability and the injection guarantee at the interface level.

options.name: Defer — design after async story is settled
options.detail: The right Driver shape depends on whether queries are sync or async. Wait until Jet's async/concurrency model is ratified, then design Driver once with the right shape. Risk: blocks any new database backends in the meantime.

comparisons.note: Generic DB interface with parameterized queries via ? placeholders. Drivers register themselves. No string-building API at the interface level — close to what Jet is proposing.
Macro-verified parameterized queries checked against a live DB at compile time. Stronger than Go but requires a live DB in CI — Jet's approach is lighter.

decisions.title: Web backend: hybrid JS-DOM for views + WASM for logic?
decisions.gist: Jet has no web target. The proposal is to compile view/UI code to JS DOM operations and logic/compute code to WASM, letting the JS bridge own the DOM while WASM handles the heavy work. This is the proceed/kill gate for any web target at all.
decisions.explainer: A hybrid JS+WASM target is the front door to replacing TypeScript. All-WASM hits a known bottleneck: WASM cannot touch the DOM directly without JS glue, so all-WASM still produces JS glue; the question is whether that glue is generated by Jet or hand-written. All-JS transpile loses the safety and performance properties that make Jet worth using. The hybrid strategy matches how wasm-bindgen and Emscripten actually work in practice. This decision gates the JS/Swift interop card (D-JSWIFTFFI1) and interacts with the one-type-system-wire decision (c23wsw4) and reactive-ui.
decisions.story: I write my app logic in Jet and get WASM performance for data processing. My view layer auto-generates efficient DOM updates. I never write TypeScript.

options.name: Hybrid: JS-DOM for views, WASM for logic
options.detail: Jet's codegen partitions the program: UI/view declarations compile to a thin JS driver that issues DOM operations; pure logic functions compile to WASM. The JS driver calls into WASM for compute. Avoids the WASM-DOM roundtrip bottleneck for event-heavy UI while keeping compute fast.

options.name: All-WASM with generated JS glue
options.detail: Compile everything to WASM; generate the JS DOM glue automatically. Simpler codegen split; JS glue is still emitted, just hidden. The WASM-DOM roundtrip cost remains and is harder to optimize without the partition.

options.name: All-JS transpile
options.detail: Compile Jet directly to JavaScript — no WASM. Simple toolchain; no compile step for small scripts. Loses memory safety enforcement, type-system guarantees at runtime, and performance on compute-heavy paths. Jet becomes a TypeScript replacement without the performance story.
options.code:
// jet build --target js
// -> app.js  (no WASM, no safety guarantees at runtime)

options.name: Defer web target
options.detail: No web backend now. Focus on native and CLI targets first. Keeps the target matrix small; blocks the TS-replacement use case indefinitely. Re-evaluate post-Epoch 3.
options.code:
// status quo: jet has no web/WASM target
// jet build --target web  ->  error: target not supported

comparisons.note: wasm-bindgen compiles Rust logic to WASM and generates JS bindings for DOM calls — the hybrid pattern Jet would adopt. Framework crates (Leptos, Yew) sit on top.
Elm compiles to JS only (all-JS), not WASM. Excellent correctness story but no WASM performance path — the tradeoff of option C.
comparisons.code:
-- Elm: compiles entirely to JS, no WASM
main = Browser.sandbox { init = 0, update = update, view = view }

decisions.title: Concurrency model for Go-scale networking: green-threads/M:N over task+channel, or add @async/await?
decisions.gist: Epoch 3 requires an async runtime capable of 100k+ concurrent connections. The shipped model teaches tasks and channels; the question is whether to keep that model and add an M:N scheduler under it, or introduce @async/await coloring. This is the keystone Epoch 3 decision — coroutines, structured concurrency, and deadline cards all depend on it.
decisions.explainer: The function-color problem (async infects call sites) is the core tradeoff. @async/await requires every function that awaits to be marked, propagating annotation up the call graph — the 'color' spreads. Green-threads / M:N scheduling makes all tasks implicitly concurrent; blocking calls yield automatically; no call-site annotation. Jet already ships `task { }` and channels; green-threads extend that model with a scheduler, not a new surface. @async/await introduces new syntax (D-level decision), a new execution model, and a bifurcated function space — a second way to mean 'this function may yield' next to the task model, which violates I8. A hybrid adds both costs. This decision must be made before coroutines-prim, structured-concurrency, or deadline cards proceed.
decisions.story: I write a server that handles 100,000 simultaneous WebSocket connections. I don't want to mark half my functions `@async` just because they read from a socket. I want to write normal-looking code and have the runtime handle the concurrency.

options.name: Green-threads / M:N scheduler under the task+channel model
options.detail: Add an M:N thread scheduler to the runtime. `task { }` blocks become green-thread yields; socket/IO calls park the task and wake it on readiness. No new surface syntax; no function coloring; the existing task/channel API gains concurrency scale without user changes. Matches Go's goroutine approach. Aligns with the shipped teaching model.

options.name: @async/await + futures
options.detail: Add `@async fn` and `await` expressions. Explicit at every call site that yields; type system tracks async-ness. Functions bifurcate into async/non-async. Introduces function coloring and a second 'this yields' mechanism alongside tasks — I8 tension. Familiar to Rust/JS developers.

options.name: Hybrid: M:N scheduler + @async opt-in for fine-grained control
options.detail: Ship the M:N green-thread scheduler (option A) as the default; allow `@async fn` for callers who need explicit future/poll control (e.g. embedding in C event loops). Two mechanisms for yielding — violates I8 unless the `@async` path is kept to an expert escape hatch with a narrow, documented use case.

comparisons.note: Go's goroutines are the green-thread / M:N model: write normal blocking code, the scheduler handles concurrency. No function coloring; 100k+ goroutines are routine.
Rust uses async/await + a future executor. Every async call site must be marked; function color propagates. High performance, but the bifurcation is a known ergonomics cost.
BEAM spawns millions of lightweight processes (green-threads) with no async annotation. Concurrent IO is the default; no function color. The closest prior art to option A at scale.
comparisons.code:
handle(Socket) ->
    {ok, Data} = gen_tcp:recv(Socket, 0),
    gen_tcp:send(Socket, process(Data)),
    handle(Socket).

decisions.title: Ship user-authored derives + typed reflection (Epoch 3 exit criterion)?
decisions.gist: Libraries need to author derives (like #[Serialize], #[Codable]) using a typed reflection API. The Epoch 3 exit criterion includes this. The v1 ceiling is already ratified: reflection + derives only, no arbitrary macros. This is the umbrella proceed/kill gate; D-METAREFLECT1 (read API) and D-METADERIVE1 (output) are sub-decisions that open only if this passes.
decisions.explainer: Today only builtin derives exist. User-authored derives require two things: (1) a typed reflection API that lets comptime code inspect a type's fields, types, and markers (D-METAREFLECT1); and (2) a mechanism for derive output to re-enter the compiler and be sema-checked (D-METADERIVE1). D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratifies the architecture rule (output must re-enter sema, not bypass it). The v1 ceiling (no arbitrary macros) is the I8 guard: derives are a single, scoped metaprogramming job; general macros would be a second surface that can do the same job. Deferring blocks any library that needs Serialize, ORM field mapping, or any type-driven code generation until post-v1.
decisions.story: I'm writing a serialization library. I want to derive Serialize on any user struct automatically — inspect its fields at comptime and emit the encode/decode implementation. I should not need to hardcode this into the compiler.

options.name: Ship user derives + typed reflection within the ratified ceiling
options.detail: Approve opening D-METAREFLECT1 and D-METADERIVE1. Delivers the Epoch 3 exit criterion; enables third-party derive libraries (Serialize, ORM, validation); keeps the ceiling at reflection+derives (no arbitrary macros). D-CTCODEGEN1's architecture constraint (output re-enters sema) applies.

options.name: Builtin derives only; no user-authored derives
options.detail: Keep derives as a closed set in the compiler. No reflection API, no derive output mechanism. Library authors cannot add new derives; every new derive requires a compiler PR. Blocks the serialization, ORM, and validation library ecosystem.

options.name: Defer to post-Epoch 3
options.detail: Treat user derives as post-v1. Epoch 3 ships without a derive authoring API. Third-party serialization/ORM libraries cannot work without manual impl. Re-evaluate after the runtime, async, and other Epoch 3 exits are done.

comparisons.note: Rust derive macros are proc-macros that receive a TokenStream and emit a TokenStream — powerful but operate on syntax trees, not typed reflection. Jet's typed reflection API is safer and simpler.
Swift's Codable is a compiler-synthesized protocol conformance — a builtin derive only. Third-party derives are impossible; every new derive requires a Swift compiler change.

decisions.title: Derive output: emit Jet source via $ splice, re-parsed and sema-checked?
decisions.gist: User-authored derives need a way to emit code. D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratifies that output must re-enter lexer/parser/sema (never bypass it). This decision fixes the surface: the `$` splice inside `comptime { }` is the output mechanism. Opens only if D-USERDERIVE1 passes.
decisions.explainer: D-CTCODEGEN1 forbids derives from emitting Rust directly or manipulating the AST in-place — all output must be Jet source that re-enters the front end. The `$` splice already exists for comptime value injection. The question is whether derive output is the same `$` splice mechanism (extended to emit function/impl blocks) or a separate API (typed AST builder). A typed AST builder is a second mechanism for emitting code — I8 violation. The `$` splice path means all derive errors appear in Jet source terms, not in opaque AST operations (I2/I3 compliant). The main risk is that splicing multi-line impl blocks requires the splice to carry statement-level fragments, not just expressions — a small extension to the existing mechanic.
decisions.story: My derive_Serialize function builds up a String of Jet source for the encode/decode methods, then splices it in with `${ ... }`. The parser re-reads it; sema checks the types; if I made a mistake, the error points at the generated Jet, not at rustc output.

options.name: $ splice emits Jet source fragments, re-parsed and sema-checked
options.detail: Extend the existing `$` splice to carry statement- and item-level Jet source (not just expressions). The emitted text re-enters the lexer and parser exactly as user-written Jet would. Sema sees the expanded code; errors appear in Jet source terms. One mechanism for comptime output; I8 satisfied; I2/I3 satisfied.

options.name: Typed AST builder API
options.detail: Derives call a builder API (`ImplBlock.new()`, `.add_method()`, etc.) that constructs a typed AST node directly. No string parsing; type-safe at the builder call sites. A second mechanism for emitting code alongside the `$` splice — I8 tension. Builder API surface must be designed, stabilized, and versioned separately.

options.name: Defer derive output mechanism
options.detail: Approve D-USERDERIVE1 and D-METAREFLECT1 but leave the output mechanism open. Reflection ships; derives cannot emit code yet. Partial; blocks the actual derive use cases; not a useful intermediate state.

comparisons.note: Rust proc-macros receive and emit `TokenStream` — effectively source text in token form, re-parsed by the compiler. The `quote!` macro is the ergonomic surface. Jet's `$` splice is the same concept with Jet syntax.
Zig comptime functions return types directly — a typed approach closer to option B. No string emission; the comptime function is the mechanism. Works because Zig's type system is the API surface.

decisions.comment: Reconciled 2026-06-27 from docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md and decision-ballots.md: derive Trait for T + Jet source-fragment re-entry via $ splice.

decisions.title: Should Jet commit to a layered reactive UI stack as a strategic pillar?
decisions.gist: The proposed stack is: reactivity → view model → typed styles → headless+styled component kit → motion/app kit — each layer building on the previous. This is the TypeScript/Swift UI replacement play. Gated on D-REACTCORE1 (how reactivity works) and D-RENDERTGT1 (backend seam). No layer of this stack should be built until those two gate decisions are made.
decisions.explainer: Committing to this stack means Jet's stdlib eventually includes a full UI framework, not just a signal library. That is a large scope addition — UI frameworks are notoriously hard to get right and to maintain. The payoff is that Jet becomes a genuine TS/Swift alternative for app developers. The risk is years of stdlib work that distracts from language correctness and performance. This decision is about strategic direction, not immediate implementation — no code ships before D-REACTCORE1 and D-RENDERTGT1 are resolved. I8: the stack must have one canonical mechanism at each layer, not multiple competing approaches.
decisions.story: I want to build a web or native app entirely in Jet — not reach for React or SwiftUI. That means Jet needs a first-party UI layer that is reactive, composable, and ships real components.

options.name: Adopt layered stack, sequenced after gate decisions
options.detail: Commit to the strategic direction. Build each layer in order, gated on D-REACTCORE1 + D-RENDERTGT1. No code before those are decided. Long roadmap but gives Jet a genuine app-dev story.

options.name: UI is third-party only
options.detail: Jet ships no UI framework. The signal library (D-REACT1) is the ceiling of stdlib UI support. Third parties build frameworks on top. Keeps stdlib small; risks ecosystem fragmentation (multiple incompatible UI libs).

options.name: Defer — decide at v1
options.detail: No commitment now. Revisit after the language core is stable. Safe for the near term but defers the TS/Swift replacement play indefinitely.
options.code: // No decision — UI story TBD post-v1

comparisons.note: Apple committed to a layered reactive UI stack (Combine → SwiftUI) early. The two-layer seam (reactive model + declarative views) has held up well across platforms.
Elm built the reactive model into the language (The Elm Architecture) and owns the full UI stack. Extremely coherent but brittle to extend beyond its core use-case.
comparisons.code: update Increment model = { model | count = model.count + 1 }

decisions.title: Should Jet's runtime adapt behavior to environmental signals (battery, network, load, carbon)?
decisions.gist: The idea is a runtime that reads environmental conditions and adjusts behavior — throttles work on low battery, degrades quality under load, shifts tasks to low-carbon windows. This is a New idea with no existing card. The question is whether this belongs in the language/runtime or in a library that apps call.
decisions.explainer: Environmental adaptation is inherently app-specific policy — what 'degrade under load' means for a video encoder is different from a web server. Baking adaptation into the runtime (option B) risks making the default behavior magical and hard to audit (I1: safe/predictable defaults). A library that exposes signals (battery level, network quality, carbon intensity) and lets app code choose the policy is more composable and auditable. Carbon intensity data requires an external API (electricityMap, WattTime) — the runtime cannot self-contain it. This overlaps with D-ADAPTFID1 (fidelity knob) and D-CARBON1; all three should fold into one decision.
decisions.story: I'm shipping a background sync task. I want it to pause when the battery is below 20%, slow down on metered connections, and prefer running when the grid is clean — without writing platform-specific code for each.

options.name: Library exposing env signals + policy hooks
options.detail: Stdlib exposes a thin `Env` API: battery level, network quality, estimated carbon intensity (via OS/external). App code reads these and sets its own policy. Predictable, auditable, no hidden runtime behavior. Correct match for I1.

options.name: Runtime-managed adaptation
options.detail: The runtime automatically throttles tasks, degrades quality, or defers work based on environmental conditions. Magic and convenient but opaque — hard to debug when behavior differs across devices. Violates predictability (I1 concern).

options.name: Defer / don't add
options.detail: Niche use case. Most apps handle this ad-hoc or via platform APIs. Add only if there is clear demand. Fold the three adaptive cards (runtime, fidelity, carbon) into one decision when the time comes.
options.code: // No stdlib env-adaptation; apps use platform APIs directly

comparisons.note: Constraint-based scheduling (battery, network, idle) as library/framework, not language primitives. Policy is explicit in code.
OS signals exposed as library APIs; apps poll or observe and apply their own policy. No automatic adaptation.

decisions.title: Add a full logic-programming subset (backtracking, multi-answer relations) to Jet?
decisions.gist: Research notes caution against a full logic-programming subset. The gentler slice — failure-aware iterators and comprehensions — is already on the roadmap. The question is whether to add true multi-answer relations and backtracking on top of that, or hold the line.
decisions.explainer: Full LP (Prolog-style) requires unification, a choice-point stack, and a non-deterministic execution model that cuts across Jet's deterministic ownership semantics. It would introduce a second execution model with different rules for variable binding, mutation, and resource cleanup — directly conflicting with I8 and with the safety-by-default guarantee. The failure-aware-comprehension card covers the practical 90% case (generators that can fail or produce multiple results) without a separate execution model. A full LP subsystem would also complicate the JIT tier and codegen.
decisions.story: I want to write a solver that enumerates valid configurations of a constraint system — like a puzzle solver or a type-inference engine — without shelling out to Prolog.

options.name: Reject full LP — keep failure-aware iterators only
options.detail: The failure-aware-comprehension card already targets the practical use cases. Full backtracking introduces a second execution model (choice points, unification) incompatible with deterministic ownership. Recommend keeping the door closed.

options.name: Adopt a scoped LP subset (relations block)
options.detail: A `@logic { }` block opts in to a Datalog-style subset: finite relations, no function symbols, stratified negation. Bounded and terminating, so no infinite search trees. Still a second execution model — variables inside the block bind differently — which violates I8.

options.name: Far-horizon: post-v1 constraint/solver research
options.detail: Park LP as a research item. A future constraint-programming library (not a language feature) could implement backtracking via a continuation monad or explicit search stack, keeping the language surface clean. No language change needed.

comparisons.note: Full LP with backtracking and unification. Powerful for combinatorial search but the non-deterministic execution model is notoriously hard to reason about for programmers from imperative backgrounds.
comparisons.code:
path(X, Z) :- edge(X, Y), path(Y, Z).
?- path(1, Z).
Z = 2 ;
Z = 3.

comparisons.note: A minimal logic DSL embedded in a host language. It works but requires the programmer to think in a completely different evaluation model — the very friction Jet wants to avoid.
comparisons.code:
(run* (q)
  (fresh (x y)
    (== q (list x y))
    (membero x '(1 2))
    (membero y '(a b))))

decisions.title: Commit to a structural (AST/semantic) merge tool for Jet version control?
decisions.gist: Structural merge resolves version-control conflicts using the program's AST or semantic identity rather than line-based text diff. This is new and not yet carded for implementation. It depends on content-addressed definitions and a semantic index, neither of which is built.
decisions.explainer: Line-based merge fails when two branches rename a function, reorder arguments, or extract a helper — producing conflicts that are trivially safe or spurious conflicts that obscure real ones. A structural merge tool would compare AST nodes by identity (name + signature or content address), resolve renames and moves automatically, and surface only semantic conflicts. Prerequisites: stable AST serialization, content-addressed definitions (its own unbuilt card), and a semantic index API. This is a tooling feature, not a language feature — it does not touch syntax or sema, so I1/I8 are not at risk. But it is a large, standalone project that competes for capacity with in-flight compiler work.
decisions.story: I refactored a module across two branches — one renamed a function, the other added parameters. Git thinks it's a conflict. A structural merge tool would see they touched different things and merge cleanly.

options.name: Far-horizon: capture, don't build now
options.detail: Record the idea and its prerequisites (content-addressed defs, semantic index). Build neither until those foundations exist. The semantic index and content-addressed-definitions cards must land first; revisit structural merge after they do. No current action.

options.name: Build a structural merge tool now
options.detail: Start the tool alongside the compiler. Requires inventing an AST serialization format and a merge algorithm before the AST is stable. High risk of rework as the language evolves. Not recommended.

options.name: Reject — out of scope
options.detail: Structural merge is a tooling feature orthogonal to the language. Jet can ship v1 without it; existing Git workflows are sufficient. The effort is better spent on the compiler. Reject and don't revisit.
options.code:
// No action. Developers use standard git merge.
// Conflict resolution is a developer workflow problem, not a language problem.

comparisons.note: A structural diff tool using tree-sitter grammars. Shows diffs in terms of AST nodes rather than lines. Does not do merging — only diffing — but demonstrates the value of structural comparison.
comparisons.code:
# difftastic output (not Jet):
# left.py            right.py
# def foo(x):        def foo(x, y):  # added param
#     return x + 1       return x + y

comparisons.note: GitHub's experimental semantic merge tool parsed code into typed syntax trees and merged on AST identity. Abandoned in 2021 — the project underestimated the complexity of a language-agnostic merge algorithm.
comparisons.code:
# github/semantic (archived)
# semantic diff --language python a.py b.py
# → proved the concept; proved it was hard to generalize

decisions.title: Which crypto primitive backend powers `crypto.seal/open` + `sign/verify`? (I6 owner gate)
decisions.gist: D-CRYPTOENV1=A ratified the seal/open + sign/verify envelope. This is an I6 external-dependency approval gate for the underlying AEAD/signature primitives. Pure-Rust is preferred for the native-ize end-state.
decisions.explainer:
Hand-rolling primitive crypto is a footgun (constant-time, audited impls). A vetted backend is required; I6 governs which: runtime-side only, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation. Differentiator is the backend's I6 posture. Blast radius: a stdlib `crypto` module + `.jet/lock` pin.

Recommendation: A — RustCrypto is pure Rust with no C/asm, the closest of the three to the I6 end-state and simplest to re-implement first-party.

options.name: Pure-Rust RustCrypto (aes-gcm/chacha20poly1305/ed25519-dalek)
options.detail:
Audited pure-Rust crates, gated runtime-side like Cranelift.

I6: pure Rust, no C/asm — closest to the native-ize end-state, easiest to re-implement first-party.

box@ Bytes = crypto.seal(key, plaintext)?
sig@ Bytes = crypto.sign(privkey, msg)
crypto.verify(pubkey, msg, sig)?

options.detail:
Battle-tested, fast.
I6: pulls in C + assembly, needs a C toolchain, pins a non-Rust core — furthest from the end-state.

options.name: libsodium via FFI
options.detail:
Bind system libsodium through the stdlib FFI-bridge pattern.
Widely audited, misuse-resistant — but an external C library + system dep (nixpkgs-interim), heaviest to native-ize, worst non-Nix story.

comparisons.note: RustCrypto offers pure-Rust AEADs, hashes, signatures, and traits with broad audit attention and no C toolchain.

decisions.bestCurrent: RustCrypto: RustCrypto offers pure-Rust AEADs, hashes, signatures, and traits with broad audit attention and no C toolchain.
decisions.recommendation: Use RustCrypto behind Jet’s misuse-resistant envelope. Jet can expose fewer knobs than Rust while keeping pure-Rust portability.

decisions.gist: Partition inference requires a `Browser` effect (or equivalent named call-graph rule) as its engine — the current D-EFF4 closed set has no such entry. The JS/WASM boundary is bidirectional (WASM→JS exports and JS→WASM callbacks) and interacts with the D-SIGNAL1 reactive graph. Before this decision can be ratified, D-WEBKIND1 (WASM target) and D-JSBIND1 (boundary types) must exist as ballot cards, and the inference engine must be defined precisely enough to snapshot-test.
decisions.story: Priya writes a dashboard. Her chart view responds to clicks in the browser, but CSV export and matrix transforms should run in WASM. She does not want to annotate a hundred helper functions; she wants Jet to send pure compute to WASM and keep browser API code in JS.

comparisons.note: Modern web frameworks infer client/server splits from imports and boundaries, minimizing manual export markers.

options.name: Infer from `Browser` effect + allow module-level target ceilings (recommended)
options.detail: Amend D-EFF4 with a `Browser` effect and use effects as the default partition engine: browser/DOM APIs imply JS; pure/compute code is WASM-eligible. Add the useful part of B as expert control: a module may declare `#Target(Wasm)` or `#Target(Js)` as a ceiling/default, and sema validates it against the inferred effects. This keeps beginner magic (no required module declarations) and gives large teams auditable module-level placement. Per-function `#Wasm`, `#Js`, and `#WasmExport` remain overrides. GATES: D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 still need ballots before implementation.

options.name: Module-level `#Target(Wasm)` / `#Target(Js)` declarations + sema validation
options.detail: Each module declares its default compile target in the header. All functions in the module inherit the default; per-function overrides allowed. Inference validates: a `#Target(Wasm)` module calling a Browser-effect function is a compile error. Explicit, auditable, and no language-gate dependency (no comparison-operator or compiler-type-family changes required). Less magic than Option A for beginners; more auditable for large teams. Does not require amending D-EFF4. Compatible with D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 being raised later.

options.name: Defer web partitioning to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not decide the JS/WASM boundary now. D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 are unraised cards that must precede a sound partition model. D-EFF4 may need amending. D-SIGNAL1=A reactive primitives have no boundary model. D-PLUGIN1's Component Model may or may not compose with the web-backend WASM target. Deciding D-WASM1 before these gates produces a model that will be revised within the same epoch.
options.code:
// No web target partition policy yet.
// Epoch 6 revisit after D-WEBKIND1, D-JSBIND1, and D-EFF4 amendment are settled.

decisions.recReason: Effects already encode the information. Inference gives beginner magic and keeps target details out of normal Jet code; explicit markers remain possible later for exports, not partitioning every helper.
decisions.title: For the web backend, how does Jet partition JS DOM code and WASM logic while preserving expert control?
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: pure inference is not enough for experts. Best shape is inferred default plus explicit markers and a partition report. Compared with Next/SvelteKit, Jet should keep the magic boundary inference but add typed bridge/audit reports. Compared with wasm-bindgen, Jet should require less manual glue and own all diagnostics. Adversarial pass: override markers can create unsound crossings. Patch: sema rejects browser handles in WASM, checks bridgeable types/effects, emits a build manifest, and snapshots boundary diagnostics.
decisions.bestCurrent: SvelteKit / Next.js: Modern web frameworks infer client/server splits from imports and boundaries, minimizing manual export markers.
decisions.recommendation: Use effect inference by default plus module-level `#Target` controls (Option A). Pure B makes every beginner choose a target; hybrid A gives magic out of the box and expert visibility where teams need it.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: We must ensure full expert control & auditability. Reconsider this ballot with devil's advocate, make it best in the world.
Agent answer: Updated. New rec: C, not pure inference. Default is inferred from effects and browser API use; experts can pin #Wasm, #Js, #WasmExport, then inspect `jet build --target web --explain-partition`. Devil's advocate: overrides can create unsound crossings. Patch: sema checks all boundary types/effects, rejects browser handles in WASM, emits a bridge manifest, snapshots boundary diagnostics.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): INFERENCE ENGINE GAP: D-EFF4 (ratified) closed the effect vocabulary at ten effects with no Browser/Dom entry; Option C inference has no implementation foundation without amending D-EFF4 or introducing a parallel ad-hoc tracking pass (I8 violation). Option F (add Browser effect) is the I8-coherent path. PURE ≠ WASM: #Pure (empty effect set) ≠ "WASM candidate" — wasm32-wasip2 allows Net/Fs effects in WASM; correct inference rule is "no Browser effect in transitive closure," blocked on D-WEBKIND1. CALLBACK BRIDGE MISSING: #WasmExport covers WASM→JS direction only; JS→WASM callbacks are absent from all options, gated on D-JSBIND1. D-PLUGIN1 COHERENCE: D-PLUGIN1=B (WASM Component Model) and this web-backend WASM model are two distinct incompatible WASM compile targets — neither ballot acknowledges the other.

log.text: Owner asked why not module-level declarations; Option A now includes module-level `#Target` as expert control while keeping inference default.
Ballot cleanup: rec key fixed, detail deduplicated, naming corrected.
Adversarial pass complete: options hardened, challenges documented in detail field.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation (adversarial pass + recommendation fused), rec moved to A.

decisions.gist: M:N green threads are decided. This card chooses the runtime implementation behind blocking-looking socket/file APIs. It is not user syntax: user code keeps `task { }`, channels, and ordinary reads/writes.
decisions.story: Gary runs a chat server with 50,000 open TCP connections. Most sockets are idle. `socket.read()` should park the Jet task and free the OS thread until the socket is ready, without Gary learning epoll, kqueue, or IOCP.

comparisons.note: Go parks goroutines on epoll/kqueue/IOCP through platform-native netpollers, enabling high concurrency.

options.name: Own platform-native backends (recommended)
options.detail: Implement Linux io_uring/epoll, macOS/BSD kqueue, and Windows IOCP behind one runtime trait. No external event-loop dependency. Highest ceiling and matches Go/BEAM shape: one scheduler, native pollers, task parking, timers, cancellation, and metrics under Jet control.

options.name: Own portable poller first
options.detail: Start with epoll/kqueue/IOCP readiness only; defer `io_uring` batching. Still no external dependency and simpler to test, but leaves Linux peak throughput on the table.

options.name: Use libuv through C FFI
options.detail: Battle-tested portability. Requires explicit owner approval for a runtime external C dependency and a system-library story. Good fallback if owned backends stall, but not the best Jet identity.

decisions.recReason: Owning native backends gives Jet the highest performance ceiling, no foreign event-loop dependency, and full observability/control for the task-scope/task runtime. It keeps the user surface unchanged while letting experts tune the runtime.
decisions.title: Which OS readiness backend parks M:N tasks on I/O?
decisions.explainer: The scheduler needs one park/wake layer per platform. The decision is between owning native backends, owning a lowest-common-denominator poller, or depending on libuv. I6 matters: compiler Source has zero external crates, and runtime-side deps still need owner approval. The E3 goal is better-than-Go networking, so the backend must support task-per-connection scale, O(ready events) wakeups, low allocation pressure, and runtime observability.
decisions.bestCurrent: Go: Go parks goroutines on epoll/kqueue/IOCP through platform-native netpollers, enabling high concurrency.
decisions.recommendation: Build own platform-native backends. Jet needs Go-class scaling as the floor and a higher ceiling through native pollers, structured cancellation, deadlines, and runtime metrics.
Use a closed ABI-safe subset with generated adapters (Option A).

decisions.gist: The web backend needs either a small runtime shim or raw generated DOM calls.

decisions.title: UI tree node shape: typed enum vs dynamic record
decisions.gist: Should UI view-model nodes be a typed enum (Text, Box, Button) or a dynamic tagged record?
