decisions.story: Dorothy is building a to-do app. She needs text labels, containers, buttons, and input fields. She wants the compiler to catch a typo in a node kind at build time, not at runtime.

options.name: Typed constructors: ui.text(), ui.box(), ui.button() (recommended)
options.detail: Each node kind is a distinct constructor. The compiler knows statically that ui.button() produces a button node and ui.text() produces a text node. No stringly-typed fields, no runtime kind-check. Consistent with closed-type direction.

options.name: Dynamic tagged record: ui.node({ kind: "text", content: "..." })
options.detail: A single ui.node() function accepts a record with a "kind" string field. Flexible for dynamic node creation but kind typos are runtime errors. Inconsistent with Jet's static-safety direction.

decisions.comparisons:
SwiftUI:      Text("hello") / VStack { ... } / Button("ok") {}  — typed constructors, each is a distinct type
Flutter:      Text("hello") / Column(children:[...]) / ElevatedButton(...)  — same pattern
React JSX:    <Text>hello</Text> / <View> / <Pressable>  — tagged strings compiled to typed calls
HTML:         <div> / <span> / <button>  — string tags, no compile-time kind checking
Android XML:  android:layout_width="match_parent"  — string attributes

decisions.title: Style API shape: flat record vs builder chain
decisions.gist: Should ui.Style be a flat value record or a builder-method chain?
decisions.story: Walter is styling a submit button: red background, white text, 12px padding, 80px wide. He wants to define the style as a reusable constant and pass it to multiple buttons.

options.name: Flat value record: Style { color: rgb(255,0,0), width: px(80) } (recommended)
options.detail: Style is a pure value — comparable, hashable, passable as a constant. Consistent with Jet's value semantics: no mutable builder state, no object identity, no method chain side effects. A partial style (only some fields set) uses default values for the rest.

options.name: Builder chain: Style.new().color(rgb(255,0,0)).width(px(80))
options.detail: Familiar from many UI frameworks but introduces mutable builder state. A Style mid-chain is not a value — you cannot store it, compare it, or pass it without calling a terminating method. Inconsistent with Jet's value-oriented surface.
options.code:
// Not easily reusable as a constant:
SUBMIT_STYLE :: Style.new()
    .background(rgb(220, 38, 38))
    .color(rgb(255, 255, 255))
    .padding(px(12))
    .width(px(80))
    .build()   // or is this the value? when is it a value?

decisions.comparisons:
SwiftUI:     Text("hi").foregroundColor(.red).frame(width: 80)  — builder chain on the node, not style
Flutter:     TextStyle(color: Colors.red, fontSize: 16)              — flat struct
CSS:         { background: red; width: 80px; padding: 12px }        — flat key-value
Tailwind:    "bg-red-500 text-white p-3 w-20"                       — string class list
React:       {{ backgroundColor: 'red', width: 80, padding: 12 }}   — plain object
SwiftUI (StyleSheet): not idiomatic — styles via modifiers on views

decisions.title: Motion timing: injectable Clock vs global time signal
decisions.gist: Does core.motion.spring() take a Clock capability parameter, or does it read a global time signal?
decisions.story: Doris is building a loading spinner that animates with a spring. She needs to write a unit test that asserts the spinner reaches its target position after 300ms — without waiting 300 real milliseconds.

options.name: Injectable Clock: spring(target, clock, stiffness, damping) (recommended)
options.detail: Clock is passed in explicitly. Tests inject FakeClock.new() and call clock.advance(ms) for deterministic results. Production code passes the real system clock. Consistent with D-DET1 (all time/randomness is injectable). Flutter uses the same pattern (TickerProvider).

options.name: Global time signal: core.motion.time_signal() read internally
options.detail: Motion reads a module-level time signal automatically. Simpler call site but tests must stub the global, which requires framework-level mocking support (jest.useFakeTimers equivalent). Less consistent with D-DET1.

decisions.comparisons:
React Spring:   useSpring({ from: {x:0}, to: {x:1} })          — global RAF/time; not testable without mocking
Framer Motion:  useAnimate(), animate(el, {x:1}, {duration:0.3}) — global time; testing needs jest fake timers
SwiftUI:        withAnimation(.spring()) { state = 1 }           — global CADisplayLink; XCTest uses waitFor
GSAP:           gsap.to(el, {x:1, ease:"elastic.out"})          — global ticker; test with gsap.ticker.tick()
Flutter:        AnimationController(vsync: this, duration: ...)  — vsync injected via TickerProvider (close to option A)

decisions.title: A11y diagnostic gating mechanism
decisions.gist: How are accessibility diagnostics triggered — automatic on --release, explicit jet lint --a11y, or per-file #A11yStrict?
decisions.story: Hank's team ships a web app. He wants his CI to catch missing ARIA roles and unlabeled buttons before they reach users. But he doesn't want beginners running jet build to see a wall of a11y warnings on their first hello-world.

options.name: --release build flag enables a11y lints automatically
options.detail: Hank runs jet build --release for production and a11y lints fire automatically. But a beginner who runs jet build --release for their first deployed app also sees a wall of a11y errors on components they didn't write. Surprise on first real build.
options.code:
jet build --release
# output includes:
# W2930: button "X" has no accessible label (E2930)
# W2931: ui.text used as interactive element without role (E2931)
# 2 accessibility warnings — use --no-a11y to suppress

jet build              # no a11y lints (dev builds)
jet build --release    # a11y lints fire automatically

options.name: jet lint --a11y explicit separate step (recommended)
options.detail: A11y linting is an explicit step Hank adds to CI. It never surprises beginners. Consistent with existing lint profile pattern — same as running jet lint --unused or jet lint --style.
options.code:
# CI pipeline (Hank adds this step):
jet lint --a11y

# output:
# src/nav.jet:3: W2930: button "X" has no accessible label
# src/nav.jet:4: W2931: interactive text missing role
# 2 accessibility issues

# Beginner dev loop:
jet build     # no a11y lints — not surprised
jet run       # no a11y lints
jet lint      # base lints only
jet lint --a11y  # only when explicitly requested

options.name: #A11yStrict file-level opt-in marker
options.detail: Files with #A11yStrict at the top get a11y lints; others don't. Hank can enforce it on specific modules. Very granular but obscure — beginners don't know to add it, and it requires discipline across a large team.

decisions.comparisons:
ESLint a11y:    eslint --rule jsx-a11y/...  explicit plugin; CI adds --rule flags
axe-core:       separate npm run a11y  — entirely separate tool run
Lighthouse:     CI step: lighthouse --only-categories=accessibility
SwiftUI:        XCUIAccessibilityAudit  — explicit test call in test suite
Android:        AccessibilityScanner    — separate IDE plugin, not build-time

decisions.title: Native OS platform gating for #Extern backends (Phase 8 blocker)
decisions.gist: How does Jet source say "this function/module only compiles on Linux (or macOS, or Windows)" so a native GTK/AppKit/Win32 FFI backend doesn't break builds on the other two platforms?
decisions.story: Walter is shipping a desktop app. His `LinuxWindowBackend` calls into GTK via #Extern C FFI. He needs the compiler to leave that code out entirely when building on macOS (no GTK there) and swap in an AppKit-backed implementation of the same JetBackend trait instead — without a runtime crash or a linker error on the wrong platform.

options.name: Extend the existing #Target marker with OS variants (recommended)
options.detail: D-WASM1 already established #Target as "module-level target marker" with Browser/Wasm/Js as the first instances. Add Os.Linux / Os.Macos / Os.Windows as more instances of the SAME marker family, so there is exactly one marker for "what environment does this code run under" (web bucket or native OS) — I8 one-way-to-mean-it. Sema rejects mixing a web variant and an OS variant on the same item (two different axes, one marker, mutually exclusive values).

options.name: New dedicated #Os marker, separate from #Target
options.detail: #Target's existing job (web WASM/JS partitioning) is a genuinely different compilation axis from "which native OS." A distinct #Os(Linux) marker keeps the two concerns from ever being conflated in sema, at the cost of one more marker family to learn.

options.name: Manifest-level gating (pkg.jet / env.jet), no in-source marker
options.detail: No per-function marker at all — the whole file/package is included only when the target platform in pkg.jet's payload matches. Coarser granularity (whole file, not per-impl), and inconsistent with how every other conditional-compilation-flavored feature in Jet (#Reactive, #Extern, #Unsafe, D-WASM1's #Target) is an in-source marker, not a manifest switch.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust: #[cfg(target_os = "linux")] — attribute-based, same shape as option A/B.
Swift: #if os(macOS) ... #endif — source-level directive, same shape.
React Native: Button.ios.js / Button.android.js — filename convention, same shape as option C.
Zig: builtin.target.os.tag comptime check — comptime-if, closer to option A/B than C.

decisions.title: File-level + manifest-level default build target (web without --target=web every time)
decisions.gist: A .jet file (or its pkg.jet once it's a managed package) can declare "I'm a web app" so jet run/dev/build default to the web backend without --target=web typed every time.
decisions.story: Nate is iterating on a loose example file and is tired of typing --target=web on every jet dev invocation. Once he promotes the file into a real package, he wants that same intent to live in pkg.jet instead of the source file, since a packages target is project config, not a per-file concern.

options.name: #Target(Web) file-level marker + pkg.jet target: "web" field, CLI flag always wins
options.detail: Extends the EXISTING #Target(...) marker (today only #Target(Wasm)/#Target(Js), both already file/module-scope-only ceilings, never per-function) with a third value, Web -- distinct in meaning (default backend selection, not a partition ceiling) but same lexical form, no new marker family (I8). pkg.jet's payload gains a parallel target: "web" key. Precedence: --target=<x> CLI flag overrides pkg.jet target which overrides file-level #Target(Web) which overrides the native default. No automatic file-to-manifest migration tool for now -- a manual edit, or a later jetpack convenience, not blocking this decision.
options.code:
#Target(Web)
use core.ui as ui
fn main() { ... }

$ jet dev counter.jet                 // infers web from the marker
$ jet dev counter.jet --target=native  // flag still overrides

decisions.title: Explicit companion-HTML marker for jet build/dev --target=web
decisions.gist: Replace the silent <stem>.html filename convention with an explicit #Html("path.html") marker at the top of the .jet file, so the pairing is visible in the source and errors loudly if the file is missing.
decisions.story: Nate renamed a file mid-project and jet dev silently started serving the generic fallback page instead of his real one -- no error, just a confusingly plain-looking dashboard. He wants the source itself to say which HTML file it pairs with.
decisions.inWild:
#Target(Web)
#Html("dashboard.html")
use core.ui as ui
fn main() { ... }

$ jet dev app.jet   // uses dashboard.html, or a clear error if it's missing
decisions.detail: AMENDED 2026-07-01: option B added — manifest-level pairing for managed packages composes with the file marker; single-option ballots decide nothing.

options.name: #Html("path.html") file-level marker, same family as #Target(Web)
options.detail: Precedence when building for web: explicit #Html(...) wins; else the existing sibling <stem>.html convention (kept for backward-compat with 190-197's existing examples, none of which will be forced to add the marker); else the generic auto-generated page. A referenced #Html(...) path that doesn't exist on disk is a build-time error naming the missing file, not a silent fallback.
options.code:
#Target(Web)
#Html("dashboard.html")
use core.ui as ui
fn main() { ... }

options.name: pack.jet target field for managed packages, #Html(...) for single files — composed
options.detail: Once a project has a manifest, pairing belongs with the target declaration: executable { entry: "src/run.jet", html: "dashboard.html" }. Single-file apps keep the #Html marker (option A). Precedence: CLI flag > manifest field > file marker > sibling <stem>.html > generated page. Missing referenced file is a build error either way.

decisions.title: Next-generation FFI: what one structure makes every foreign language near-trivial to wrap, replace in situ, and tap immediately?
decisions.gist: Pick the architecture every foreign language shares: per-language namespaces with pluggable binders, uniform extern blocks, typed projection importers, or runtime-broker sidecars.
decisions.explainer: Jet already speaks two foreign languages, each with its own shape: Rust via extern rust "crate@version" { … } (S50) and C via generated bindings mounted at c.<lib> with a user overlay (S59). JS is sequenced next, Swift later (D-JSWIFTFFI1). The owner's bar: using a library from almost any language should feel almost as easy as using a Jet package — every ecosystem's work immediately usable, and any foreign dependency replaceable later by a native Jet implementation without touching call sites (in-situ replacement). This ballot picks the one structure all languages share. How deep each language's binding goes (shallow declaration binding, full typed projection, or a runtime broker) is a per-language follow-up ballot on top of the winning frame — the frame is what must never vary.
decisions.story: Doris is building a lab-data tool in Jet. The only mature reader for her instrument's file format is a Python package; the best plotting library is on npm; a checksum routine she needs ships as a C header. She wants all three working this afternoon, each behind an ordinary typed Jet API with honest effects — and when a native Jet plotting package appears next year, she wants to swap it in by changing one dependency line, not rewriting call sites.
decisions.inWild:
use py.h5instrument as h5     // Python package, typed surface
use js.plotly as plot          // npm package (D-NPMTYPE1 stubs)
use "xxhash.h" as xx           // C header, script tier (S59)

fn main() #(Fs, Proc) {
    run := h5.read("run-0142.h5")
    print(xx.hash64(run.raw))
    plot.line(run.times, run.values)
}
decisions.detail: A, C, and D compose rather than exclude: A is the surface law (namespaces, three tiers, overlay, in-situ shadowing, lockfile provenance); C and D are per-language binder strategies BEHIND that surface — projection importers for static languages (C, Swift, Rust), a broker likely right for Python/JS dynamic tails, shallow declaration binding where that's enough. Ratifying A means: the surface ships now; follow-up ballots (D-FFI-PY1, D-FFI-JS1 folding in D-NPMTYPE1, D-FFI-SWIFT1 honoring D-JSWIFTFFI1 sequencing) pick each language's strategy on the common frame. Existing ratifications are preserved, not reopened: S59 is already the C instance of A; S50's extern rust block becomes the rust binder's declaration format inside rust.*; D-DEP1's vendoring/hash-pinning law extends to every language's refs. I8: one FFI structure for all languages is the point — shipping B alongside A would be two spellings for one job. I1/I2 hold in every option: user code is safe unless #Unsafe; no foreign toolchain's errors ever reach the user unlaundered — binder diagnostics are Jet diagnostics with codes and snapshots (I4). Recommendation rationale: A is the only option that is uniform (one structure to learn), immediate (a new language needs only a binder, at whatever depth exists first), deep where it counts (projection strategy per language later), and structurally in-situ-replaceable — rank on beginner experience, one-path, and long-term correctness.

options.name: Language namespaces + pluggable binders (recommended)
options.detail: Generalize S59's proven C structure into the law for every language. Each foreign world mounts as a namespace <lang>.<lib> with the same three tiers everywhere: script tier (use "xxhash.h" as xx — bind on first compile), project tier (use py.h5instrument as h5 with the dep pinned in pkg.jet), overlay tier (#Extern module py.h5instrument { … } to refine generated types; overlay wins). `jet bind <lang>` is a per-language binder producing inspectable, committable bindings in .jet/bindings/<lang>/<lib>.jet. Safety: generated bindings are safe wrappers by construction (marshaling internals compiler-vetted like std internals — I1); calling a foreign symbol outside a binding requires #Unsafe("reason"). In-situ replacement is structural: any <lang>.<lib> can be shadowed by a Jet package exporting the same surface — call sites never change. Per-language depth (projection vs broker vs shallow) is chosen behind this surface, one follow-up ballot per language.

options.name: Uniform extern blocks (generalize S50)
options.detail: Every language uses S50's declaration-first shape: extern <lang> "ref@version" { fn … = "path" }. Maximal explicitness — every crossing is written in the file — and one grammar for all languages. The cost is the wall: wrapping a real library means hundreds of declaration lines per library (generated or not, they live in your project), there is no namespace to shadow so in-situ replacement means hand-built wrapper modules, and 'almost trivial' is exactly what it isn't.

options.name: Typed projection importers only
options.detail: Every language gets a full compiler importer (Swift-Clang-importer style): use py.h5instrument elaborates the package's surface — from type stubs and introspection — directly into checked Jet types with effects and ownership mapped; overlays refine (raw pointer -> checked handle). The deepest 'feels native' ceiling, and the right end-state for static languages. As the only mechanism, it makes every new language wait for a full importer before ANY access exists — the opposite of tapping ecosystems immediately.

options.name: Runtime broker sidecars only
options.detail: Foreign runtimes run as supervised sidecar processes with a typed message boundary; py.* calls marshal to a Python worker (Mojo's play). Any language with a runtime works day one and effects are honest (#(Proc) on every call) — but values are serialized at every crossing (no zero-copy, no shared memory), C headers and Rust crates don't fit the model at all, and production binaries grow a process tree. Right as a per-language strategy for dynamic tails; wrong as the only structure.

comparisons.note: @cImport makes C trivial — but only C. The lesson: binder-in-the-compiler is magic; the miss: no structure for a second language.
Clang importer: full typed projection of C/ObjC — foreign APIs feel native. The depth ceiling to aim per-language binders at.
comparisons.code: import Accelerate   // C library, arrives as typed Swift

comparisons.note: Imports any Python module day one via a runtime broker — instant ecosystem reach, marshaled boundary. The play for dynamic-language tails.
comparisons.code:
from python import Python
let np = Python.import_module("numpy")

comparisons.note: P/Invoke plus WinRT projections: two tiers under one runtime — proof that shallow decls and deep projections coexist behind one surface.
Polyglot: many languages, one VM — reach bought with total runtime lock-in; the anti-goal for an AOT language.

decisions.title: Style length spelling: unit literals vs Length wrappers vs bare numbers
decisions.gist: How a user writes a length like 320 pixels in a UI style.
decisions.story: Betty is laying out the settings page of her recipe app: a card 320 wide, 180 tall, 12 of padding. She wants to type those three numbers once, have the compiler catch a unit typo, and not wonder later whether 320 meant pixels or something else.

options.name: Unit-family literal: width: 320px (recommended)
options.detail: core.ui.style declares a #UnitFamily(length) { px } (D-QUAL3), so the ratified unit-literal syntax (D-UNITLIT1) applies: 320px is a compile-checked Px value. One canonical unit mechanism in the whole language (I8) — style lengths use the same machinery as 500ms and 12.50usd. Unit typos are compile errors (E0134); if a second unit ever ships, cross-unit math is a compile error too (E0127). Reads like the CSS every beginner has already seen.

options.name: Enum with per-unit variants: width: .Px.{value: 320.0}
options.detail: Length is an enum whose variants carry the value: Length { Px(value: Float) }. Fully typed and pattern-matchable, and the field type stays a single Length even if more units are added. But it duplicates what unit families already do with a second, style-only mechanism (I8), and every length costs a variant-construction spelling.

options.name: Flat pair record: width: Length.{value: 320.0, unit: .Px}
options.detail: Length is a two-field struct (value + LengthUnit enum) — the shape Phase 3's example shipped. Plain user-space types, nothing new to learn beyond structs. But it's the most ceremony per length, the unit and value can be read independently without matching (a backend can use .value and forget .unit), and it's a second unit mechanism next to unit families (I8).

options.name: Bare Float logical pixels: width: 320.0
options.detail: No Length type at all — style dimensions are Float, pixels by convention, like SwiftUI/Flutter. Least typing and no unit concept for beginners to learn. But the unit lives in documentation instead of the type: 320.0 could be anything, a duration mixed into a width compiles fine, and adding real units later changes every Style field's type.

options.name: CSS string: width: "320px"
options.detail: Lengths are strings parsed at render time, exactly like inline CSS. Familiar to web developers and trivially copy-pasteable from CSS. But every typo becomes a runtime failure in the user's running app, the compiler can't help with math on lengths, and stringly-typed values are the opposite of the typed-styles goal this phase exists for.

decisions.comparisons:
CSS:            width: 320px;              — unit-suffix literal, the shape every web tutorial teaches
Jetpack Compose: Modifier.width(320.dp)     — typed Dp via extension property; 320 alone is a type error
SwiftUI:        .frame(width: 320)         — unitless CGFloat points, unit is implicit convention
Flutter:        SizedBox(width: 320)       — unitless logical pixels, same implicit convention
React inline:   {{ width: 320 }}           — bare number silently means px; {{ width: '320px' }} string also accepted
Typst:          width: 320pt               — unit-suffix literal, checked at compile time
decisions.rec: A — reuses the one ratified unit mechanism (D-QUAL3 + D-UNITLIT1), so `320px` is compile-checked with zero ceremony and no second style-only unit system (I8).
decisions.recommendation: A — reuses the one ratified unit mechanism (D-QUAL3 + D-UNITLIT1), so `320px` is compile-checked with zero ceremony and no second style-only unit system (I8).

decisions.title: Phase 8 native UI backends: how do GTK/AppKit/Win32 toolchain deps enter the dev environment?
decisions.gist: Building a real native UI backend needs OS toolkit headers/libs the dev shell does not have; decide how they get there.
decisions.story: Hank wants the reactive UI showcase to open a real Linux window instead of the web renderer. The compiler side (OS gating, renderer seam) is ready, but the flake devShell has no GTK headers or pkg-config, so nothing can link. Nothing an agent does can proceed until the dependency route is chosen.

options.name: nixpkgs devShell deps now (recommended)
options.detail: Add gtk4 + pkg-config (Linux) to the flake devShell per the existing owner guidance for native deps (nixpkgs stopgap, jetpack core provider owns it long-term). macOS/Windows backends wait for contributors on those hosts. Non-Nix users get a clear "install gtk4" message.
options.code:
# flake.nix devShell
buildInputs = [ gtk4 pkg-config ];

# then Phase 8 builds:
nix develop -c jet run ui_showcase.jet   # real window

options.name: Defer Phase 8 to Epoch 4
options.detail: Ship Epoch 3 UI as web-renderer only; native backends land with the jetpack core provider that owns native deps properly.
options.code:
// e3: web target stays the only real renderer
jet build --target=web ui_showcase.jet

options.name: Headless native backend first
options.detail: Build the native backend against a stub/offscreen renderer (no toolkit linkage) so the seam is exercised end-to-end; real toolkits follow later behind A or B.
options.code:
#Target(Os.Linux)
impl HeadlessBackend: JetBackend { /* draws to a buffer, asserts in tests */ }

comparisons.note: system gtk4 via pkg-config; user installs it (apt/brew/nix).
bundles its own engine — zero system deps, huge binary.
comparisons.code: flutter build linux   # no gtk headers needed

decisions.rec: A — matches the ratified native-deps guidance (nixpkgs stopgap while jetpack matures); unblocks Phase 8 for the primary dev host without new invariant pressure.
decisions.recommendation: A — matches the ratified native-deps guidance (nixpkgs stopgap while jetpack matures); unblocks Phase 8 for the primary dev host without new invariant pressure.

decisions.title: How does ungated code get "the impl for this OS"?
decisions.gist: #Target(Os.*) now gates impls, but plain main has no ratified way to construct/dispatch to whichever gated impl survived the build.
decisions.story: Doris writes a desktop app. She gates LinuxBackend and MacosBackend impls per D-OSTARGET1. Now her ungated main needs a backend value. Constructing LinuxBackend directly in main is (correctly) E-OSTARGET-UNMATCHED-CALL — main is not Linux-only. There is no blessed way to say "give me the one that matched this build."

options.name: fn-level #Target(Os.*) + one-survivor rule (recommended)
options.detail: Extend gating to fns: several fns share one name/signature, each gated to a different OS, exactly one survives per build; ungated code calls it like any fn. Missing an OS the build targets = compile error listing covered OSes. Mirrors Rust cfg/Go build tags; no new expression syntax.

options.name: Comptime OS switch expression
options.detail: A compiler-known comptime value (e.g. build.os) usable in a match whose non-matching arms are discarded before OS-gating checks run. More general (any per-OS choice), but new comptime surface + a second way to express what A does (I8 pressure).

options.name: Status quo — gated modules own the choice
options.detail: Ungated code never touches gated types; each app ships a per-OS gated module exporting a common fn. Works today only if fn-level gating exists somewhere, which it does not — effectively forces apps to gate their whole main, hollowing the check.
options.code: // every call chain from main must itself be OS-gated — main per OS.

comparisons.note: #[cfg(target_os)] fns — one survives per build.
build tags: one file per OS defines the same fn.
comparisons.code:
//go:build linux
func newBackend() Backend { return gtk{} }

comparisons.note: comptime switch on builtin.os.
comparisons.code: const b = switch (builtin.os.tag) { .linux => Gtk{}, .macos => AppKit{}, else => unreachable };

decisions.rec: A — smallest ratified-shape extension (same marker, fns instead of impls), proven pattern in Rust/Go, keeps one dispatch idiom (I8).
decisions.recommendation: A — smallest ratified-shape extension (same marker, fns instead of impls), proven pattern in Rust/Go, keeps one dispatch idiom (I8).

decisions.title: Python binder depth: how deep does `use py.<lib>` reach into CPython?
decisions.gist: The D-FFI-UNIFY1 frame is law; this picks Python's binder strategy behind it. Python's ecosystem is C-extension-heavy (numpy, torch), so the binder must reach real CPython. Choose the host model: crash-isolated sidecar broker, in-process libpython embed, Python-on-WASM, or a shallow script shim.
decisions.explainer: The owner's bar (card #180) is tapping any ecosystem immediately. Python is the biggest prize and the hardest: its value lives in native C-extension packages, so a pure reimplementation or a WASM-only path forfeits most of the ecosystem. Two real hosts remain: an in-process libpython embed (zero-copy on buffer-protocol arrays, but a buggy native extension can take the whole process down and the GIL must be managed) and a supervised sidecar worker (a crashing extension dies with the worker, honest #(Proc)-style effect, but values marshal across a process boundary — no zero-copy of large tensors). Under I1, crash containment argues for the broker as the safe default; the embed is the expert performance tier for hot numeric paths, mirroring how D-PLUGIN1 made the WASM sandbox the default and native the opt-in. One `use py.X` surface either way; the host tier never moves call sites. Adds a `#(Py)` effect to the D-EFF4 set (owner-visible).
decisions.story: Doris is building a lab-data tool. The only mature reader for her instrument's file format is a Python package, and numpy is her numeric stack. She wants both working this afternoon behind an ordinary typed Jet API with honest effects — and she does not want a segfault in someone's C extension to take down her whole program.
decisions.detail: All options honor D-FFI-UNIFY1: `<lang>.<lib>` namespace, three tiers, `jet bind py` emitting inspectable `.jet/bindings/py/<lib>.jet`, safe wrappers by construction, `#Unsafe` only to reach a raw symbol outside a binding. The choice is only the host/depth. Marshalling law (all options): scalars<->Int/Float/Bool, str<->String, bytes/buffer-protocol arrays<->[T] or zero-copy View<T> in embed / copied in broker, dict<->struct or Map, list/tuple<->[T], None<->optional, Python exception->Jet Result + E-code (never a raw traceback). Async: asyncio coroutine -> Jet async task. Distribution: PyPI ref pinned in pkg.jet, wheel fetched + vendored + hash-pinned (D-DEP1); the CPython interpreter/libpython is a native runtime dep provisioned by jetpack/nixpkgs (ballot D-DEP-PY1). I1/I2/I4 hold in every option.

options.name: Sidecar-broker default + opt-in embed tier (recommended)
options.detail: The default host is a supervised CPython worker process (reuse the jetpack `services` supervision seam) with a typed message boundary — a crashing native extension takes down the worker, not your program, and the compiler restarts it. `#(Py)` effect on every call. An opt-in `py@embed` (dep flag or `#Embed` marker on the import) switches to in-process libpython for zero-copy on buffer-protocol arrays, for hot numeric paths. One `use py.X` surface; the tier is a distribution/perf choice, never a call-site change. Mirrors D-PLUGIN1's sandbox-default / native-opt-in shape.

options.name: Sidecar broker only
options.detail: Every py.* call marshals to a supervised worker; no in-process path ever. Maximum crash isolation and the simplest safety story; large arrays always copy across the process boundary, so a tensor-heavy inner loop pays a serialization cost with no escape hatch.

options.name: In-process libpython embed only
options.detail: Every py.* call runs in-process against linked libpython, GIL-scoped, zero-copy on buffer-protocol types. Fastest and simplest to reason about for numeric code; a faulty native extension segfaults the host process (weaker isolation), which sits uneasily with I1's crash-containment posture as an unconditional default.

options.name: Python-on-WASM sandbox
options.detail: Run CPython compiled to WASM (Pyodide/CPython-wasi) on the already-approved wasmtime runtime. Fully sandboxed and I1-clean by construction, and reuses the #5 runtime — but the C-extension long tail (arbitrary wheels, native torch) does not run under it, so it forfeits the exact packages that make Python worth calling. Right as a niche isolation tier, wrong as the reach story.
options.code: use py.pure_python_lib as p        // sandboxed; native wheels unavailable

options.name: Subprocess script shim (shallow)
options.detail: `jet bind py` emits thin declarations that shell out to `python -c`/script invocations per call. Trivial to stand up; no persistent interpreter, so state does not carry between calls, everything re-imports each time, and rich values degrade to stringly-typed exchange. Below the frame's typed-surface bar.
options.code: use py.h5instrument as h5          // each call = a fresh python process

comparisons.note: Imports any Python module day one via an in-process CPython embed — the reach bar to match. Mojo accepts the embed's coupling; Jet's I1 posture pushes the safe default toward isolation with embed as the opt-in.
comparisons.code:
from python import Python
let np = Python.import_module("numpy")

comparisons.note: In-process libpython with GIL tokens and typed conversions — the mechanism the embed tier wraps. Shows zero-copy buffer-protocol bridging is a solved shape.
Out-of-process typed boundary with supervision — the broker model. Proven isolation; the cost is marshaling, which is why large-array paths want the embed escape hatch.

decisions.title: Approve a CPython runtime dependency for the Python binder
decisions.gist: The Python binder needs a real CPython interpreter — libpython linked in-process (embed tier) and/or a CPython executable for the sidecar worker. That is a new runtime-side external dependency, an I6 owner decision, exactly parallel to D-DEP-WASM1 for wasmtime.
decisions.explainer: I6 keeps the compiler (Source/) zero-external-crate forever and requires owner approval for any new stdlib/runtime external dependency. D-FFI-PY1's reach depends on real CPython: the sidecar broker needs a CPython executable present, and the embed tier links libpython. This is runtime-side only — never in Source/ — mirroring how D-DEP-WASM1=A approved wasmtime for plugins. The dependency is provisioned per the ratified native-deps policy (nixpkgs interim, jetpack core provider long-term), carries a native-ize obligation (the frozen end-state), and is hash-pinned in .jet/lock. Without this approval the Python binder cannot ship at any depth except the WASM-sandbox tier (which forfeits the C-extension ecosystem).
decisions.story: The build needs numpy to actually run. That means a CPython the compiler can drive — linked or spawned. Before any code assumes libpython is on the link line, the owner decides whether Jet takes that runtime dependency and how it is provisioned.
decisions.detail: Runtime-side only (I6 holds — never in Source/). Provisioning follows the ratified native-deps policy: nixpkgs where the user has Nix, jetpack core provider long-term, with a clear message on machines lacking both. Native-ize obligation recorded (parallel to D-DEP-WASM1's frozen own-runtime end-state). Hash-pinned in .jet/lock (D-DEP1). Only pulled in when a project actually uses py.* — a pure-Jet project never acquires it.

options.name: Approve CPython runtime dep (libpython embed + broker interpreter), provisioned via nixpkgs/jetpack (recommended)
options.detail: Sanction CPython as a runtime-side dependency for the Python binder: libpython on the link line for the embed tier, a CPython executable for the sidecar worker. Never in Source/ (I6 holds). Provisioned by nixpkgs (interim) / jetpack core provider (long-term); hash-pinned; native-ize obligation recorded; acquired only when a project uses py.*. This is the D-DEP-WASM1 precedent applied to Python and unblocks D-FFI-PY1 at full depth.
options.code:
deps: { numpy: py@">=1.26" }   // pulls the approved CPython runtime
// pure-Jet projects never acquire it

options.name: Broker interpreter only (no libpython linkage)
options.detail: Approve only a CPython executable for the sidecar worker; never link libpython. Keeps the dependency at arm's length (out-of-process only) and avoids in-process linkage entirely; forecloses the zero-copy embed tier of D-FFI-PY1, so large-array numeric paths always marshal.
options.code: deps: { numpy: py@">=1.26" }   // worker process only; no embed tier

options.name: No CPython dep — WASM-sandbox Python only
options.detail: Decline the CPython runtime dependency; the Python binder is limited to the Python-on-WASM tier on the existing wasmtime. No new dep at all, fully sandboxed — but the native C-extension ecosystem (numpy/scipy/torch) does not run, gutting the reason to call Python.
options.code: use py.pure_python_lib as p    // native wheels unavailable

comparisons.note: The exact precedent: a runtime-side external dep approved for a capability (plugins), never in Source/, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation. Option A is the same shape for Python.
comparisons.code: // wasmtime approved runtime-side for target: plugin

comparisons.note: Both bundle or link a CPython to reach the ecosystem — the accepted cost of real Python interop.
comparisons.code: // libpython embedded in the distributed binary

decisions.title: npm / PyPI / SwiftPM as jetpack registry providers
decisions.gist: `use js.lodash` / `use py.numpy` / `use swift.Alamofire` must fetch from foreign registries. This decides whether jetpack gains npm/PyPI/SwiftPM providers (like the Nix bridge U16), and the network/trust/vendoring policy for them.
decisions.explainer: The FFI binders are only 'trivial' if the dependency is fetched as easily as a Jet package. That means jetpack reaching npm, PyPI, and SwiftPM registries. D-DEP1 already fixes the mechanics (fetch -> vendor -> hash-pin -> lock), and U16 already set the precedent of jetpack consuming a foreign ecosystem (Nix). What is an owner call is the policy: do foreign registries become first-class providers resolved by `<lib>: <lang>@"ref"` in pkg.jet, and how do they obey the ratified jetpack laws — U29 offline guarantee (no network when the lock is satisfied, `--offline` makes any fetch a loud error), U21 channels (a floating `@latest` npm ref resolves only during update, never in CI), U28 no-daemon, and trust/provenance on fetched artifacts. Recommended: first-class providers under the existing provider seam, every foreign artifact vendored + hash-pinned into the hangar exactly like a Jet package, subject to the same offline/lock/trust laws. This is one gate shared by all three per-language ballots' distribution stories.
decisions.story: Doris types `use js.plotly`, `use py.h5instrument`, `use swift.Alamofire` and expects `jet build` to fetch each from its home registry, lock it exactly, and rebuild offline forever after — the same contract she gets from a Jet package.
decisions.detail: Extends D-DEP1 (vendor + hash-pin every language's refs) and the U16 foreign-ecosystem-provider precedent. Must obey the ratified jetpack laws: U29 (offline/lock), U21 (channel refs resolve only on update, exact in lock, unlocked ref in CI = error), U28 (no daemon), U24 (provenance envelope on fetched objects), U23 (honest message on machines that cannot reach a registry). Foreign artifacts land in the hangar like Jet objects and GC per U22. Trust: fetched artifacts are hash-verified on arrival; a registry compromise cannot alter a locked build.

options.name: First-class npm/PyPI/SwiftPM providers under the jetpack provider seam (recommended)
options.detail: Each foreign registry is a provider resolved by `<lib>: <lang>@"ref"`, fetching into the hangar, vendored + hash-pinned to .jet/lock, obeying every ratified jetpack law (U29 offline, U21 channels, U28 no-daemon, U24 provenance, U23 honest fallback). Foreign artifacts are hash-verified on arrival so a registry compromise cannot alter a locked build. One uniform distribution story across all three binders.
options.code:
deps: { lodash: js@"lodash@4", numpy: py@">=1.26" }
// resolved by the npm / pypi providers; locked exactly; offline-safe after

options.name: Manifest-declared registry endpoints only (no built-in providers)
options.detail: No first-party providers; the user declares each foreign registry endpoint and credentials in pkg.jet and jetpack fetches generically. Maximum control for private registries; every project re-specifies boilerplate and there is no curated default, so `use js.lodash` does not just work out of the box.
options.code:
registries: { npm: "https://registry.npmjs.org", pypi: "https://pypi.org/simple" }
deps: { lodash: js@"lodash@4" }

options.name: Vendor-only, no live registry fetch
options.detail: jetpack never contacts a foreign registry; users vendor foreign packages into the repo by hand (or via an external tool) and jetpack only hash-pins what is already present. Strongest supply-chain posture and zero network policy to design; but it forfeits the 'trivial to use any library' bar — adding a package is a manual vendoring chore.
options.code: // user vendors node_modules / wheels by hand; jetpack only locks them

comparisons.note: Already-ratified precedent: jetpack consumes a foreign ecosystem as a provider with honest gating. Option A applies the same model to npm/PyPI/SwiftPM.
comparisons.code: jet run nixpkgs@tool   // foreign provider, gated, locked

comparisons.note: Fetch npm/PyPI into a hermetic, hash-locked store obeying an offline/repro contract — the shape of option A under Jet's U29/U21 laws.

decisions.title: Editor engine architecture
decisions.gist: What machinery answers the editor: today's per-file re-checker, a grown semantic index, or one incremental compiler service shared by everything.
decisions.explainer: Glossary. LSP = the background program editors (VS Code, Zed, Cursor) talk to for errors, completion, rename, go-to-definition. Incremental = after a keystroke, re-analyze only what changed, not the whole file or project. Semantic index = a persistent map of every symbol in the project (where defined, where used), kept up to date as you type. Today jet lsp re-parses and re-checks a whole file on each request and mostly sees one file at a time; jet-semindex exists as a separate batch tool.
decisions.story: Priya has a 30-file Jet web service open in VS Code. Every keystroke re-checks her 2,000-line file from scratch; renaming a function she can only trust for files that are open; the outline pane is empty; project-wide symbol search finds nothing. She never reads the compiler's carefully written error copy — she judges Jet entirely by this laggy hour in her editor. The engine choice decides the ceiling for every editor feature Jet will ever have.
decisions.detail: Recommend C. One semantic brain is the only shape where editor truth and compiler truth cannot drift (I8), it makes jet check/jet dev warm-instant for free, and #182's bidirectional visual editor needs exactly this engine. B is the fallback shape if C is declined — it reaches feature parity sooner but permanently owns a two-brain alignment burden.

options.name: Extend the per-request checker
options.detail: Keep today's shape: each LSP request re-runs parse+check on the current file, plus targeted cross-file lookups. Add features one by one on top. Stays closest to today's shape, but every feature re-derives the world; big files pay full re-check per keystroke, and project-wide answers (rename, find-references, symbols) stay best-effort rather than guaranteed.
options.code:
// What today's shape gives — and its ceiling:
$ edit routes.jet (2,000 lines)
  keystroke -> re-parse + re-check whole file   ~80ms today, grows with file
  F12 on auth.current      ok (single hop)
  rename orders_for        edits OPEN files; closed callers found by re-scan,
                           no guarantee mid-edit state is consistent
  workspace symbol search  full project re-scan per query

options.name: Index-backed engine (grow jet-semindex)
options.detail: Promote jet-semindex (whose versioned query API is already ratified, D-SEMINDEX1) from batch tool to the live heart of the LSP: a persistent project-wide symbol database, updated incrementally on every change. All features (rename, references, symbols, outline, call hierarchy) become index queries. The compiler front end stays as-is; the LSP maintains the index beside it. This is the gopls / clangd shape.
options.code:
$ jet lsp   # first open: index 30 files once (~1s), then:
  keystroke -> re-index one file's symbols       ~few ms
  rename orders_for        index knows all 14 callers, open or closed
  workspace symbol 'ord'   instant — index lookup
  call hierarchy           who-calls-whom already materialized
// Risk to own: two brains — checker semantics vs index semantics
// must be kept in agreement by tests, or they drift.

options.name: One incremental compiler service
options.detail: Rebuild the front end as a demand-driven, incremental query engine (parse-of-file, types-of-item, callers-of-fn — each cached, each invalidated precisely), and make jet check, jet dev, the REPL, and the LSP all clients of that one engine. There is exactly one semantic brain, so editor answers can never disagree with the compiler (I8: one way to mean it). This is the TypeScript model — tsserver IS the compiler — and the road rust-analyzer wishes rustc had taken from the start. Largest rebuild; also the foundation the self-host era and #182 (Blueprint visual editor, which needs live bidirectional semantics) will stand on.
options.code:
$ jet lsp        # same engine as jet check — literally the same queries
  keystroke -> invalidate routes.jet's parse query; types re-derive
               only for items whose inputs changed   ~1-5ms
  rename orders_for        exact: the engine's own resolution data
  editor squiggles         byte-identical to `jet check` output, always
$ jet check      # warm daemon answers from the same cache — instant
// One brain: a fix to type inference fixes the editor the same second.

comparisons.note: tsserver is the compiler — one incremental engine serves tsc, editors, everything. Widely considered the best editor experience in the industry; never drifts.
comparisons.code: tsc --watch and VS Code share one Program instance model

comparisons.note: The cautionary tale: rust-analyzer is a second front end beside rustc. Years of duplicated work, subtle disagreements, and a still-running project (polonius/chalk era) to merge them back.
comparisons.code: rustc says error; rust-analyzer says fine — the bug class Jet can refuse to have

comparisons.note: gopls is index-backed (option B shape) over the go/types checker. Excellent, but gopls and the compiler have disagreed, and keeping them aligned is ongoing work.
comparisons.code: gopls: persistent file cache + per-package invalidation

decisions.title: Editor capability bar
decisions.gist: Which editor features jet lsp must serve — full protocol parity, a curated professional dozen, or beginner-first waves.
decisions.explainer: What exists today: hover, go-to-definition, references, rename, dot-completion, semantic tokens, inlay hints, formatting, code actions. What is missing: outline (the file's structure pane), workspace symbol search, signature help (parameter hints while typing a call), folding, highlight-other-occurrences, incremental sync (today the editor re-sends the whole file every keystroke), snippet/auto-import completion, call hierarchy, prepare-rename validation, semantic token deltas. 'Full parity' means every LSP 3.17 feature that makes sense for Jet.
decisions.story: Ben, week one with Jet, types `svc.request(` and waits for parameter hints that never come — he opens the docs in a browser to remember the four arguments. Ctrl+Shift+O for the file outline: empty. Ctrl+T to find a type project-wide: nothing. Each miss is a moment where the language that promises magic out-of-the-box feels like a prototype. The capability bar decides what 'Jet has great tooling' means, feature by feature.
decisions.detail: Recommend A, delivered in C's order (signature help + outline first). Master-of-all means the tooling bar is parity, not a subset; every advertised capability carries a test, so the surface stays honest (I4 spirit). Effort is the currency we spend.

options.name: Full LSP 3.17 parity
options.detail: Everything applicable to Jet, as one program with exit criteria: incremental sync, outline, workspace symbols, signature help, folding, occurrences, selection ranges, snippets + auto-import completion, prepare-rename, semantic token range+delta, call hierarchy, type hierarchy, document links, code lens (off by default). Each feature lands with an lsp test and a line in the editor README. Delivery ordered by beginner impact (signature help and outline first), but the bar is: all of it.
options.code:
// Exit criteria, testable:
$ cargo test --test lsp
  signature_help_mid_call ........ ok
  document_symbol_outline ........ ok
  workspace_symbol_cross_file .... ok
  incremental_sync_partial_edit .. ok
  folding_regions ................ ok
  occurrences_highlight .......... ok
  completion_auto_import ......... ok
  call_hierarchy_incoming ........ ok
  ... (every capability advertised = every capability tested)

options.name: Curated professional dozen
options.detail: The ~12 features that define how a language feels, then stop: incremental sync, signature help, outline, workspace symbols, folding, occurrences, snippets + auto-import, prepare-rename, semantic deltas, call hierarchy. Skip long-tail protocol surface (type hierarchy, document links, code lens, monikers) until someone asks. Smaller advertised surface, honestly complete.

options.name: Beginner-first waves, re-decide between waves
options.detail: Wave 1: signature help, outline, completion quality (auto-import, snippets). Wave 2: workspace symbols, incremental sync, folding, occurrences. Wave 3: call hierarchy, code lens, the rest. Owner reviews after each wave and re-aims. Most control, three decisions instead of one.

comparisons.note: Ships essentially full parity plus extensions; that completeness is a large part of Rust's professional reputation.
comparisons.code: outline, signature help, 30+ assists, call/type hierarchy, semantic deltas

comparisons.note: Deliberately curated (option B shape) — smaller surface, everything it advertises is polished.
comparisons.code: no code lens by default; core dozen kept excellent

decisions.title: What a change must pass before it lands
decisions.gist: How much of the test suite (and which extra gates) run on every pull request versus nightly.
decisions.explainer: Today CI runs 5 of the ~70 test files: unit tests, truthfulness, diagnostic snapshots, golden examples, cross-compile. The other 65 — LSP, formatter, REPL, jetpack, workspace, web build, ownership, debugger, everything else — only run when a developer remembers to run them locally. CI also still calls the frozen old board path (tools/Tower/Tower.mjs). 'Sharded' = split the suite across parallel CI machines so the wall-clock stays short. 'Ratchet' = a number (coverage, binary size, compile time) that may improve but never regress.
decisions.story: A contributor's PR goes green in 12 minutes and merges. It broke jet fmt's round-trip, two REPL commands, and a jetpack flow — none of which CI ran. The breakage surfaces days later on someone else's machine, bisecting costs an afternoon, and 'CI is green' quietly stops meaning anything. For a language whose examples are the executable spec (I5), the suite that isn't run is a spec that isn't enforced.
decisions.inWild:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — the entire test gate today:
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --lib
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test truthfulness
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test golden
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test cross
# not run on any PR, ever: lsp, fmt, repl, jetpack, workspace, web_build,
# ownership, debug, modules, generics, effects ... (65 files)
# also: - run: nix develop -c node tools/Tower/Tower.mjs status   # frozen dir, per MOVED.md
decisions.detail: Recommend A. The suite is the spec (I4/I5); a gate that skips 65 of 70 files lets the spec be broken silently, and this repo has already paid that bisect tax. Whichever option wins, the frozen tools/Tower CI step is corrected as part of it.

options.name: Everything on every PR; nightly adds the slow science
options.detail: PR gate = the full cargo test suite, sharded across parallel jobs, plus grammar-drift and docs-build checks. Nightly = multi-OS matrix (Linux/macOS), perf-regression harness (tools/perf) with ratchets, fuzzing cadence, coverage report. Green means green: no change lands without the whole spec passing. Costs more CI minutes; sharding keeps wall-clock near today's.
options.code:
# PR (sharded, ~4 parallel jobs):
test-shard-1: lexer parser fmt grammar ui...
test-shard-2: sema ownership generics effects...
test-shard-3: golden examples, codegen, cross
test-shard-4: lsp repl debug jetpack workspace web...
gates: grammar-drift, docs-build, tower status (new path)
# nightly: macOS + Linux, perf ratchet, fuzz 30min, coverage

options.name: Two lanes: fast PR, full suite gates the merge
options.detail: PR lane stays fast (today's five targets + build + lint), and the full suite runs in a merge queue / on master after merge, auto-reverting or red-flagging on failure. Cheap PRs, but a window exists where broken code is on master and someone else pulls it.
options.code:
PR:     12 min — compile, golden, snapshots, lint
merge:  full suite on the merge commit; failure -> auto-revert + card
# the gap: between merge and full-suite result, master may be broken

options.name: Full suite nightly only
options.detail: PRs unchanged; one nightly run of everything files a card on failure. Minimal CI spend; a full day of changes can land between a breakage and its discovery, and the bisect cost returns.
options.code: nightly: cargo test (all) -> on failure: tower card add --kind bug ...

comparisons.note: Nothing merges without the full suite: bors merge queue, every PR fully tested on the merge commit. This is why 'rustc is green' is trusted absolutely.
comparisons.code: @bors r+ -> full CI on the exact merge -> only then master moves

comparisons.note: TryBots on every CL run the broad suite; slower builders complete post-submit. Two-lane, but the fast lane is already broad.

decisions.title: Warning and style policy for the compiler codebase
decisions.gist: Whether the Rust codebase must build warning-free, and how work-in-progress code marks itself so cleanup never amputates a feature.
decisions.explainer: The workspace currently builds with warnings allowed (one live dead-code warning in jet-jit today). Rust's `#[expect(lint, reason = "...")]` is a lint gate that also fails when the lint stops firing — so an exception can't outlive its cause. `-D warnings` in CI = any new warning is a red build. rustfmt/clippy = the standard Rust formatter and lint suite; both are configurable and neither touches this repo's PascalCase file naming.
decisions.story: An agent sweeping the codebase sees `fn scrutinee_bool` flagged dead and deletes it — not knowing it's the next stage of the JIT, mid-build on another card. The reverse also happens: genuinely dead code survives for months because nobody can tell it from in-progress work. This repo has hit both. The policy question: does 'dead code' explain itself, or does every reader have to guess?
decisions.detail: Recommend A. It resolves the standing tension between 'keep the build clean' and 'dead code may be an unbuilt feature' by making the code say which it is — and the expect self-expires when the feature lands.

options.name: Warning-free gate + card-referenced expects
options.detail: CI adds `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`, and a curated clippy set (correctness + suspicious lints on; style lints that fight house conventions off). Every intentional exception must be `#[expect(dead_code, reason = "#125: JIT tier-1a, wired in next stage")]` — self-documenting, and when the code goes live the expect itself errors and gets removed. Dead code without a card reference is deletable on sight, by rule.
options.code:
#[expect(dead_code, reason = "#125: JIT tier-1a scrutinee lowering, next stage")]
fn scrutinee_bool(&mut self, cond: &str) -> Result<Value, String> { ... }

$ cargo build   # clean — zero noise, every exception explains itself
# ...later, when #125 wires it in:
error: this lint expectation is unfulfilled  // <- expect must be deleted: self-expiring

options.name: Warning-free except dead_code
options.detail: `-D warnings` for everything else; dead_code stays advisory so in-progress features need no annotation. Keeps builds mostly clean but preserves exactly today's ambiguity for the one lint where ambiguity has already caused damage.
options.code:
$ cargo build
warning: method `scrutinee_bool` is never used   // still: delete or feature?

options.name: Status quo — warnings advisory
options.detail: No gate. Warnings accumulate until someone sweeps; sweeps risk deleting in-progress work; the build output slowly stops being read.
options.code: $ cargo build 2>&1 | wc -l   # a number that only grows

comparisons.note: Unused variable is a compile error, full stop — the language forces option A's discipline with no escape hatch.
comparisons.code: declared and not used: x   // does not compile

comparisons.note: `#[expect]` (stable 1.81) was added precisely for this: exceptions that expire themselves.

decisions.title: Build graph UX: what commands explain targets, generated files, and rebuild causes?
decisions.gist: Choose the inspection surface for graph, provenance, and why-rebuilt answers.
decisions.story: Grace changes an OpenAPI file and twenty generated modules rebuild. She needs to ask Jet what depended on that file, what generated a changed module, and why a cache miss happened, without reading lock internals.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet graph --target service
$ jet explain-build build/api_client.jet
$ jet explain-build openapi-client --why-rebuilt
$ jet query build "targets depending_on api/openapi.json" --json
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: command-line explainability and editor UX should share the same model. Recommendation is CLI-first commands plus LSP/editor surfaces over the same graph/provenance API.

options.name: CLI commands plus shared editor/query API (recommended)
options.detail: `jet graph` visualizes, `jet explain-build <target/file/action>` explains provenance/rebuilds, `jet query build` gives CI-friendly structured queries, and the LSP uses the same data for hover/go-to-def/generated-file provenance.
options.code:
$ jet graph --target service
$ jet explain-build build/api_client.jet
$ jet query build "generated_by openapi-client" --json
// editor hover: produced by openapi-client, cache miss reason shown

options.name: One explain command only
options.detail: A single `jet explain-build` handles everything. Simpler vocabulary, but graph exploration and CI queries become cramped.
options.code:
$ jet explain-build --graph service
$ jet explain-build --query "generated_by openapi-client"

options.name: JSON lock only
options.detail: Expose `.jet/lock` and let tools inspect it. Machine-readable, but bad human UX and easy to break when lock internals evolve.
options.code: $ cat .jet/lock | jq ...

options.name: LSP/editor only
options.detail: Show provenance in editor UI but keep CLI minimal. Good interactive UX, weak CI/script story.
options.code: // hover generated file -> produced by openapi-client

comparisons.note: Bazel query/aquery explain graph shape and actions.
Ninja can explain why outputs are dirty.
Cargo metadata is useful for tools but not a complete build-action graph.

decisions.title: Web backend TIR boundary
decisions.gist: Whether browser builds must use the same executable TIR as every other target.
decisions.story: Mara ports a Jet UI from native dev mode to the browser. A branch works in one target and not the other because the web emitter read older AST shapes instead of the checked TIR. That breaks the promise that rustc and target backends never become alternate semantic judges.

options.name: TIR-only web execution
options.detail: All executable web bodies lower through sema/TIR first. Unsupported web features produce Jet diagnostics before emission. This keeps one semantic pipeline and one source of truth across dev, JIT, AOT, and web.
options.code:
$ jet build --target web app.jet
Error [E-WEB001]: this effect is not available in the browser target
Fix: move file IO behind a server boundary or choose a native target.

options.name: Explicit web carve-out
options.detail: Allow the web backend to keep a separate AST emitter for a documented subset. The docs must say web is a distinct semantic path with its own conformance suite. This is a real exception to R7/R12.

options.name: Freeze web target until TIR-ready
options.detail: Stop growing the web backend until all executable emission can come from TIR. This avoids split semantics, but browser examples remain frozen while the backend catches up.
options.code:
$ jet build --target web app.jet
Error: web target is frozen until TIR lowering is complete.

comparisons.note: One typed core feeds JavaScript output; JS is not a second checker.
The compiler can emit JS even with type errors unless configured; Jet should not copy that split.

decisions.title: Fidelity signal API
decisions.gist: Choose the API apps use to read and pin runtime fidelity.
decisions.story: Mira tunes a Jet game across laptops and handhelds. Effects can scale down, but no user function may disappear because the machine is hot, and tests need deterministic pins.
decisions.inWild:
use core.perf.{Perf}
fidelity :: Perf.fidelity()

options.name: `core.perf.Perf` static API
options.detail: One runtime-global signal: read, override, reset. App code decides behavior; runtime never silently changes semantics.

options.name: Scoped override block
options.detail: Cleaner test isolation, but adds a second control shape beyond read/override/reset.
options.code: Perf.with_fidelity(0.2) { render_frame() }

options.name: Task-local fidelity
options.detail: Expert isolation, but less direct and conflicts with runtime-wide signal wording.
options.code: task.spawn(() => { Perf.override_fidelity(0.2)? })

comparisons.note: Global quality knobs are read by app code.

decisions.title: Platform signal provider surface
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet exposes battery, thermal, network, load, or carbon facts in Epoch 3.
decisions.story: Noor ships a tablet field app. Battery and network facts could tune sync, but Jet must not silently change scheduling, storage, or cleanup policy.
decisions.inWild: Signals.current() // if accepted

options.name: No platform providers in Epoch 3
options.detail: Keep only the ratified fidelity signal. Other facts remain platform packages or research notes.
options.code:
use core.perf.{Perf}
if Perf.fidelity() < 0.5 { draw_low_detail() }

options.name: Read-only `Signals.current()`
options.detail: Expose facts as one read-only value. Apps choose behavior explicitly.
options.code: signals :: Signals.current()

options.name: Injectable provider interface
options.detail: Deterministic and expert-controlled, but becomes a real platform abstraction layer.
options.code: Signals.use_provider(SignalProvider.fixed(...))

comparisons.note: Battery/network facts are readable; apps decide policy.

decisions.title: Explicit solver library
decisions.gist: Choose whether Core gets a finite constraint solver API in Epoch 3.
decisions.story: Iris writes a level generator with keys, doors, and enemies under constraints. She wants deterministic search with normal Jet ownership, not hidden backtracking.
decisions.inWild:
use core.solve.{Solver}
solver.require(path_exists(start_room(), key))

options.name: Core finite solver library
options.detail: Add `core.solve` with explicit solver state, deterministic order, ordinary values, and iterator output. No syntax.
options.code:
solver :: Solver.new(42)
solver.require(x + y == 10)

options.name: Experimental package first
options.detail: Explore API evidence without making Core law.
options.code: use core.experimental.solve.{Solver}

options.name: Defer solver API
options.detail: Keep logic work out of Epoch 3 Core. Use normal iterator adapters and keep examples research-only.
options.code: rooms().filter((r) => path_exists(start, r))

comparisons.note: Explicit solver objects keep search visible to host code.

decisions.title: Structural merge command surface
decisions.gist: Choose how users invoke Jet structural diff and merge.
decisions.story: Sam renames a type while Priya moves methods into a new module. Text merge conflicts, but Jet can see program entities and should expose one Jet-aware merge path.
decisions.inWild:
jet diff --structural main...feature
jet merge --structural base.jet ours.jet theirs.jet

options.name: `jet diff --structural` and `jet merge --structural`
options.detail: One command surface for read-only diff and three-way merge. Git/editor integration can call it later.
options.code:
jet diff --structural main...feature
jet merge --structural base.jet ours.jet theirs.jet --out merged.jet

options.name: Dedicated structural commands
options.detail: Plain feature name, but creates a parallel command family.
options.code: jet structural-diff main...feature

options.name: Git-only merge driver
options.detail: Convenient when installed, poor for learning, debugging, CI, and editor reuse.
options.code: git config merge.jetstruct.driver ...

comparisons.note: Text merge is default; drivers are opt-in per repo/path.

decisions.title: Public conflict identity model
decisions.gist: Choose what identity Jet shows in structural conflict reports.
decisions.story: Lena reviews a CI merge report. She needs to know whether a function changed, moved, or became a different definition without reading internal hashes first.
decisions.inWild: conflict: fn Parser.parse_expr(self, TokenStream) -> Expr

options.name: Human identity plus stable internal ID
options.detail: Reports show module/type/function/signature first and include stable IDs for tools and rename tracking.
options.code:
conflict: fn Parser.parse_expr(self, TokenStream) -> Expr
stable id: def:7YDK4Q6V

options.name: Name/path identity only
options.detail: Readable, but rename/move cases lose the proof structural merge exists to preserve.
options.code: conflict: Source/Parser.jet Parser.parse_expr changed

options.name: Content IDs first
options.detail: Precise for machines, weak beginner report.
options.code: conflict: def:7YDK4Q6V changed

comparisons.note: Structured identity internally, human names in UI.

decisions.title: Structural conflict report shape
decisions.gist: Choose how structural merge conflicts are shown to humans and tools.
decisions.story: Owen hits CI after two refactors. Terminal output must be readable; editor and review bots need structured facts from the same model.
decisions.inWild: jet merge --structural base.jet ours.jet theirs.jet --report json

options.name: Human text only
options.detail: Best direct CLI, but tools must scrape text.
options.code: conflict: fn Parser.parse_expr changed on both sides

options.name: JSON only
options.detail: Machine-stable, weak direct CLI experience.
options.code: {"kind":"signature_conflict","identity":"fn Parser.parse_expr"}

options.name: One schema, text/JSON/editor renderers
options.detail: One typed conflict model. CLI renders Jet-style text, JSON writes same facts, editor consumes same schema.
options.code:
jet merge --structural base ours theirs
jet merge --structural base ours theirs --report json

comparisons.note: Human diagnostics plus JSON output for tools.

decisions.title: Git and VCS integration policy
decisions.gist: Choose how structural merge plugs into Git and other VCS tools.
decisions.story: A team adopts Jet in a monorepo. Beginners keep normal Git; release engineers enable structural merge for `.jet` files in CI and protected branches.
decisions.inWild: jet merge install-driver --repo .

options.name: Opt-in Git driver generated by Jet
options.detail: Jet configures `.jet` paths for this repo. Other VCS tools call the same structural merge command.
options.code: jet merge install-driver --repo .

options.name: Always-on Git replacement
options.detail: Strong stance, but adds source-control ceremony before identity safety has proven out.
options.code: git merge feature

options.name: Standalone only
options.detail: Simple boundary, but misses where conflicts happen.
options.code: jet merge --structural base ours theirs --out file.jet

comparisons.note: Syntax-aware diff is opt-in around Git.

decisions.title: Core data surface
decisions.gist: Choose the public Core API for tables, series, stats, and plots.
decisions.story: Mira analyzes support tickets from CSV in one file. She wants typed rows, grouped summaries, and a small plot without first learning Python, SQL, or package manifests.
decisions.inWild:
use core.data
summary.plot.bar(x: .team, y: .p95_minutes).save("ticket-p95.svg")?

options.name: One `core.data` facade
options.detail: Tables, series, stats, CSV, and plot builders live behind one beginner import; expert modules remain below with same operation names.
options.code:
use core.data
rows :: data.csv<Ticket>("tickets.csv")?

options.name: Split by domain modules
options.detail: Ownership explicit, but first tutorial spreads across several namespaces.
options.code:
use core.table
use core.stats
use core.plot

options.name: Method-only table API
options.detail: Compact call sites, but reusable stats/plot vocabulary hides inside table values.
options.code: Table.csv<Ticket>("tickets.csv")?.group_by(.team)

comparisons.note: Composable pipelines are strong; Jet should keep column misses as Jet diagnostics.

decisions.title: Data bridge providers
decisions.gist: Choose how Python, R, and accelerator bridges are named and imported.
decisions.story: Ishan has a mostly native analytics job, with one Python clustering step and one accelerator kernel. He needs bridges visible, typed, and replaceable.
decisions.inWild:
use py.sklearn as sklearn
model :: sklearn.KMeans(k: 8).fit(customers)?

options.name: Use provider roots directly
options.detail: `py.*` and other accepted bridge roots stay visible under the FFI structure law; data APIs accept typed bridge results and report status.
options.code:
use py.sklearn as sklearn
use r.forecast as forecast
use gpu.cuda as cuda

options.name: Nest bridges under `core.data.bridge`
options.detail: Discoverable from data, but creates a second spelling for foreign providers.
options.code: use core.data.bridge.py.sklearn as sklearn

options.name: Manifest-named accelerators
options.detail: Policy control, but hides bridge authority from single-file readers.
options.code: deps: { sklearn: py@sklearn#"1.6.0" }

comparisons.note: Provider identity is obvious, but native replacement status is absent.

decisions.title: Native replacement status
decisions.gist: Choose how users see which data steps are native, bridged, or missing.
decisions.story: Rae moves notebook work into Jet for a regulated report. She must prove which steps are native, which bridge into Python or R, and which replacements exist.
decisions.inWild:
data.status().write("data-status.json")?
jet dossier data analysis.jet

options.name: `jet dossier data` lens plus API
options.detail: Machine status via Core API; canonical human view through the D-WD dossier umbrella.
options.code:
data.status().write("data-status.json")?
jet dossier data analysis.jet

options.name: Standalone `jet data status`
options.detail: Discoverable for analysts, but adds another explain surface beside dossier.
options.code: jet data status analysis.jet --json

options.name: Build warning summary only
options.detail: Visible during run, weak for audits unless another artifact appears.
options.code:
jet run analysis.jet
Data status: native, bridged

comparisons.note: Stable scriptable graph/report views work well.

decisions.title: Deterministic plotting policy
decisions.gist: Choose the first plotting backend and deterministic output rule.
decisions.story: Noor checks a generated report into CI. Charts must be readable and golden-test stable across host fonts, timestamps, and graphics libraries.
decisions.inWild: summary.plot.bar(x: .region, y: .revenue).save("revenue.svg")?

options.name: First-party deterministic SVG plus text fallback
options.detail: Core emits stable SVG with pinned layout and a text backend for terminal/CI. Bitmap export can layer on the same model later.
options.code:
plot.save("revenue.svg")?
plot.save("revenue.txt")?

options.name: Text plots only in Core
options.detail: Maximally stable, weaker beginner report story.
options.code: plot.save("revenue.txt")?

options.name: Backend package required
options.detail: Maximal backend control, too much setup for first chart.
options.code: plot.render(svg.backend()).save("revenue.svg")?

comparisons.note: Portable declarative specs are useful; Jet can own a smaller typed model first.

decisions.title: Game asset handles
decisions.gist: Choose how game assets are declared, loaded, and diagnosed.
decisions.story: Lena makes a platformer. She wants a typed `player_sprite` handle everywhere and a Jet diagnostic if a PNG is missing or used as a sound.
decisions.inWild: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Scene asset registry with typed handles
options.detail: Assets load through `scene.assets`, returning typed handles tied to scene identity.
options.code:
player :: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?
jump :: scene.assets.sound("assets/jump.wav")?

options.name: Top-level loaders
options.detail: Flexible, but weakens scene-owned diagnostics and editor identity.
options.code: player :: game.asset.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Manifest asset catalog
options.detail: Strong packaging provenance, more ceremony for one-file games.
options.code: targets: { game: { assets: { player: "assets/player.png" } } }

comparisons.note: Resource handles are editor-friendly; Jet should keep them typed and source-owned.

decisions.title: ECS over Scene
decisions.gist: Choose the component and query API that layers over `Scene`.
decisions.story: Omar starts with a simple scene, then adds hundreds of enemies. Components and queries should be another view over the same scene data, not a second engine.
decisions.inWild:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.query(Position, Velocity)

options.name: `component` declarations plus `scene.query`
options.detail: Components are typed declarations; queries are scene methods, preserving one scene identity.
options.code:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
loop item in scene.query(Position, Velocity) { }

options.name: Struct marker components
options.detail: No new declaration form, but component intent is less visible.
options.code:
struct Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.component<Velocity>()

options.name: System functions over query parameters
options.detail: Concise for experts, but puts scheduler vocabulary before the beginner scene story.
options.code: system move(pos: Position mut, vel: Velocity, frame: Frame) { }

comparisons.note: Typed queries are strong; Jet should hide scheduler complexity until needed.

decisions.title: Game input bindings
decisions.gist: Choose how input bindings and per-frame snapshots are named.
decisions.story: Aya wants keyboard today and gamepad later. Replay files should store actions, not raw device quirks, so logic is deterministic across dev, CI, and builds.
decisions.inWild:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Scene bindings plus frame snapshot
options.detail: Bindings live on `scene.input`; frame logic reads deterministic `frame.input` snapshots.
options.code:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Global input map
options.detail: Short, but weak multi-scene/editor isolation.
options.code: game.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])

options.name: Typed action enum
options.detail: Explicit and replay-friendly, more ceremony for tiny games.
options.code:
enum Action { jump }
frame.input<Action>().pressed(Action.jump)

comparisons.note: Action maps are beginner-friendly and replayable.

decisions.comment: Both A & C

decisions.title: Game replay contract
decisions.gist: Choose the replay API, file format, and determinism contract.
decisions.story: Ben gets a physics bug report. The player sends one replay file; Ben runs it under `jet dev` and compiled mode and gets the same frame transcript.
decisions.inWild: game.Replay.record("runs/bug-142.jreplay")

options.name: `game.Replay` API plus `.jreplay` artifact
options.detail: First-party typed artifact contains input actions, seeds, fixed-step timing, backend identity, and budget events.
options.code:
game.run(scene, replay: game.Replay.record("run.jreplay"))
game.Replay.play("run.jreplay", scene)?

options.name: CLI-only replay
options.detail: Keeps source clean, weakens tests that need replay facts.
options.code: jet game record game.jet --out run.jreplay

options.name: User serialization hooks
options.detail: Expert control, but no shared deterministic contract.
options.code: scene.on_snapshot((frame) => writer.write(frame.input))

comparisons.note: Input-stream replay is proven; Jet should type and version the artifact.

decisions.title: Game backend selection
decisions.gist: Choose how renderer, audio, and editor backends are selected.
decisions.story: Sana starts with a no-op CI backend, develops on raylib, and later targets wgpu. Gameplay code should not change when backend changes.
decisions.inWild: game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Typed `game.Backend` value
options.detail: Backends are explicit typed values passed to `game.run`; beginners can omit for the default headless/no-op path.
options.code:
game.run(scene)
game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Manifest target backend
options.detail: Fits packages, but single-file games need hidden defaults or a second path.
options.code: targets: { game: { backend: { renderer: core.raylib } } }

options.name: CLI-selected backend
options.detail: Useful for CI, harder to audit from source.
options.code: jet run game.jet --game-renderer=core.raylib

comparisons.note: Plugins are flexible; Jet should keep one stable Core scene API above replaceable backend packages.

decisions.title: Game budgets
decisions.gist: Choose how frame, memory, asset, and draw-call budgets attach and report diagnostics.
decisions.story: Nico ships a handheld build with strict frame, memory, and draw-call ceilings. Violations should be Jet diagnostics with replay context.
decisions.inWild: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Scene/package budgets, same model
options.detail: Budgets attach to scenes for one-file games and package targets for projects; sema/runtime treat both as one fact model.
options.code: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Package-only budgets
options.detail: Clean for CI, but one-file games lose budget diagnostics unless packaged.
options.code: targets: { game: { budgets: { frame: 16.ms } } }

options.name: Runtime watcher API
options.detail: Dynamic control, weaker build/dossier/CI facts.
options.code: budget_watch.attach(scene)
