options.detail: A single source-backed generation engine owns identity, atomic switch, history, collision policy, and GC rooting for every profile object; `profile.<name>` is the sole package-profile declaration and `user.<name>` composes profiles by reference, amending D-JOS-USERENV1, D-JOS-USERAPPLY1, and D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1 only to share the engine. `jet profile plan/build/switch/rollback/generations` mirrors the ratified `jetos user` verb set, with D-JPK-OSGEN1 auto-naming plus `--name` and the ratified plan-before-apply UX on every mutation. A profile composed into an active user environment has exactly one history: switching it records a new generation through the same engine, so the Jetpack and JetOS views can never drift. Non-JetOS platforms get full parity per D-JPK-PLATFORM1; generations are JP4 GC roots with retained-generation defaults experts may tune.

comparisons.note: Per-user profiles provide atomic generations and rollback.
comparisons.code:
nix profile install nixpkgs#ripgrep
nix profile rollback

comparisons.note: User environment composition is separate from low-level Nix profiles.

decisions.title: Registry, publisher, and cache trust root
decisions.gist: Choose the trust architecture for registry metadata, publishers, caches, and offline verification.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A's TOFU defends none of the story's attacks and is already listed as a production blocker in the plan. Option B forbids identity-based signing, hurting key-loss recovery; option C is strongest but leaves bootstrap distribution, transparency-log checkpoint pinning, recovery drills, and the beginner verdict surface unstated, and both B and C amend D-PKGSIGN1, which does not appear in the ratified digest — that reference needs reconciliation at ratification. The hybrid keeps C's architecture and closes bootstrap, agility (D-PQCRYPTO1), offline-grace (D-JPK-OFFLINE1), and audit-UX gaps.
decisions.story: Martha's registry timestamp key is stolen. Attackers must not replace packages, roll clients back, freeze updates, or make a new publisher key look legitimate on first use.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet audit trust
root: 3-of-5 offline threshold
registry snapshot: current
publisher: verified identity bundle
cache builder: approved provenance
result: trusted
decisions.detail: Automatic beginner verification plus exact expert roots, thresholds, privacy, offline, and recovery controls.

options.name: Author TOFU plus Git index
options.detail: Keep first-seen Ed25519 author keys and current Git history as the principal trust model.
options.code: trust: first seen key for acme/web

options.name: TUF thresholds plus long-lived author keys
options.detail: Offline threshold root, delegated targets, snapshot/timestamp freshness, rotation/revocation; public-registry releases require publisher Ed25519/KMS signatures, explicitly amending D-PKGSIGN1 there. Private registries may set an equally explicit signature policy.
options.code:
root: 3-of-5
publisher: ed25519/acme

options.name: TUF thresholds plus hybrid publisher identity
options.detail: TUF secures registry authority/freshness; trusted-root bootstrap, monotonic updates, bad clocks, expiry, and signature stripping fail closed. Public-registry releases require either Sigstore identity bundles or Ed25519/KMS/HSM publisher signatures, explicitly amending D-PKGSIGN1 there; private registries choose an explicit offline policy. SLSA provenance covers builders.
options.code:
root: 3-of-5, monotonic + unexpired
publisher: required sigstore bundle OR offline key
builder: signed provenance

options.name: TUF + hybrid publisher identity, pinned bootstrap, agile algorithms (hybrid)
options.detail: TUF secures registry authority: offline threshold root, delegated targets, snapshot/timestamp freshness, consistent snapshots, monotonic versions; expiry, rollback, bad clocks, and signature stripping fail closed with named E12xx, while already-realized environments keep working offline per D-JPK-OFFLINE1. The trusted root ships pinned inside the jet toolchain object, so bootstrap never trusts first network contact; rotation, revocation, and threshold-minus-one recovery are drilled surfaces, and all signature algorithms ride the D-PQCRYPTO1 agility seam over the D-DEP-CRYPTO1 backend. Public-registry releases require a Sigstore identity bundle verified against a pinned transparency-log checkpoint OR an offline Ed25519/KMS/HSM publisher signature — both feed one monitorable audit stream — explicitly amending D-PKGSIGN1 there; private registries set an equally explicit offline policy. Cache builders and remote executors hold distinct identities with SLSA provenance bound to action and output digests. `jet audit trust` gives beginners one verdict line; `--json` exposes every role, threshold, and expiry.
options.code:
$ jet audit trust
root: 3-of-5 offline, pinned via toolchain, unexpired, monotonic
publisher: sigstore bundle (log checkpoint verified)
builder: SLSA provenance, approved identity
result: trusted
$ jet audit trust --json   # full chain: roles, thresholds, expiry

comparisons.note: Separates offline root, delegated targets, snapshot, and timestamp roles.
Binds ephemeral keys to workload/user identity with transparency proof bundles.

decisions.title: Shared-cache writer authority
decisions.gist: Choose which builders may publish objects that others consume as trusted.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A is the poisoning hole the story describes — a signature proves who, not build integrity. Option B kills all developer sharing and never defines builder approval; option C is the right shape but leaves credential lifetime, the approval evidence set, read-path verification, and compromised-builder revocation unstated. The hybrid keeps C's namespace split and pre-execution approval, then adds verify-on-read, provenance field law, quarantine-on-revocation, and the explain surface implementers need.
decisions.story: Frank's laptop builds a package with a locally modified compiler. That result may be useful to him, but it must not silently become the organization's trusted cache hit.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet build
cache write: private/frank
$ jet release
cache write: shared/release (approved builder + provenance)
decisions.detail: Fast local sharing never weakens organization-wide trust.

options.name: Any authenticated developer writes shared
options.detail: A cache token grants read/write to the common namespace; consumers verify object signatures only.
options.code: cache: shared write accepted from frank

options.name: Hosted release builders only
options.detail: Only centrally configured builders may write shared cache; all developer outputs stay local.
options.code: cache: shared write denied; builder not allowlisted

options.name: Private and shared namespaces
options.detail: Developers write private namespaces. Shared namespaces accept only builders approved before execution with action/platform/sandbox/policy/reproducibility proofs. An unapproved result must rebuild on an approved builder; provenance cannot retroactively promote authority. Read/write credentials are separate.
options.code:
cache write private/frank: accepted
cache promote shared: rebuild on approved release builder

options.name: Namespaces plus provenance-bound writers, verify-on-read, revocation (hybrid)
options.detail: Developers write private namespaces with short-lived write-scoped credentials; read and write credentials are always separate. Shared/trusted namespaces accept only builders allowlisted in source policy before execution, and every upload carries signed provenance binding action digest, output digest, platform, sandbox class, and policy hash — provenance can never retroactively promote authority. Consumers re-verify digest and signature on every hit in every namespace (Law 3: no trust by location); an unapproved result is rebuilt on an approved builder, never copied across on assertion. Revoking a builder quarantines every object it signed until re-verified or rebuilt. `jet build` prints the namespace of each cache write, and `jet explain --lens cache` states why a hit was trusted or refused.
options.code:
$ jet build
cache write private/frank: accepted (write-scoped token, 1h)
$ jet release
cache promote shared: rebuild on approved release builder
$ jet explain --lens cache pkg:foo
hit shared/release: digest ok, sig ok, builder approved, sandbox=strong

comparisons.note: Common guidance separates cache consumers from trusted CI writers.
Remote cache authorization is separate from action correctness.

decisions.title: Multiple-version resolution law
decisions.gist: Choose when two versions of the same package may coexist.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A is the Go-style global straitjacket that turns every major-version ecosystem migration into a flag day; B reproduces npm/cargo one-process ABI splits. C is sound but under-specified: it never says who proves isolation, gives no diagnostic quality bar, and forces unification even where cargo-style major coexistence is provably safe. The hybrid keeps C's typed domains, adds compiler-proven major coexistence with version-qualified identity, PubGrub causal proofs on E1201, and an audited expert escape recorded in the lock.
decisions.story: Alice builds a server whose code generator needs protobuf 3 while the runtime needs protobuf 4. Global unification fails; unrestricted duplication can split one runtime ABI.
decisions.inWild:
tool protobuf@3   domain: build/x86_64-linux
lib  protobuf@4   domain: target/aarch64-linux
both locked; runtime link domain remains coherent
decisions.detail: Avoids global straitjacket and uncontrolled duplication through typed isolation.

options.name: One version globally
options.detail: Every package name resolves once across the whole workspace and every build/target role.
options.code: Error: protobuf 3 and 4 cannot coexist

options.name: Unrestricted duplicates
options.detail: Every dependency edge may select its own version, even inside one runtime/link domain.
options.code:
app -> protobuf 4
plugin -> protobuf 3
both enter same process

options.name: One version per typed domain
options.detail: Identity is provider + namespace + name. Unify inside a domain; duplicate only across a proven isolation boundary for build/host/target, platform, runtime, linkage, or ABI. Feature differences alone do not prove isolation. Amends E1201 to reject incompatible versions in one typed domain.
options.code:
build domain: protobuf 3
target domain: protobuf 4
shared runtime/link domain: unify or E1201

options.name: Typed domains plus proven-safe major coexistence and causal proofs (hybrid)
options.detail: Identity is provider + namespace + name; one version unifies inside each typed domain, and duplication is automatic only across proven build/host/target, platform, runtime, linkage, or ABI boundaries — feature differences never prove isolation. Distinct semver majors may additionally coexist inside one domain only when the compiler proves no type or value crosses versions (identities are version-qualified); any crossing is E1201 carrying a PubGrub causal proof naming both requirement chains and the smallest fix. Experts may force a named coexistence via policy.resolution.allow_duplicate(package, domain, reason), recorded in lock rationale and audit output. Every coexistence appears in `jet explain duplicates` with its proving boundary.
options.code:
$ jet build
E1201: protobuf 3 and 4 meet in one runtime/link domain
  proof: server -> grpc 2.1 -> protobuf 4; codegen -> protobuf 3
  smallest fix: update codegen to >=1.8 (uses protobuf 4)
$ jet explain duplicates
protobuf: 3 [build] / 4 [target] — boundary: build/target roles

comparisons.note: Can resolve multiple crate versions but feature/type identity surprises remain.
Package identity includes settings/options/dependency identities.

decisions.title: Package variant vocabulary
decisions.gist: Choose the axes used to match package producers and consumers.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A pushes linkage/ABI/role back into ad-hoc recipes and recreates the vcpkg triplet explosion; B is Gradle's open-attribute ambiguity, an explicitly rejected anti-pattern. C names the right axes but omits the matching/defaulting law where Gradle actually hurts (ambiguous candidates), never binds the selected variant into action keys and the lock (JP15), and gives the closed set no evolution path. The hybrid states total defaults, deterministic tie-break with a naming diagnostic, lock/key entry, and ballot-gated axis growth.
decisions.story: George needs a static musl library for an ARM target, a native code generator for macOS, and a shared debug library for local tests. Variant facts must be precise and finite.
decisions.inWild:
need: role .Target, os .Linux, arch .Aarch64, libc .Musl, linkage .Static
selected: exact compatible artifact
decisions.detail: Captures real compatibility without Gradle-style unbounded ambiguity.

options.name: Platform only
options.detail: Selection considers OS and architecture; recipes handle linkage, ABI, runtime, and role ad hoc.
options.code: variant: aarch64-linux

options.name: Open attribute maps
options.detail: Providers and packages invent arbitrary keys; a generic matcher picks compatible maps.
options.code: variant: { os: linux, fooMode: turbo, abiX: 7 }

options.name: Typed core axes plus namespaced provider facts
options.detail: Closed native axes: build/host/target role, OS, arch, runtime/libc, linkage, ABI, artifact kind, feature set. Providers may preserve extra facts, but native selection uses them only after explicit mapping.
options.code:
variant: Variant.{ role: .Target, os: .Linux, arch: .Aarch64, linkage: .Static }
providerFacts: { conan.compiler.runtime: "libstdc++11" }

options.name: Closed axes, total defaults, deterministic match, ballot-gated growth (hybrid)
options.detail: Native selection uses only the closed typed axes — build/host/target role, OS, arch, runtime/libc, linkage, ABI, artifact kind, feature set — and every axis has a defined default derived from the requesting context, so beginners never write variants. Matching is exact-then-compatible under one total documented order; an ambiguous tie is an E12xx listing the candidates and the first distinguishing axis, never a silent pick. The selected variant enters the action key and the semantic lock. Provider facts persist under namespaced keys and influence selection only through explicit variant_map declarations in source policy; adding a native axis requires a decision ballot.

comparisons.note: Variant-aware resolution matches producer/consumer attributes.
Triplets encode platform/linkage/runtime choices.

decisions.title: New-release maturity default
decisions.gist: Choose whether newly published third-party versions wait before fresh resolution.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A leaves the compromised-account story wide open, and option C makes safety opt-in — a direct philosophy violation. Option B is correct but hard-codes 24h for every source including your own registry, and never resolves the ugly case where the held release is itself the security fix. The hybrid keeps B's transparency-anchored clock and exact exceptions, zeroes the window for first-party sources, makes it policy-tunable per registry, and surfaces the advisory conflict with a guided audited override.
decisions.story: Doris runs `jet update` minutes after a popular package account is compromised. Existing exact locks should keep working, while new resolution gets time for yanks and trust evidence.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet update http
held: http 4.8.1 (published 37m ago)
selected: 4.8.0
Fix: audit and grant an exact exception
decisions.detail: Beginner protection is automatic; audited exact overrides preserve urgent expert control.

options.name: No maturity delay
options.detail: Any valid new release is immediately eligible under version and trust policy.
options.code: selected 4.8.1, published 37m ago

options.name: 24-hour default with exact exception
options.detail: New direct and transitive third-party versions wait 24 hours from first immutable inclusion in trusted, monotonic signed registry/transparency metadata—not publisher, mirror, or local timestamps. Existing exact locks are unaffected. Exceptions bind one package/version plus that inclusion/evidence identity.
options.code:
held 4.8.1 until maturity
policy exception may name exactly 4.8.1

options.name: Opt-in maturity policy
options.detail: Default stays immediate; projects enable a delay in workspace policy.
options.code: module workspace { policy: Policy.{ release_maturity_hours: 24 } }

options.name: 24h default, policy-tunable per source, advisory-aware exact exceptions (hybrid)
options.detail: New direct and transitive third-party versions wait 24 hours from first immutable inclusion in trusted monotonic signed registry/transparency metadata — never publisher, mirror, or local timestamps; existing exact locks and realized environments are untouched (D-JPK-OFFLINE1). Workspace policy may raise or lower the window per registry or source class; first-party and workspace-internal sources default to zero. When a held version fixes a published advisory affecting the currently selected version, `jet update` says so and offers the audited exception; every exception binds exactly one package#version plus its inclusion/evidence identity, reviewer, and expiry in `policy.trust`. CI evaluates the same policy deterministically, and held versions print with age and the one-line fix.
options.code:
$ jet update http
held: http 4.8.1 (published 37m ago; matures in 23h)
selected: 4.8.0
note: 4.8.1 fixes advisory JSA-2026-114 affecting 4.8.0
Fix: jet trust grant release-exception:http#4.8.1 --expires 7d

comparisons.note: Supports minimum release age and trust-policy exclusions.
Default resolution has no maturity delay.

decisions.comment: the version specifier is package#version, not package@version

decisions.title: Upstream build and install hook approval
decisions.gist: Choose when third-party package scripts may execute.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A converts sandbox containment into authorization and auto-runs third-party code; option B's name-scoped approval that survives script changes is the classic worm vector and leaves CI undefined. Option C has the right binding law but a cold policy error on `jet add` is beginner-hostile, and it never states that approval keeps the sandbox, nor grant revocation or transitive review aids. The hybrid keeps C's exact digest+capability binding, adds a guided interactive path and diff-on-change, mandates sandbox-after-approval, and allows only digest-bound curated allowlists.
decisions.story: Hank adds an npm tool whose transitive package has a postinstall script. The metadata can be read safely, but executing code needs an authority decision bound to what will run.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet add npm:sharp
blocked hook: sharp#0.34 install
requests: exec, filesystem write
$ jet trust grant package-hook:sharp#0.34
grant binds script digest + capabilities
decisions.detail: One approval mechanism covers providers and keeps both beginners and CI safe.

options.name: Run sandboxed hooks automatically
options.detail: All provider-declared hooks run inside the strong sandbox with declared/default capabilities.
options.code: install hook: auto-approved sandbox

options.name: Prompt on first execution
options.detail: Interactive users approve the package name once; later hook changes inherit approval.
options.code: Run sharp install hook? [y/N]

options.name: Deny unreviewed; exact intent approval
options.detail: Hooks never run during metadata probing. Approval binds package identity, script/recipe digest, provider/source, and capability set in source policy. Any change re-prompts. CI fails with the exact source fix.
options.code:
Error: unreviewed hook
Fix: `jet trust grant package-hook:sharp#0.34` drafts policy.trust

options.name: Deny unreviewed; guided exact grants, always sandboxed, CI fix line (hybrid)
options.detail: Metadata probing never executes upstream code; unreviewed hooks are held, not run. Interactive `jet add` shows package identity, provider/source, script digest, and requested capabilities, and one confirmation drafts an exact `policy.trust` grant binding all four; any digest or capability change re-prompts with a diff of what changed. Approval authorizes execution but never removes containment — approved hooks still run inside the strong sandbox with only their granted capabilities, under D-BUILDPOLICY1 tier rules. CI never prompts: it fails with the exact `jet trust grant package-hook:...` source fix, and grants are listable and revocable via `jet trust`. A workspace may pin a signed curated allowlist feed as pre-review evidence; feed entries are digest-bound, never name wildcards.
options.code:
$ jet add npm:sharp
held hook: sharp#0.34 install (digest sha256:4c11)
requests: exec, write $out
approve and record in policy.trust? [y/N] y
~ runs sandboxed with granted caps only
CI: Error [E12xx] unreviewed hook — Fix: jet trust grant package-hook:sharp#0.34

comparisons.note: Explicitly approves dependencies allowed to run install scripts.
build.rs executes as part of builds; sandboxing is external.

decisions.title: Pinned Nix compatibility baseline
decisions.gist: Choose which Nix version and experimental features define the parity contract.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A amputates flakes, contradicting the epoch exit claim and the dominant real-world nixpkgs entry point. C promises bit-parity with dynamic derivations and IFD — experimental moving targets — even though IFD's hidden store coupling is a plan-listed rejected anti-pattern, and C states no baseline-advancement law. The hybrid keeps C's full coverage claim and its good impure trust-grant law, delivers IFD/dynamic through the already-gated JP21 typed staging instead of Nix's mechanism, and adds the machine-readable matrix plus a corpus-gated re-pin procedure that A/B/C all lack.
decisions.story: Walter compares Jetpack against Nix after a Nix upgrade changes derivation behavior. A pinned baseline tells CI whether Jetpack diverged or the oracle changed.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack compatibility
Nix baseline: 2.34 stable
nixpkgs: <pinned commit>
flakes: yes
CA derivations: yes
dynamic derivations: staged compatibility
decisions.detail: Meets the requested full pinned parity while keeping unsafe/impure behavior isolated from Jet authoring.

options.name: Stable Nix surface only; narrow parity claim
options.detail: Pin latest stable Nix language/store protocol; exclude flakes and experiments. Selecting this explicitly amends the epoch exit claim and drops flake/experimental compatibility.
options.code:
baseline: Nix stable
parity exceptions: flakes, experimental features

options.name: Stable plus selected production experiments
options.detail: Pin Nix 2.34 stable plus flakes, new CLI lock/registry behavior, and CA derivations. Dynamic/recursive/IFD and impure derivations remain named compatibility exceptions, narrowing full Nix parity.
options.code:
baseline: Nix 2.34
features: flakes nix-command ca-derivations

options.name: Full pinned Nix compatibility
options.detail: Pin one Nix release and implement its stable plus experimental package-manager/evaluator/store features, including flakes, CA, dynamic/recursive derivations, IFD, and impure compatibility. Impure Nix is never enabled by import/default: an explicit trust grant binds host/network/env capabilities; results stay private, untrusted, and non-promotable unless rebuilt hermetically.
options.code:
baseline: Nix 2.34
features: full pinned set
impure: explicit capability grant -> private/untrusted output

options.name: Pinned full baseline: tiered core/staged features, granted impurity (hybrid)
options.detail: Pin Nix 2.34 plus a nixpkgs commit as the sole parity oracle. The core tier — stable language/store/protocol, flakes, nix-command, and CA derivations — carries full bit-parity by default; IFD and dynamic/recursive derivations form a staged tier that lowers to the D-JPK-DYNAMICPLAN1 finite typed-staging mechanism, never Nix's hidden store coupling, and until that ballot ratifies such refs fail with one E-code naming the construct, tier, and fix. Impure evaluation is never enabled by import or default: an explicit `jet trust` grant binds host/network/env capabilities, and outputs stay private, untrusted, and non-promotable unless rebuilt hermetically. `jetpack compatibility` emits a machine-readable feature matrix; a baseline re-pin requires the full differential corpus green under the new pin and is recorded as a decision amendment.
options.code:
baseline: Nix 2.34 + nixpkgs <pin>
core: stable flakes nix-command ca-derivations -> bit parity
staged: ifd dynamic-derivations -> JP21 typed staging (ballot-gated)
impure: explicit trust grant -> private/untrusted output
$ jetpack compatibility --json

comparisons.note: Many important capabilities remain behind experimental feature flags.

decisions.title: Canonical Nix store-path execution without installed Nix
decisions.gist: Choose how unmodified Nix binaries with embedded `/nix/store` references run from Hangar.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: C violates ratified D-JPK-NODAEMON1 (no root, no mutable global host state) and should be flagged as contradicting ratified law; B's byte relocation is unsound for hash-embedded Nix artifacts and forks cache identity. A is correct but silent on the common case of unprivileged user namespaces being disabled (hardened kernels, CI containers) and on hosts that already have a real /nix/store. The hybrid keeps A's projection and fail-closed macOS/Windows law while adding a deterministic verified fallback ladder with degraded-provenance marking, so beginners keep a working default and no path ever trusts location or silently relocates.
decisions.story: Earl fetches Firefox from cache.nixos.org on a machine with no Nix installation. Its loader and libraries contain canonical `/nix/store/...` paths that must resolve exactly.
decisions.inWild:
$ env -u NIX_STORE_DIR jetpack run nixpkgs:hello
Hello, world!
proof: canonical /nix/store closure projected from Hangar; no installed Nix
decisions.detail: Preserves bit-compatible cached artifacts while keeping rootless host state and Jetpack ownership.

options.name: Sandbox-projected canonical store
options.detail: Hangar owns bytes and references. Linux uses a rootless mount namespace. macOS uses an explicitly approved narrow helper/broker when rootless projection is unavailable; otherwise fail closed. Windows treats Nix binaries as Linux-target artifacts executed remotely/VM, never relocates silently. Cross-references SANDBOX2/MULTIUSER1.
options.code:
Linux: user+mount namespace -> /nix/store
macOS: approved projection helper or fail
Windows: Linux remote/VM target

options.name: Relocate and patch binaries
options.detail: Rewrite interpreter/RPATH/text references to Hangar paths and prove semantic equivalence per artifact.
options.code: patchelf --set-rpath /hangar/...

options.name: Require a real host `/nix/store`
options.detail: Jetpack installs or asks an admin to create the canonical global directory even without the Nix program.
options.code: sudo mkdir /nix/store

options.name: Projected canonical store with deterministic verified fallback ladder (hybrid)
options.detail: Hangar owns bytes and references; Linux projects canonical `/nix/store` through a rootless user+mount namespace. When the kernel denies unprivileged namespaces, the fallback ladder is deterministic and ordered: reuse an existing host `/nix/store` read-only with every object digest-verified before use (no trust by location); else an audited userspace path-translation backend whose provenance is marked degraded and whose outputs never promote to trusted cache; else fail closed with one E-code naming the kernel knob and both fixes. macOS uses the explicitly approved narrow helper/broker or fails closed with the same diagnostic; Windows treats Nix binaries as Linux-target artifacts realized via declared WSL2/VM/remote builders, never silent relocation. Jetpack never creates a root-owned host `/nix/store` (upholds D-JPK-NODAEMON1); byte relocation exists only as an explicit expert tool whose output is a new derived identity that can never substitute the canonical digest. Cross-references SANDBOX2/MULTIUSER1 and JP11 build-environment facts.
options.code:
Linux: user+mount ns -> /nix/store
fallback 1: verified host store (read-only)
fallback 2: userspace translation [degraded, non-promotable]
else: E13xx kernel denies userns -> both fixes listed
macOS: approved helper or fail closed | Windows: WSL2/VM/remote

comparisons.note: Store paths are canonical and embedded in runtime artifacts.
Projects a Nix store through user-space mechanisms.

decisions.title: Remote builder declaration and control surface
decisions.gist: Choose how teams declare builders, capabilities, credentials, trust domains, and fallback.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option C puts endpoints and credentials in flags, directly violating the plan's typed-credential law (JP12: secrets never in argv/env/logs) and making builds unreviewable and unreproducible; B hides builder policy from code review entirely, so team graph policy drifts per machine. A has the right authority lattice but never states the binding verb, the flag law, or the explain surface, leaving `--builder ssh://...` holes open. The hybrid keeps A's intersection lattice, aligns with D-BUILDREMOTE1's separate cache/exec grants, restricts credentials to typed providers, and forbids flag-introduced endpoints.
decisions.story: Betty develops on macOS and sends a Linux ARM build to two workers. The graph policy belongs in source; private credentials and machine availability do not.
decisions.detail: One source-backed scheduling policy; secrets and physical endpoints remain local, scoped, and replaceable.

options.name: Source policy plus local credential binding
options.detail: Reviewable `build.remote` policy declares maximum/requested capability, trust, and fallback. Stricter user/org policy may refuse or narrow it; repositories cannot force remote use, choose credentials/trust roots, weaken sandbox/trust, or make fallback authoritative. Host config binds names to endpoints and scoped credentials.
options.code:
source: arm-ci requires .Release
host policy: allows arm-ci, local fallback denied
host credential binding: scoped pipe

options.name: User configuration only
options.detail: Builders, selection, trust, and fallback live outside repositories; source graphs name only platforms.
options.code: ~/.config/jet/builders: arm-ci=ssh://...

options.name: Per-command endpoints
options.detail: Every build supplies remote endpoints and credentials through flags; nothing persists in source.
options.code: jet build --builder ssh://arm-ci --fallback local

options.name: Source grant lattice, typed host bindings, no endpoint flags (hybrid)
options.detail: Reviewable `build.remote` declares requested/maximum capability, trust domain, and fallback; the effective grant is its intersection with stricter user/org policy, and remote cache and remote execution remain the separate grants D-BUILDREMOTE1 ratified — repositories can never force remote use, name endpoints, choose credentials or trust roots, or weaken sandbox. `jet remote bind/list/remove` manages the one host config mapping builder names to endpoints and typed credential providers (OS keychain or scoped pipe); secrets never enter URLs, argv, environment, logs, locks, or provenance. `--builder <name>` may only select among already-granted named builders — no flag or environment variable ever introduces an endpoint or credential. With no bindings every build is local and silent; an unreachable builder follows the effective fallback, and `jet explain build --lens remote` names the chosen builder, trust domain, fallback decision, and provenance.
options.code:
module build.remote { builders: [Builder.{ name: "arm-ci", platform: linux.arm64, trust: .Release }], fallback: .Local }
$ jet remote bind arm-ci ssh://build1.corp --credential keychain:jet/arm-ci
$ jet build --target aarch64-linux   # grant intersection selects arm-ci
$ jet explain build --lens remote    # builder, trust, fallback, provenance

comparisons.note: Builders are machine specifications in config/files.
Remote executor/cache endpoints are client configuration.

decisions.title: Store operation command family
decisions.gist: Choose how users access verify, repair, copy, import/export, sign, and closure queries.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A resurrects `jet store gc` against amended D-JPK-GC1 — `jet clean` is ratified as the one GC+optimize verb — and adds a second top-level store noun; C denies experts verify/repair/export entirely, contradicting JP19's parity-plus mandate. B is the right split but states no placement law, no destructive-op gating, and no import trust rule, so `hangar optimize` or a stray second home could sneak back in. The hybrid hardens B with an I8 placement law, plan-before-apply plus --json on mutations, quarantined verified imports, and an explicit optimize exclusion.
decisions.story: George sees a corrupt cache object and needs to verify, repair, copy it to an air-gapped machine, and explain its roots without learning a second low-level CLI.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet hangar verify
$ jet hangar repair package:foo
$ jet explain package:foo --lens why-live
$ jet clean   # only GC + optimize intent
decisions.detail: Preserves Jet's few-intents UX while giving experts full store control and keeping `jet clean` canonical.

options.name: Every operation under `jet store`
options.detail: Mirror the Nix command family with a new top-level store noun. Selecting this explicitly retires/amends D-JPK-GC1's sole `jet clean` intent; both verbs may not coexist as GC mechanisms.
options.code:
jet store verify
jet store repair foo
jet store gc

options.name: Hangar operations plus existing explain/clean intents
options.detail: Physical operations live under `jet hangar`; causal queries stay `jet explain`/`jet dossier`; `jet clean` remains the sole GC+optimize intent per D-JPK-GC1.
options.code:
jet hangar verify
jet hangar repair foo
jet hangar export foo
jet explain foo --lens closure
jet clean

options.name: No low-level public operations
options.detail: Only automatic verify/repair/copy exists; experts inspect internal files or JSON APIs.
options.code: jet build --repair

options.name: Hangar owns physical verbs; explain owns why; clean stays sole GC (hybrid)
options.detail: `jet hangar` owns exactly the physical object operations — verify, repair, copy, import, export, dump/restore, sign — while causal questions stay `jet explain`/`jet dossier` lenses and `jet clean` remains the sole GC+optimize intent per amended D-JPK-GC1; optimize never reappears under hangar. Placement law: a verb that mutates or moves physical objects lives under `jet hangar`, anything answering "why" is an explain lens, and a proposed operation fitting neither home is rejected with the existing path named (I8). Mutating hangar verbs use the ratified plan-before-apply UX and versioned `--json`; repair verifies from ordered caches then deterministic rebuild per JP4. Imported objects are digest- and signature-verified and quarantined before registration — no trust by location (Law 3).
options.code:
$ jet hangar verify                 # read-only report
$ jet hangar repair package:foo     # plan -> apply; caches, then rebuild
$ jet hangar export foo > foo.jetobj
$ jet hangar import foo.jetobj      # verify + quarantine before registration
$ jet explain package:foo --lens why-live
$ jet clean                         # sole GC + optimize intent (D-JPK-GC1)

comparisons.note: Exposes a broad `nix store` command family.
Porcelain commands hide most object-database plumbing but retain fsck/bundle.

decisions.title: Provider reference spellings for external ecosystems
decisions.gist: Choose how Maven, NuGet, Conan/vcpkg, Homebrew, OCI, and binary sources appear in Jet refs.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: B forks the ratified npm@/py@/cargo@ direct-root spelling (D-WD6, D-JPK-EXTPROV1) into a second generic prefix and weakens per-provider selector validation; C's mandatory alias ceremony breaks zero-ceremony single-file scripts (D-JPK-SCRIPTDEP1) and copy-paste discoverability. A is closest but leaves private-mirror/dependency-confusion mapping, version-shorthand consistency, and root-reservation governance unstated. The hybrid keeps A's lossless selector law and folds C's authority control into policy.providers source mapping without changing spellings, so beginners paste refs and experts pin authority in one reviewable place.
decisions.story: Doris imports a polyglot service with Maven, NuGet, Conan, Homebrew, and OCI dependencies. Every source must be explicit without inventing five dependency mechanisms.
decisions.detail: Direct roots are easiest to discover and teach; one internal model prevents semantic fragmentation.

options.name: Direct provider roots
options.detail: Each ecosystem gets a readable prefix under one dependency/action/lock model. Provider selectors remain lossless: version+revision, baseline+features, bottle digest+platform, OCI digest, or binary digest+platform. Unhashed mutable-only refs are rejected; digest-qualified URLs/tags are non-authoritative locators, while digest+platform is identity.
options.code:
maven@org.slf4j/slf4j-api#version=2.0.17
conan@openssl#version=3.5.0&revision=<rev>
vcpkg@openssl#baseline=<commit>&features=tls
oci@ghcr.io/acme/tool#sha256:<digest>
binary@https://acme/tool#sha256:<digest>&platform=linux.arm64

options.name: One generic registry prefix
options.detail: All external sources use `registry@kind/target`; fewer reserved roots, more repeated provider tags.
options.code: registry@maven/org.slf4j/slf4j-api#2.0.17

options.name: Named sources only
options.detail: Users define source aliases in workspace policy, then dependencies refer only to alias-qualified packages.
options.code:
sources: { java: Provider.maven(...) }
deps: { logging: java@org.slf4j/slf4j-api#2.0.17 }

options.name: Direct roots with policy-mapped authority and lossless selectors (hybrid)
options.detail: Each ecosystem keeps a readable direct root under the one dependency/action/lock model, matching ratified npm@/py@/cargo@ spellings (D-WD6, D-JPK-EXTPROV1); bare `#2.0.17` remains shorthand for `#version=` per D-JPK-SCRIPTDEP1. Selectors stay lossless — version+revision, baseline+features, bottle digest+platform, OCI digest, binary digest+platform; unhashed mutable-only refs are rejected, digest-qualified URLs/tags are non-authoritative locators, and digest+platform is identity. Every root binds a default authority in `policy.providers` (D-JPK-PROVIDERAUTH1), and a workspace may remap a root or namespace to a private mirror/source-map without changing dep spellings — NuGet-style anti-confusion mapping instead of alias indirection. Locks always record the canonical fully-qualified ref plus resolved source; new roots are reserved only by owner ballot.

comparisons.note: D-WD6 already ratifies federated providers under one authority graph.
Input types are encoded in URLs/registry entries.

decisions.title: Immutable registry transport and governance
decisions.gist: Choose the registry architecture for metadata, blobs, namespaces, yanks, mirrors, and recovery.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A retains pre-sparse crates.io pathologies — unbounded index growth, namespace authority by repo permission, no transactional publish, undetectable mirror equivocation — and cannot pass the plan's registry lane. B lacks any equivocation witness, so a compromised registry plus timestamp key serves split views invisibly; C fixes that but hard-couples to an unratified trust-root outcome and is silent on migration, offline checkpoints, mirror-failure behavior, and yank/version-reuse law. The hybrid states all of these: fail-closed mirror consistency, pinned checkpoints for offline, never-reused versions, lossless Git-index migration, and a clean degradation path across TRUSTROOT1 outcomes.
decisions.story: Hank and an attacker race to publish the same version while a mirror serves stale metadata. Consumers need one immutable winner, consistent history, and recoverable ownership.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet publish
+ source blob sha256:...
+ metadata snapshot 481
+ transparency checkpoint ...
registry: one immutable version committed
decisions.detail: Fast sparse resolution, offline threshold trust, and observable history prevent mirror/registry equivocation.

options.name: Keep Git JSONL index
options.detail: Metadata and history remain Git commits; artifact delivery is added beside it. Namespace control follows repository permissions.
options.code: git push registry-index

options.name: TUF-signed sparse HTTP registry
options.detail: Per-package sparse metadata plus content-addressed blobs, ETags, transactional publish, namespace authority, signed yanks, consistent snapshots, mirrors. Requires D-JPK-TRUSTROOT1 outcome B or C.
options.code:
GET /index/ac/me/acme
GET /blobs/sha256/...

options.name: Sparse registry plus append-only transparency
options.detail: Option B plus an append-only consistency log/checkpoints across mirrors and ownership events. Requires D-JPK-TRUSTROOT1 outcome C: TUF remains the offline trust root; transparency witnesses equivocation.
options.code:
snapshot: 481
log checkpoint: signed tree root
mirror consistency: proven

options.name: TUF sparse registry, transactional publish, witnessed transparency (hybrid)
options.detail: Per-package sparse TUF-signed metadata plus content-addressed blobs, with transactional publish yielding exactly one immutable winner; version numbers are never reused, and signed yanks stop new selection while exact locks still resolve. An append-only transparency log covers publishes, yanks, ownership transfer/recovery, and mirror checkpoints; clients verify inclusion when online, pin the last verified checkpoint into offline snapshots, and reject any mirror that cannot present a consistent checkpoint — never silently trust it. The existing Git JSONL index migrates losslessly into the log and leaves product paths. The wire format carries checkpoints from day one; full client witnessing requires D-JPK-TRUSTROOT1 outcome C, and under outcome B the log runs operator-side until C is adopted.
options.code:
$ jet publish
publish txn: snapshot 481 + blob sha256:... (atomic, one winner)
log: leaf 90412 under checkpoint sha256:... — inclusion proven
$ jet fetch --offline
snapshot 481 @ pinned checkpoint
mirror-b: checkpoint fork detected -> rejected (E12xx)

comparisons.note: Sparse registry fetches per-package metadata over HTTP.
Proxy and checksum database provide cached modules plus append-only consistency.

decisions.title: Package policy and exception source surface
decisions.gist: Choose where license, advisory, source, maturity, hook, cache, and exception policy lives.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option B makes policy ambient and invisible to review — the exact opposite of the one-diff requirement — and lets two machines resolve different worlds; C scatters exceptions across every dependency line with no conflict, expiry, or transitive law. A is directionally right but never anchors Policy to the already-ratified policy.trust/providers/replacements namespace, does not mandate exception scope/expiry, and leaves the explain surface vague. The hybrid unifies one policy namespace, mandates expiring package-edge exceptions that fail closed, and wires JP20's provenance-and-smallest-fix explain output.
decisions.story: Martha's team requires approved sources, mature releases, MIT/Apache licenses, fresh advisories, reviewed hooks, and one expiring CVE exception. Reviewers need one diff.
decisions.detail: One authority lattice: source request/max plus reviewed exceptions, intersected with stronger organization/host policy, with provenance for every effective rule.

options.name: Typed workspace policy plus CLI drafting
options.detail: Workspace source declares requested/max policy and source-reviewed exceptions. Organization/host policy may strengthen or refuse but never weaken it; source exceptions cannot override stronger policy. Effective policy is their auditable intersection. CLI commands only draft source edits; user config supplies credentials.
options.code:
$ jet policy draft exception CVE-... --expires 2026-08-01
+ module workspace { policy: Policy.{ ... } }

options.name: Global/user configuration
options.detail: Rules and exceptions live in user/organization config outside repositories; projects inherit ambient policy.
options.code: ~/.config/jet/policy.jet

options.name: Markers beside each dependency
options.detail: Every dependency carries inline license/source/freshness/hook exceptions for maximum locality.
options.code: foo: npm@foo#1.2 #AllowLicense("GPL-3.0") #AllowFresh

options.name: One policy namespace, drafted source diffs, expiring scoped exceptions (hybrid)
options.detail: All package policy — sources, licenses, advisories, maturity, hooks, cache roles, exceptions — lives in the one ratified `policy:` namespace of the workspace manifest beside `policy.trust`, `policy.providers`, and `policy.replacements` (D-JPK-GRANTSCHEMA1, D-JPK-PROVIDERAUTH1, D-JPK-REPLACEPOLICY1); no second config file and no inline dependency markers. Absent policy means the ratified safe defaults; effective policy is the auditable intersection of the source request/max with stronger org/host policy, which may refuse or narrow but never weaken, and source exceptions cannot override stronger policy. Every exception is a typed record with mandatory id, exact package-edge scope, reason, and expiry, and fails closed on expiry. `jet policy draft ...` only writes reviewable source diffs per the D-JPK-OVERLAY1 drafting pattern, and `jet explain <pkg> --lens policy` names the effective rule, its provenance layer, the evidence, and the smallest source fix per JP20.

comparisons.note: Constraints enforce repository-wide dependency policy.
Package source mapping binds package patterns to sources.

decisions.title: Binary-cache and mirror configuration surface
decisions.gist: Choose where cache order, trust roots, read/write scope, credentials, and private behavior are declared.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option C leaks keys through environment and argv — violating the plan's credential law — and makes cache order an unreproducible per-invocation accident; B strips repositories of any declarable trust posture, so CI and developers silently diverge. A is closest but states no precedence law among mirrors, no offline interaction, no write-grant linkage, and no beginner default. The hybrid adds the ordered-mirror verified-first-hit law, Law-3 verification regardless of source, --offline supremacy, separate write grants per D-BUILDREMOTE1/D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1, and a zero-config beginner path with pinned trust roots.
decisions.story: Frank uses a public read-only cache, an organization release cache, and his private developer cache. Repository policy may request acceptable roles, but stricter user/organization policy controls endpoints, credentials, and whether remote use is allowed.
decisions.detail: Source states a maximum/request; stricter host and organization policy owns secrets, endpoints, and final authority.

options.name: Source trust policy plus user endpoint bindings
options.detail: Canonical `module workspace { policy: Policy.{...} }` declares maximum/requested cache roles and trust. Stricter user/org policy may refuse or narrow it; repositories cannot force cache use, add trust roots, choose credentials, or weaken sandbox/trust. Host config binds names to endpoints and scoped keychain/provider pipes.
options.code:
module workspace { policy: Policy.{ cache_read_roles: ["release"] } }
# host config: release -> endpoint + credential pipe

options.name: User config only
options.detail: Every cache URL, priority, key, and write rule is machine-local; repositories cannot demand a trust posture.
options.code: ~/.config/jet/caches.toml

options.name: Environment variables and flags
options.detail: Cache URLs/keys/order are supplied per command or environment.
options.code: JET_CACHE=https://... jet build --cache-write

options.name: Role trust in one policy namespace, bound mirrors, verified-first-hit (hybrid)
options.detail: Workspace `policy:` declares requested/maximum cache roles and trust posture in the same single ratified policy namespace; stricter user/org policy may narrow or refuse, and repositories never name endpoints, keys, or credentials. `jet cache bind` manages the one host config mapping roles to ordered mirror endpoints and typed credential providers (OS keychain or scoped pipe); no environment variable or flag may introduce an endpoint or key, and secrets never enter URLs, argv, environment, logs, or locks. Read law: mirrors are tried in bound order, the first hit that verifies digest and signature against the role's trust roots wins regardless of location (Law 3), negative-cache hints stay mirror-local, misses fall back to source build, and `--offline` (D-JPK-OFFLINE1) beats everything. Writes require the separate D-BUILDREMOTE1/D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1 grant; zero-config beginners get the ratified default read set with pinned trust roots and never see cache jargon, and `jet explain <pkg> --lens cache` shows every decision.
options.code:
module workspace { policy: Policy.{ cache_read_roles: ["public", "release"], cache_write_role: "release" } }
$ jet cache bind release https://cache.corp.example --credential keychain:jet/release
$ jet build                                # ordered mirrors, verify, miss -> source build
$ jet explain package:foo --lens cache     # role, mirror, verification, fallback

comparisons.note: Substituters and trusted keys are nix.conf settings.
Build cache endpoints and push policy are configured separately.

decisions.title: Store endpoint interoperability scope
decisions.gist: Choose which native and Nix store endpoints Jetpack must speak.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A contradicts the plan's JP5 card, which already requires daemon/SSH/file/HTTP/S3 endpoints, and abandons real air-gap and builder workflows; C adopts Nix URI vocabulary as canon, violating Law 7 (compatibility is not canon). B has the right scope but is vague on write authority, credential handling, NAR fingerprint round-tripping, mirror ordering, and failure UX. The hybrid pins those down with typed capability records, dual identity for exact re-signing, D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1 write grants, typed credential providers, and deterministic mirror-to-source fallback.
decisions.story: Earl copies a locked closure among a laptop, an SSH builder, an air-gapped file cache, and S3-backed CI cache. One store abstraction should preserve integrity everywhere.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to builder-arm
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to file:///mnt/airgap
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to s3://release-cache/prefix
decisions.detail: Native design stays canonical while interoperability covers real Nix/cache/air-gap workflows.

options.name: Jetpack-native endpoints only
options.detail: Support local Hangar, native HTTP, and native remote executor; Nix caches only through NAR HTTP import.
options.code:
local://
https://jet-cache/...

options.name: Native plus Nix-compatible endpoint adapters
options.detail: Support local Hangar, native HTTP, SSH, file, S3-compatible cache, and Nix daemon/SSH/file/HTTP adapters. All lower to verified Jetpack object/closure APIs.
options.code:
hangar://local
ssh://builder
file:///cache
s3://bucket
ssh-ng://nix-host

options.name: Nix store URI semantics everywhere
options.detail: Adopt Nix store URL vocabulary/protocol as Jetpack's primary store abstraction.
options.code:
daemon
ssh-ng://host
https://cache.nixos.org

options.name: Native plus Nix adapters with typed capabilities and dual identity (hybrid)
options.detail: Support local Hangar, native HTTP cache, SSH, file, S3-compatible, and Nix daemon/SSH/file/HTTP adapters; every endpoint declares a typed capability record (read, write, remote-execute, trust domain, credential provider) and all transfers lower to verified Jetpack object/closure APIs — no trust by location. Objects crossing a Nix endpoint record dual identity — canonical Jetpack digest plus NarHash/signed fingerprint — so round-trips re-verify and re-sign exactly. Write access is a separate grant under D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1; credentials come only from typed providers and never enter URLs, argv, logs, or locks. Mirrors are ordered with deterministic fallback to source build; a capability gap fails with one E-code naming the endpoint, the missing capability, and the nearest supported path. Nix store URI spellings are accepted as endpoint addresses only, never as Jetpack's canonical vocabulary (Law 7).
options.code:
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to ssh-ng://nix-host
endpoint: nix-daemon adapter [read+write, trust: team]
verified: canonical digest + NarHash fingerprint
$ jet hangar copy package:foo --to s3://release-cache
E13xx: endpoint grant is read-only
fix: jet trust cache --write s3://release-cache

comparisons.note: Store backends include local, daemon, SSH, file, HTTP, and S3 binary caches.
CAS/remote execution normally use HTTP/gRPC services.

decisions.title: Dependency update and verification modes
decisions.gist: Choose how users request conservative, latest, lowest, and cross-platform resolution.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: C is expert-hostile and cannot satisfy the plan's binding lowest/latest resolver lane without manual constraint surgery. A and B are artificially siloed halves of one mechanism: A leaves CI matrices as unreviewable copy-pasted flags with no default-strategy or lock-mutation law; B buries the standard vocabulary behind mandatory policy ceremony. The hybrid merges them — fixed vocabulary with conservative default, optional source-declared profiles that can only bundle that vocabulary, non-mutating typed proof artifacts, and tested byte-stability of unrelated lock records.
decisions.story: Betty updates one HTTP library, then CI proves the workspace works at lowest-direct constraints and on Linux/macOS/Windows without rewriting unrelated locks.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet update http --strategy conservative
$ jet prove --lens dependencies --strategy lowest-direct --platform linux,macos,windows
lock: unrelated records unchanged
decisions.detail: Common default stays simple; explicit strategies make compatibility proof discoverable and reproducible.

options.name: Explicit update/verify strategies
options.detail: One resolver exposes conservative/default/latest/lowest/lowest-direct strategies. `jet update` may write the selected closure; the ratified `jet prove` umbrella evaluates dependency matrices without mutating the canonical lock unless asked.
options.code:
jet update http --strategy conservative
jet prove --lens dependencies --strategy lowest-direct

options.name: Source-defined resolution profiles
options.detail: Named strategies and platform matrices live only in workspace policy; commands select a profile.
options.code:
module workspace { policy: Policy.{ resolution_profiles: { oldest: ... } } }
jet prove --lens dependencies --profile oldest

options.name: Fixed policy only
options.detail: `jet update` is always conservative; CI users edit constraints to test latest/lowest manually.
options.code: jet update http

options.name: One strategy vocabulary, source profiles, non-mutating proof artifacts (hybrid)
options.detail: One resolver exposes the fixed vocabulary conservative/latest/lowest/lowest-direct; `jet update <pkg>` defaults to conservative and may move only the named subtree, writing strategy and command into lock rationale (D-JPK-CHANNEL1 intact; realize verbs never resolve). Workspace policy may declare named profiles that only bundle vocabulary strategies plus platform matrices, so CI runs are source-reviewable. `jet prove --lens dependencies` never mutates the canonical lock; it emits typed .jproof matrix artifacts per D-PROVE-REPLAY1. Byte-stability of unrelated lock records is a tested guarantee.
options.code:
$ jet update http                    # conservative: only http subtree moves; rationale logged
$ jet prove --lens dependencies --strategy lowest-direct --platform linux,macos,windows
proof: .jet/proofs/deps-lowest-direct.jproof
$ jet prove --lens dependencies --profile ci-floor   # profile declared in workspace.jet
lock: unrelated records byte-identical

comparisons.note: Supports highest, lowest, and lowest-direct resolution strategies.
Conservative updates limit changes around named gems.

decisions.title: Cache policy for unreproducible outputs
decisions.gist: Choose what happens when independent builders produce different bytes for one action.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A discards the divergent bytes teams need to debug the mismatch at all; option C is trust-by-annotation — a tag that policy engines will eventually ignore, blessing a single builder's bytes against Law 3. Option B has the right namespace split but never requires evidence retention, defines the consumer opt-in, propagates taint downstream, or states how a fixed package re-earns trust. The hybrid keeps B's visible split and adds diff+provenance retention, explicit opt-in with taint propagation, and rebuild-only promotion.
decisions.story: George's package embeds the wall clock. Two approved builders disagree. Jetpack must not bless either result as a trusted shared cache hit.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet prove --lens reproducibility package:foo
mismatch: bin/foo offset 0x2a1 (timestamp)
shared cache promotion: denied
decisions.detail: Debugging remains practical without letting non-deterministic bytes satisfy trusted policy.

options.name: Reject all caching
options.detail: Unreproducible outputs remain local build results and are never uploaded to any cache.
options.code: cache publish: denied

options.name: Separate visibly untrusted namespace
options.detail: Trusted shared namespaces reject them. An explicit private/untrusted namespace may store bytes for debugging, but can never satisfy trusted/release policy.
options.code:
cache write private/unreproducible: accepted
cache promote shared: denied

options.name: Allow trusted cache with metadata tag
options.detail: Store one result in the trusted namespace if metadata says reproducibility is not guaranteed.
options.code: shared cache: accepted, reproducible=false

options.name: Untrusted evidence namespace, taint propagation, rebuild-only promotion (hybrid)
options.detail: Trusted shared namespaces accept only outputs whose action satisfied reproducibility policy. Divergent results are preserved — both builders' bytes, both provenances, and the structured first-difference diff — in a visibly untrusted `private/unreproducible` namespace, so `jet prove --lens reproducibility` can name the first differing path and producer action. Untrusted objects never satisfy trusted or release policy and are fetched only with an explicit `--untrusted-namespace` opt-in that taints every downstream output as untrusted too. Promotion happens only by fresh independent rebuilds that agree after the fix — never by relabeling stored bytes — and every denial prints the differing path plus the fix hint.
options.code:
$ jet prove --lens reproducibility package:foo
mismatch: bin/foo offset 0x2a1 (timestamp) — builders b1,b2 disagree
stored: private/unreproducible (both results + diff + provenance)
shared promotion: denied — fix determinism, rebuild independently
$ jet build --untrusted-namespace   # expert: outputs tainted untrusted

comparisons.note: `guix challenge` compares substitute results with independent builds.
Provenance describes build process but does not make differing outputs reproducible.

decisions.title: Canonical full-stack Jet application model
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet composes its already-ratified HTTP, router, reactive UI, event, style, accessibility, and web-target mechanisms into one full-stack application.
decisions.explainer:
This decision does not reopen Router, JetDom, signals, typed views, styles, accessibility, or the JS/WASM backend. It chooses where application-wide client/server/render/data metadata lives. Every option keeps executable bodies in TIR, generated source re-enters the front end, and single-file rootless applications remain complete.

Fable hybrid review: Option A never states when or how the builder is evaluated, so dynamic registration (routes added in a loop over runtime config) would silently break every whole-app guarantee it promises — the exact failure mode of Next.js static analysis; B forfeits the first-class graph that explain, adapters, and security proofs need; C forfeits static checking entirely and turns route conflicts into runtime failures. The hybrid pins the evaluation law, keeps the sema-owned graph, adds a sound declared escape for dynamic composition, and states the hydration-mismatch and effect-boundary law the ballot detail demands but no option delivers.
decisions.story: Maya starts with one file and later splits the same product into routes, server actions, streaming pages, client islands, and deployment adapters. She needs one inspectable model from the first prototype through production, without learning a second framework language.
decisions.detail: The application graph may contain typed route, data, action, asset, render-boundary, and adapter facts, but never a second executable IR. Sema owns graph validation; function bodies remain executable TIR for AOT, dev, and web. The chosen model must show nested routing, SSR streaming, hydration mismatch behavior, client/server effect boundaries, asset splitting, adapter selection, generated-plan inspection, security defaults, and exact Jet diagnostics.

options.name: Sema-owned typed application graph
options.detail: Ordinary Jet builders compose existing Core mechanisms. Sema records and validates one typed application graph, enabling whole-app route/effect/security checks, SSR and client splits, code splitting, and exact explanations. Executable code stays in TIR; any generated source re-enters parser and sema.

options.name: Compile-time Core application plan
options.detail: A Core library evaluates the same builders at compile time and emits ordinary checked Jet source. The compiler knows only the resulting declarations and TIR, not a first-class application graph. This preserves a smaller compiler surface but weakens cross-route and adapter analysis.

options.name: Runtime-only typed composition
options.detail: Router, data loaders, rendering, and actions are ordinary runtime values. The compiler type-checks each call but has no application topology. This is simple and dynamic, but forfeits whole-app effect checks, static route conflicts, optimal splitting, and build-time deployment proof.

options.name: Static-eval builder graph in sema with declared dynamic mounts (hybrid)
options.detail: Sema evaluates the `fn app()` builder chain as statically evaluable composition over TIR and records the one typed application graph (A); a route, action, or adapter constructed from a runtime value outside a declared mount is a compile diagnostic with fixes, never a silently unanalyzed edge. `.mount(prefix, handler)` declares a typed dynamic subtree whose prefix, effects, and security policy remain static facts, so conflict, splitting, and effect checks stay sound. Client/server boundaries reuse the ratified Browser-effect partition and #Target ceilings; a server-only effect reachable from an island is a whole-graph diagnostic naming the path. Hydration mismatch is law: dev shows an overlay diagnostic with both server and client spans; release keeps server HTML and emits one structured core.log event. The graph is exposed via `jet expand --facts web` and `jet explain --web-graph` with stable `--json`; bodies remain executable TIR and generated source re-enters the front end (B's re-entry law).

comparisons.note: React Compiler and Server Components provide build-wide knowledge; Next integrates routing, server functions, streaming, and splitting. Jet should gain those benefits without a separate JSX or framework language.
comparisons.code: export default async function Page({ params }) { ... }

comparisons.note: Svelte compiles fine-grained reactivity while SvelteKit unifies routes, loading, actions, SSR, and adapters. Jet already has the component primitives; this ballot chooses the application-level owner.

decisions.title: Full-stack application authoring: explicit graph and optional conventions
decisions.gist: Choose how single-file and multi-file web applications author the application model selected by D-WEBAPP1.
decisions.explainer:
R9 requires a complete rootless single-file path. Conventions may remove repetition in larger projects only when they expand visibly into the exact explicit builder model. A builder/convention collision is always a compile diagnostic; there is no precedence rule or hidden winner.

Fable hybrid review: Option A's 'a package may opt into' never says where the opt-in lives, so directory presence becomes the activator — the Next.js footgun where any stray file in routes/ silently ships as a live endpoint; C's regeneration codemod is proven drift in every framework that tried it; B pays full wiring ceremony forever. The hybrid moves the opt-in into the builder itself — visible in the one inspectable place, single-file law intact — makes expansion exhaustive with a diagnosed disposition for every file, and keeps A's both-spans conflict law.
decisions.story: Noah wants `jet dev shop.jet` to work immediately. Six months later, his team wants predictable route files and layouts, while reviewers still need one command that shows exactly what the conventions generated.
decisions.detail: All options use ordinary Jet source and the application model selected by D-WEBAPP1. Generated or convention-expanded source and graph facts are inspectable. Every option must support explicit route/data/action/effect boundaries, single-file operation, deterministic conflicts, rename-safe tooling, and stable build output.

options.name: Explicit builder plus optional visible conventions
options.detail: A single file uses the builder directly. A package may opt into route/layout/data/action file conventions; those expand into the same graph and are shown by explain/LSP. If an explicit entry and a convention claim the same semantic slot, Jet rejects both with a conflict diagnostic and fixes; neither silently wins.

options.name: Explicit builder only
options.detail: Every route, layout, loader, action, island, and adapter is registered in ordinary Jet code. This is maximally explicit and rootless but repeats wiring in large applications and gives the IDE less conventional navigation structure.

options.name: One-shot scaffold emits an explicit builder
options.detail: No live conventions exist. `jet new web shop --emit-builder` creates ordinary route modules plus one explicit app builder. Users edit generated Jet afterward; regeneration is a reviewed codemod, never a hidden build input.
options.code:
$ jet new web shop --emit-builder
created shop/app.jet
created shop/routes/home.jet
// app.jet contains the complete editable web.app() builder

options.name: Conventions opted into inside the builder, exhaustively diagnosed (hybrid)
options.detail: The explicit builder is always the canonical model and a single file is complete (B); conventions exist only when the builder itself declares them with `.routes(from: "routes")`, so no directory presence, manifest field, or scaffold state ever activates routing invisibly. Expansion is deterministic and exhaustive: every `.jet` file under the declared root either maps to exactly one graph entry, is explicitly non-routed by a leading underscore, or is a compile diagnostic — a stray file can never become a deployed endpoint. Builder/convention collisions reject both registrations with both spans (A); `jet expand --facts web` and the LSP show every expanded entry with its source file, making renames graph-checked. `jet new web` scaffolds the builder with the `.routes(from:)` line already written (C's nothing-hidden-at-birth), never a regeneration codemod.

comparisons.note: File routing is highly productive but can hide precedence and generated topology. Option A keeps the productivity while making the expansion and conflicts explicit.
Explicit registration is easy to audit and works in one file. Option A preserves that complete path rather than requiring framework layout.

decisions.title: Canonical ownership of native scientific and accelerator computing
decisions.gist: Choose the public architectural owner for arrays, optimization, automatic differentiation, and accelerator execution without creating a second language runtime.
decisions.explainer:
This umbrella chooses product ownership only. It does not pre-ratify a Tensor type, placement policy, user kernels, autodiff rules, or backend behavior; the linked ballots decide those independently. All execution still lowers beneath executable TIR and obeys AOT/dev parity.

Fable hybrid review: A names one vocabulary but leaves the physical layer unspecified, so devices/buffers/kernels risk arriving as a bolt-on second model; B inverts the priority order by making the beginner path kernel-shaped; C forecloses the expert kernel reach the owner direction and D-COMPUTE-KERNEL1 require. The hybrid keeps A's single operation family and ratifies B's substrate as the expert tier of that same family, so I8 sees one mechanism with two entrypoints.
decisions.story: Priya starts with a small CPU calculation, scales it to a GPU, differentiates a loss, and later writes one specialized kernel. She wants one Jet vocabulary and one ownership model instead of switching among NumPy, JAX, CUDA, and deployment glue.
decisions.inWild:
use core.compute

scores :: compute.array(rows).matmul(weights).softmax()
trained :: compute.optimize(loss, model) ?? panic("optimization failed")
decisions.detail: The selected owner must compose existing lists, fixed arrays, View, Vec, Matrix, columnar data, SIMD, Gpu effects, and audited Unsafe regions. Internal graph or kernel forms are implementation stages beneath TIR, not public execution seams. Provider roots such as gpu.cuda remain explicit compatibility bridges, never the native canonical model.

options.name: One first-party compute operation family
options.detail: Core owns one public operation family spanning eager use, optimization, differentiation, and expert acceleration. Separate ballots define its types and policies. Libraries and bridges integrate through the same operations and semantic facts.
options.code:
y :: compute.array(x).matmul(w).relu()
// the same operation names survive eager execution, fusion, autodiff, and explicit device policy

options.name: Kernel-first native substrate
options.detail: Core owns portable kernels, devices, buffers, and scheduling. Arrays, autodiff, ML, and dataframes are first-party libraries built above that substrate rather than one Core operation family.
options.code:
kernel :: compute.kernel(map_relu) ?? panic("kernel is not portable")
y :: kernel.launch(input, output) ?? panic("kernel launch failed")

options.name: Array-graph compiler only
options.detail: Core owns typed array operations, fusion, and autodiff. Users cannot author native Jet kernels; specialized work uses generated operations or explicit foreign providers.
options.code: y :: tensor.graph((x) => x.matmul(w).relu()).run(input) ?? panic("compute failed")

options.name: One Core operation family layered on an expert substrate tier (hybrid)
options.detail: Core owns a single public core.compute operation family spanning eager use, fusion, differentiation, and placement; the same operation names and semantic facts survive every execution stage. Beneath it Core also owns the device/buffer/stream/kernel substrate, but that substrate is the expert tier of the same family — reached through compute.* builders under the existing ownership/effect/Unsafe law, never a second public execution model. Arrays, autodiff, ML, and dataframes integrate through the operation family; graph and kernel forms remain internal stages beneath executable TIR. Provider roots such as gpu.cuda stay explicit bridges that must differentially match native semantics, never the canonical model.

comparisons.note: NumPy established a compact array vocabulary; JAX adds transformation and accelerator compilation. Jet should preserve that ergonomic progression without tracer surprises or a Python host.
CUDA gives experts direct kernels, memory, streams, and profiling. Jet must preserve that reach behind its existing ownership/effect/Unsafe law.

decisions.title: Multidimensional compute type and existing collection relationship
decisions.gist: Choose how ranked, shaped, strided, mutable, and borrowed compute values relate to existing Jet lists, fixed arrays, View, Vec, Matrix, and columnar data.
decisions.explainer:
One type cannot erase ownership or shape facts, and two types cannot perform the same job under I8. Every option must handle compile-time and runtime dimensions, rank, mutation, non-contiguous views, broadcasting, and source compatibility with existing math/data code.

Fable hybrid review: B cannot state high-rank ownership, broadcasting, or accelerator layout coherently; C imports the PyTorch/JAX track/detach boundary — a beginner trap and an I8 hazard of two overlapping array types; A is right but its 'specializations/adapters' wording is vague enough to permit hidden copying seams between Matrix and Tensor. The hybrid pins Vec/Matrix to the ratified shared substrate (zero-copy by law), unifies host and device views under one alias/residency law, and makes autodiff a transform rather than a type.
decisions.story: Elena loads a runtime-sized image batch, slices a strided view, passes a fixed 4x4 transform to existing Matrix code, and sends the batch to an accelerator without copying by accident.
decisions.inWild:
pixels :: Tensor<Float>.from(rows).reshape([batch, height, width, 4]) ?? panic("bad image shape")
crop :: pixels.view([all, 8..72, 8..72, all])
decisions.detail: Static dimensions participate in sema shape checks; runtime dimensions produce typed fallible shape operations before execution. Mutable access obeys exclusive ownership, views carry lifetime/stride/alias facts, and device views retain the same law. Conversion that can allocate or copy is explicit and auditable.

options.name: Tensor owner with View borrows and math specializations
options.detail: Tensor<T> owns ranked multidimensional storage with optional static shape facts. View<T> is the borrowed strided projection. Existing Vec and Matrix become fixed-rank specializations/adapters with source-compatible operations. Lists and fixed arrays convert explicitly when rank/storage changes; columnar tables remain relational, not tensors.
options.code:
image :: Tensor<Float>.zeros([height, width, 4])
tile: View<Float> :: image.view([0..32, 0..32, all])
m: Matrix<4, 4> :: transform
mt :: Tensor.from_matrix(m)  // explicit representation conversion

options.name: Extend lists, fixed arrays, Vec, Matrix, and View only
options.detail: No Tensor type is added. Nested lists/fixed arrays express rank; Vec/Matrix keep static shapes; a generalized View carries runtime shape and strides. This minimizes types but makes high-rank ownership, broadcasting, and accelerator layout harder to state coherently.
options.code:
image: [[[Float]]] :: load_image()
batch :: View.from_nested(images) ?? panic("ragged image batch")
result :: batch.broadcast([n, h, w]) ?? panic("shape mismatch")

options.name: NDArray storage plus differentiable Tensor values
options.detail: NDArray owns general numeric storage, shape, strides, and mutation. Tensor is a distinct immutable value only when computation history/gradients are required; it wraps or views an NDArray with explicit conversion. The jobs are non-overlapping but users cross a boundary when enabling autodiff.
options.code:
x: NDArray<Float> :: NDArray.zeros([batch, 784])
tracked: Tensor<Float> :: Tensor.track(x.view())
plain: NDArray<Float> :: tracked.detach()

options.name: One Tensor owner with unified View and zero-copy math aliases (hybrid)
options.detail: Tensor<T> is the single owner of ranked multidimensional storage with optional static shape facts checked in sema; runtime shapes go through typed fallible operations before execution. View<T> (D-DYNARRAY1) is the one borrowed strided projection for host and device memory alike, carrying identical lifetime/stride/alias/residency facts under the existing exclusive-mutation law. Vec<N> and Matrix<M,N> remain fixed-shape forms over the same substrate (D-MATHLIB1, #293), so passing them to tensor operations is zero-copy and adapter-free; only rank- or layout-changing conversions exist, each explicitly named and flagged as allocating in plan and dossier output. Differentiability is a property of the compute.grad transform, never a second type — no track/detach seam exists — and columnar tables stay relational with an explicit, audited to_tensor.
options.code:
image :: Tensor<Float>.zeros([height, width, 4])
tile: View<Float> :: image.view([0..32, 0..32, all])
m: Matrix<4, 4> :: transform
y :: tile.matmul(m)   // zero-copy: Matrix shares the substrate
flat :: image.reshape([height * width, 4]) ?? panic("bad shape")  // named, auditable when it copies

comparisons.note: Separate dynamic ndarray and statically-shaped math types preserve useful facts but create conversion seams. Jet needs an explicit law for that seam.
One Tensor carries shape, device, strides, mutation rules, and optional gradients. It is ergonomic but many failures remain runtime-only; Jet can move static facts into sema.

decisions.title: Compute placement, transfer visibility, effects, and fallback
decisions.gist: Choose when Jet selects CPU or accelerator execution and how experts audit placement, transfers, missing backends, and fallback.
decisions.explainer:
Placement never changes language semantics. Static effect inference is mandatory: any execution policy allowed to choose a GPU carries the existing Gpu effect; a CPU-pinned operation remains pure when its operations are pure. Copies and fallbacks must appear in the plan and trace.

Fable hybrid review: B hands beginners a CUDA-shaped surface; C makes #(Gpu) inference depend on an external policy file, breaking local reasoning about effects; A is the right core but omits the deployment layer services need and understates receipt stability for CI. The hybrid keeps A's call-site law, admits C's policy strictly as a narrowing overlay so effect inference stays sound, and makes every transfer and fallback a stable, diffable receipt.
decisions.story: Sam wants a notebook to use the best available device automatically, a service to require one exact GPU class, and CI to prove that no hidden CPU fallback or host-device copy changed the result or budget.
decisions.detail: The selected policy must cover allocation limits, transfer lifetime, backend absence, remote devices, multi-device placement, deterministic/reproducible profiles, cache identity, and stable audit output. A fallback may vary capability or performance only within an explicit policy; it never silently changes precision, effects, failure, or observable results.
