decisions.title: Does the board refuse rule-breaking writes, or only report them?
decisions.gist: Pick how hard Tower enforces the working rules (done-gates, ballot completeness, owner-only actions).
decisions.explainer: The repeat offenders are agents, not you. C binds them at write time — prose rules become mechanical — while your phone workflow stays one tap. A ties your hands; B is today with extra steps.
decisions.story: An agent finishes step 2 of 5 on a card, marks it done, and moves on — the remaining steps evaporate until someone notices weeks later. Another agent files your acceptance verdict as a log note where you never see it again. Today every one of these writes succeeds, because the rules live in prose the agent may never have loaded. You have had to repeat these rules angrily more than once; this ballot decides whether the board itself starts saying no.
decisions.inWild:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by helper-agent
updated card #412 -> done        # 3 of 5 checklist items still open

$ tower decision add --title 'Cache strategy' --by helper-agent
added decision D-CACHE1          # no gist, no story, no options — reaches your queue empty

$ tower card activate '#413' --by helper-agent
activated #413                   # an owner-only action, performed by an agent

options.name: Hard gates for everyone
options.detail: The store refuses rule-breaking writes no matter who writes: done requires a complete checklist, ballots must be ballot-ready to enter the queue, ratify/activate demand owner attribution, frozen cards are read-only. Maximum consistency — but it also stops you: closing a card from your phone means ticking every box first, and there is no override when you just want something gone.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by owner
E_GATE: 3 checklist items unchecked — no done until complete (no override)

options.name: Lint-only, never refuse
options.detail: All writes keep succeeding; a `tower lint` sweep (run by agents, shown on the board) reports violations: done-with-open-checklist, empty ballots, mis-attributed ratifies. Zero friction — and zero protection at the moment of the write. A weak model that never runs lint recreates today exactly.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by helper-agent
updated card #412 -> done
$ tower lint
WARN #412 done with 3 unchecked items (by helper-agent)
WARN D-CACHE1 not ballot-ready: gist/story/options empty

options.name: Agent-hard, owner-soft
options.detail: Writes with --by other than owner hit hard gates: done-gate on checklists, ballot-ready validation (a --draft flag keeps drafts out of your queue), owner-only ratify/activate unless the agent quotes you explicitly (recorded in the event log), no writes to frozen/owner-lane cards, release of a building card requires a handoff note. Your own writes bypass everything. The rules bind exactly the population that keeps breaking them.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by helper-agent
E_GATE: 3 checklist items unchecked — complete them or --release --handoff "..."

$ tower decision ratify D-CACHE1 --outcome B --by helper-agent
E_OWNER: ratify is owner-only — use --on-behalf-of-owner "<owner's words>"

$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by owner
updated card #412 -> done        # owner bypass, no ceremony

comparisons.note: Branch protection blocks contributors while admins may bypass — the standard shape for solo-owner + helpers.
comparisons.code:
Require status checks: on
Include administrators: off

comparisons.note: Hooks enforce by default with an explicit, visible escape.
The compiler refuses at the moment of the mistake instead of reporting it later — the reason the invariant holds in practice.

decisions.title: Where ratified decisions and done cards go to rest
decisions.gist: Whether finished board history stays inside tower.json or moves to a separate archive file, and what triggers the move.
decisions.explainer: A keeps you in control of when history moves (matching how you already close out epochs), keeps one mental model (tower.json = the board), and shrinks writes, backups, git churn, and phone payload all at once. B is the same end-state but moves things the instant they close — done cards vanish from the Board's Done lists into a second file mid-session. C treats the symptom (transport) and leaves the file growing forever.
decisions.story: Nate opens Tower on his phone after a ballot session. The board file is 4.2 MB, and 68% of it is history: 496 already-ratified decisions (1.7 MB) and 305 done cards (1.1 MB). Every single write — even a one-line log entry — rewrites all 4.2 MB, snapshots another 4.2 MB backup (backups/ is at 82 MB), pushes the full state over the live stream to his phone, and lands another multi-megabyte version of tower.json in git (356 versions and counting). The live working set he actually looks at is about 0.4 MB.
decisions.inWild:
$ du -h .tower/tower.json
4.2M    .tower/tower.json

$ tower state | jq '.decisions | length'
496        # every one already ratified — zero open

$ tower state | jq '[.cards[] | select(.phase=="done")] | length'
305        # of 434 cards total

$ du -h .tower/backups
82M     .tower/backups    # 20 rolling copies of the full file

$ git log --oneline -- .tower/tower.json | wc -l
356        # full-file versions in repo history
decisions.detail: Q: Does archiving lose anything?  A: No — archived items stay on disk in .tower/, stay in git, and stay greppable; they just leave the hot file. Q: Can an archived decision be reopened?  A: Yes, via an explicit restore that moves it back into tower.json first. Q: What about the docs? Ballot text for ratified syntax already lives durably in docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md; the archive is the raw record.

options.name: Explicit archive command, epoch-aligned
options.detail: New `tower archive` verb moves ratified decisions, done cards (with their questions), and events older than 30 days into .tower/archive/<epoch>.json — one file per epoch, append-only, committed to git. Run it by hand or let closing an epoch run it automatically. `tower archive list/show/restore <id>` reads it back; `tower card show` on an archived card still works (reads the archive transparently). The owner decides when history moves; nothing disappears on its own.
options.code:
$ tower archive run --by owner
archived: 496 decisions, 291 done cards, 1712 events → .tower/archive/e1.json … e6.json
tower.json: 4.2M → 0.5M

$ tower archive show D-MEM1
D-MEM1  ratified 2026-07-03 → A  (archive/e5.json)

$ tower archive restore '#188' --by owner
restored card #188 (+2 decisions) into the live board

options.name: Auto-retire on close (split live/history files)
options.detail: No command to remember: the moment a decision is ratified or a card verified done, the store writes it to .tower/history.json (append-only ledger) and drops it from tower.json on the next write. tower.json permanently contains only live work. The Board's 'Done' subgroups render from the ledger lazily. Reopen = automatic restore. History is never more than one write behind; the hot file never grows again.
options.code:
$ tower decision ratify D-X1 --outcome A --by owner
ratified D-X1 → A   (retired to history.json)

$ du -h .tower/tower.json .tower/history.json
0.4M    .tower/tower.json     # only live work, forever
5.8M    .tower/history.json   # append-only, grows cold

$ tower card show '#42'        # a done card
#42  done  (from history)  …full card, log intact…

options.name: Keep one file; slim what moves
options.detail: tower.json stays the single complete record. Instead, stop moving the whole file around: SSE frames send only diffs, backups are gzipped (4.2 MB → ~0.4 MB each), and the UI loads done cards/ratified decisions on demand. Git history still carries the full file, and every write still rewrites 4.2 MB locally, but network, phone, and backup weight drop to near-live-set size.
options.code:
$ du -h .tower/backups
8.1M    .tower/backups        # 20 gzipped snapshots

# SSE frame after a log entry (diff, not full state):
data: {"rev":2482,"patch":[{"op":"add","path":"/cards/12/log/0",
       "value":{"at":"2026-07-10","by":"claude-main","text":"started"}}]}

$ du -h .tower/tower.json
4.2M    .tower/tower.json     # unchanged, keeps growing

comparisons.note: Completed issues auto-archive after a configurable window; they leave every view but stay searchable and restorable. Nobody scrolls past them again.
comparisons.code: Settings → Projects → Auto-archive completed issues: after 1 month

comparisons.note: Same shape as loose objects vs packfiles: the hot working set stays small, history compacts into cold files that are still fully readable.

decisions.comment: But enforce stricter "done" testing & keep a buffer of decisions made pre ratification so I can walk them back before ratification if needed

decisions.title: How an agent gets its marching orders from Tower
decisions.gist: Whether starting work on a card takes one command that returns everything, a generated brief file, or native harness tools.
decisions.explainer: A collapses the error-prone five-step ritual into one call that cannot omit the ratification comment or an open question, and it works identically for Claude, codex, and bare scripts. B helps only harnesses with auto-load; C is a strong later layer on top of A (same packet, typed transport).
decisions.story: A fresh Claude session is told 'work the board'. Today it runs five commands (status, next, card show, decision list, question list), re-reads the skill doc to remember the phase rules, and only then starts. Every extra step is a place a sub-agent skips something — the cards that bounced usually bounced because the agent never saw a ratification comment or an open question sitting right on the card.
decisions.inWild:
# today: five reads before any work happens
$ tower status
$ tower next --epoch e3
$ tower card show '#412'
$ tower decision list --card '#412' --json
$ tower question list --open
# …and the ratification comment on D-X1 is 40 lines deep in JSON
# the agent never printed
decisions.detail: Q: Does this change what the owner does? A: No — pure agent surface. Q: Does it replace the skill doc? A: The rules footer travels with the packet, so a sub-agent that only ever sees the packet still knows the phase-honesty rules.

options.name: One-shot work packet: `tower brief`
options.detail: One command claims the next card (or a named one) and prints the complete packet: card body + plan, every linked decision with outcome AND the owner's ratification comment, open questions, blockers, related doc paths found in the body, and a 5-line rules footer (phase honesty, --by, expect-rev). --json for machines. A sub-agent brief becomes literally `tower brief '#412' --agent jet-impl-1`.
options.code:
$ tower brief --agent claude-main
━ #412 P1 building — Computed module fields (e3, m-comptime)
  plan: 1. parser field-expr 2. sema eval gate 3. golden
  decisions:
    D-CTMARKER1 = C  «comptime { } block + $ splice»
    owner comment: "C, but the block must nest — see my note"
  open questions: q88 [owner] "does this break pack.jet imports?"
  blocked by: —
  docs: docs/plans/epoch-5/unified-ecosystem.md
  rules: log every advance --by claude-main · verify≠builder ·
         done only after full suite green

options.name: Rendered brief file the harness auto-loads
options.detail: `tower serve` (or a githook) keeps .tower/BRIEF.md rendered with the current agent-lane queue and per-card packets. Harnesses that auto-load context files (CLAUDE.md include, AGENTS.md pointer) pull it in for free — zero commands at session start. The file is a read-only view; writes still go through the CLI.
options.code:
$ head .tower/BRIEF.md
# Tower brief — rev 2481 (auto-generated, read-only)
## Next up
1. #412 building — Computed module fields
   decisions: D-CTMARKER1=C ("C, but the block must nest…")
   open: q88 "does this break pack.jet imports?"
2. #405 verify — REPL Ctrl-C exit

# CLAUDE.md gains one line:
@.tower/BRIEF.md

options.name: Native tools: Tower as an MCP server
options.detail: `tower serve --mcp` exposes tower_next / tower_brief / tower_update / tower_ballot as typed tools. Claude and other MCP harnesses call the board without shelling out (no nix wrapper, no JSON quoting), and every write is schema-validated at the tool boundary. Shell CLI remains for humans and scripts.
options.code:
// agent-side tool call, no shell involved
tower_brief({ agent: "claude-main" })
→ { card: "#412", phase: "building",
    decisions: [{ id: "D-CTMARKER1", outcome: "C",
                  comment: "C, but the block must nest — see my note" }],
    questions: [{ id: "q88", text: "does this break pack.jet imports?" }],
    rules: ["log advances --by", "verify≠builder", "suite green before done"] }

comparisons.note: `gh issue view` prints the issue, labels, comments, and linked PRs in one call — the packet pattern, and the reason agents drive GitHub well.

decisions.title: Exit criteria live on the card and gate 'done'
decisions.gist: How a card proves it is finished: a checklist the CLI enforces, an acceptance ballot for you, or both for flagged cards.
decisions.explainer: C gives every card a mechanical floor (no more done-by-assertion) and reserves your time for the cards where your eye is the acceptance test — which is exactly where the bounces have happened. A alone leaves your verdicts informal; B alone makes you the bottleneck on all 400+ cards.
decisions.story: The frontend cards bounced twice because 'done' was claimed from the builder's own summary — no feature-by-feature evidence against the full mock, no independent check, and your acceptance verdict ended up in a card log where no process saw it. Today a card's exit criteria live in prose (body, plan, or nowhere), so nothing mechanical stops verify→done while half the list is unmet.
decisions.inWild:
# card #360, bounce round 2 — the criteria existed only as prose:
$ tower card show '#360' | jq -r .body | tail -3
Done requires feature-by-feature matrix vs FULL hybrid.html
with owner comments, verified in the owner's real terminal.

$ tower card update '#360' --phase done --by builder-agent
updated card #360 → done      # nothing checked any of that
decisions.detail: Q: Who writes the criteria? A: The planning agent, when the plan is written; you can add/edit items from the card modal. Q: Does this add owner work? A: Only where you opt a card in — everything else is agent-side enforcement.

options.name: Machine-checked criteria list
options.detail: Cards get a criteria[] field: numbered items, each open → met (builder) → verified (a different agent, recorded). `--phase done` is rejected while any item is unverified, and the verifier must differ from the assignee. The card modal shows the checklist with per-item state.
options.code:
$ tower card criteria '#360' --add "matrix vs full hybrid.html, per feature" --by planner
$ tower card update '#360' --phase done --by builder-agent
tower: E_CRITERIA — 2 of 5 criteria unverified (3,5); verifier must not be the builder

$ tower card verify '#360' --meet 3 --evidence "pty run + screenshot, all 14 features" --by jet-verify
$ tower card update '#360' --phase done --by jet-verify
updated card #360 → done

options.name: Acceptance ballot on every close
options.detail: Closing any card auto-mints a one-option-per-verdict acceptance ballot for you (accept / bounce with comment), with the evidence summary as the ballot body. Done = you ratify. Your verdicts become durable decisions instead of log lines — but every card now waits on you.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#360' --phase verify --by jet-verify
minted D-ACCEPT-360: "Accept #360?"  → your Now queue

# your phone, focus mode:
D-ACCEPT-360  Accept #360 — frontend matrix
  evidence: 14/14 features vs hybrid.html, terminal transcript attached
  [A] Accept   [B] Bounce (comment required)

options.name: A + acceptance ballot only where flagged
options.detail: Criteria list enforced everywhere (option A), and cards you flag with needs-acceptance additionally mint the acceptance ballot on close — owner-facing surfaces get your verdict as a ballot, plumbing cards close on verified criteria alone. Matches how you already ruled that sign-off verdicts must be ballots, without putting all 400 cards through your queue.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#360' --needs-acceptance --by owner   # once, at greenlight
…builder meets criteria, verifier verifies…
$ tower card update '#360' --phase done --by jet-verify
minted D-ACCEPT-360 → your Now queue    # flagged card

$ tower card update '#405' --phase done --by jet-verify
updated card #405 → done                # unflagged: criteria were enough

comparisons.note: Required reviews + status checks: merges are blocked mechanically, and review-by-author is impossible. The branch protection model, applied to cards.
comparisons.code: Settings → Branches → Require review from someone other than the author

decisions.title: Board view rebuilt for a 434-card project
decisions.gist: What the Board tab becomes now that Agents is gone: a progress roadmap, a dense worklist table, or a search-first spotlight.
decisions.explainer: Your two Board jobs are progress-scan and planning passes; A makes the first instant (burndown per epoch/milestone, computed from the event log Tower already keeps) and keeps active cards one glance deep. B optimizes bulk re-ordering you do rarely; C optimizes find, which ⌘K already covers.
decisions.story: Nate opens Board to answer one question — 'where is epoch 3 actually at, and what is moving?' — and gets a wall of collapsible accordions: 8 epochs, hundreds of tiles, Done subgroups he has to expand one by one. On the phone it is minutes of scrolling. The two things he does here (scan progress, find one card) are both slow, and neither shows burndown over time.
decisions.inWild:
# what the board holds today
$ tower status
  TOWER · Jet · epoch e3 · rev 2481
  cards: 434 total — 129 active, 305 done
  epochs: 8, milestones: 2

# owner's actual questions, unanswered by the current view:
#  - is e3 burning down or stalled this week?
#  - which milestone is at risk?
#  - what did agents move today?
decisions.detail: Q: Does Now change? A: No — Now stays the decide/greenlight queue; this ballot is only the Board tab. Q: Do card modals change? A: No. All three options keep ⌘K and the card modal exactly as they are.

options.name: Roadmap ledger — progress is the page
options.detail: Board becomes a vertical roadmap: one row per epoch with a burndown sparkline (done/total over the last 30 days, computed from events), milestone bars underneath, and only ACTIVE cards shown inline, grouped by lane. Done and frozen live on a per-epoch 'ledger' page one tap away. The page answers 'how is it going' before you scroll.
options.code:
BOARD
  E3 syntax core          ████████████░░░  118/141 · ▂▃▅▆▇ this week +9
    m: memory-v5 ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░ 7/9      m: comptime ▓▓░░ 2/6 ⚠ stalled 6d
    building(3)  #412 computed modules [claude-main]  …

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

C (a defer keyword) adds a second cleanup mechanism plus the Go leak-by-omission bug class S63 was chosen to avoid; its only unique win is errdefer-style partial rollback, not yet proven. B doesn't foreclose C — add the keyword later on evidence. defer (C) stays declined (D-SUGAR5); user-definable Drop remains the long-term roadmap item.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

questions.text: I'm leaning towards A, but how is bloat/buildup addressed? For large codebases, how will users be able to avoid 3k lines of code that are just migrations?

So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?

The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.answer: Two things were colliding on the brackets. `[Particle]` is Jet's *list type* ("a list of Particle"), NOT a generic parameter — generics stay `<T>` and are untouched by this card. The old gist's `columnar [T]` just meant "the keyword in front of a list type," where T was the element. So the real question is the *spelling* of the per-container form, and yes — a generic-style `Columnar<Particle>` is now a real option (B) alongside the prefix keyword `columnar [Particle]` (A). The difference: A reads as a storage modifier on the same list type (no new type, same API, just a layout hint), while B (`<T>`-style) makes layout part of the type identity — `Columnar<Particle>` becomes a distinct container needing conversions and its own impls/trait bounds, like `Map<K,V>`. Recommendation stays A: a layout is how a value is *stored*, not a type parameter, and the prefix keyword keeps one word (`columnar`) across both the struct attribute and the per-use form. `<T>`-style is available as B if you'd rather layout live in the type system. questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.

Brought every line to current ratified syntax: (1) marker sigil @ -> # in derive-bracket form, so a user derive reads #[Wire] exactly like the built-in #[Codable] (D-ATTR1 reversed @->#; D-ATTR2 bracket form for trait-attaching markers); (2) dotless struct literal Packet{...} -> Packet.{ ... } (D-DOTCTOR2=A); (3) Bytes / b"hi" (neither exists) -> [U8] + byte-array literal [0x68,0x69], matching embed_bytes/sized-int examples; (4) splices made bare-identifier $name via local bindings ($fname/$tn) to respect the ratified D-CTMARKER1=C grammar (no $f.name expression-splice to invent); (5) buf: Buffer -> buf: edit Buffer (D-CAP3 capability-on-type, since the encoder mutates the buffer); sibling card D-METAREFLECT1 brought to the same sigil (#[Row]/#[Skip], has_marker("Skip")). Best-in-class examples: the 'Other languages' block now shows the two canonical author-side derive systems in full — Rust proc-macro derive returning a quote! TokenStream the compiler re-parses, and Swift @attached(extension) macros returning SwiftSyntax source the compiler re-checks — and notes both emit re-checked SOURCE (never a pre-validated tree), which is precisely the recommended Option A and why errors pin at the user's tag. Added Owner Q1 flagging the one genuinely-open sub-spelling (emit-template quoting: reuse "..."/"""...""" with {}-interpolation off inside emit, vs a distinct code-quote). Rec stays A. questions.text: What is the interplay with out idea for switft style unified protocol for both server & client to prevent drift?
questions.answer: The Swift insight is the `Responder` (or `Handler`) protocol pattern used by Vapor/Hummingbird/NIO: a single trait `trait Handler { fn handle(req: Request) -> Response }` becomes the composition unit for both the server's routing stack and the client's interceptor stack. Because both sides speak the same `Request`/`Response` types, they can never drift — any middleware that works on the server (auth, logging, retry) is structurally identical to a client-side interceptor. The plan for c164 already captures this: D-HTTPLIB2=B (split client/server modules) shares core types, and D-HTTPLIB1=A (function-first mux) is the routing side. The missing piece to make it Swift-unified is an explicit `Handler` trait in `core.http` that both the client and server implement. Concretely: the client IS a handler (wraps the network connection); the mux IS a handler (dispatches to route handlers); middleware wraps one handler with another. Testing then becomes free — inject a `MockHandler` anywhere in the chain. This should be a first-class design constraint in the c164 plan, not a separate decision. Agents writing the HTTP library plan should define `core.http.Handler` as the primary abstraction before splitting into client vs. server API docs.

questions.text: What is the best of both worlds approach here? We are trying to provide best in class service & support for any use case, not just some.
questions.answer: Best of both worlds for async is M:N green threads (Option A) — here's why it delivers everything: (1) No function coloring. Beginners write `task { do_io() }` and experts write the same thing. There is no async/non-async split to manage. Go demonstrates this at Internet scale. Java added Project Loom (virtual threads) specifically because async/await (Option B) proved inadequate — the industry has already run this experiment. (2) High concurrency for free. An M:N scheduler parks threads on IO waits and runs other tasks, achieving 100k+ connections without any new syntax. (3) Expert control is still available: task handles give you priorities, pinning, cancellation, monitoring. Channels give you explicit synchronization. These are the expert levers, just not a second concurrency MODEL. Why not Option C (hybrid M:N + @async)? I8: having two yielding mechanisms (green-thread park and @async fn future) is two ways to write concurrent code. Teams standardize on one and the other becomes dead weight or, worse, they mix and no one can read the code. The apparent limitation of Option A — 'I can't explicitly control when I yield' — is the Go objection, and Go's answer is: you don't need to. Task/channel primitives cover all real expert needs. Recommendation: Option A. It IS the best of both — simplicity without sacrificing power.

questions.text: Give me the tradeoffs, limitations, and benefits that we would get from having both A & B as the selected option
questions.answer: Having both A ($ splice source fragments) and B (typed AST builder API) simultaneously: BENEFITS — (1) $ splice covers quick, copy-modify derives (easy to read, errors in Jet source terms); (2) AST builder covers programmatic generation without string concatenation or escaping; (3) users can pick the right tool for their derive's complexity. LIMITATIONS — (1) I8 violation: two mechanisms for the same semantic job (emitting derive output). Real codebases will use both; code review becomes harder. (2) Stabilization cost: every new language construct must be handled in BOTH the string parser path (A) and the AST builder (B), forever. Miss one and the two systems diverge. (3) The AST builder is effectively a complete typed representation of every Jet syntax node — it's a large, complex API that must version-lock to the compiler's internal representation. (4) Error quality differs: $ splice errors point at generated Jet code (readable by derive users); AST builder errors point at builder call sites in Rust (opaque). VERDICT: the costs outweigh the benefits. Teams will converge on one; having both means maintaining two. Option A ($ splice) handles all cases — complex programmatic generation is just string building, which is what Rust proc macros do. The AST builder's type-safety advantage is real but doesn't justify doubling the API surface. Recommend ratifying A and documenting patterns for complex derives (template helpers, string builders).

questions.text: Give me other syntax options that read a little better, i am potentially ok with A but want multiple options, can have more than 3
questions.answer: Updated D-IGNORERET2 with six options. Best revised rec: `.ignore("reason")`. It reads better than `!_`, is attached to the value being dropped, and creates an audit trail. Devil’s advocate: method shape can look ordinary. Patch: sema treats it as a blessed escape, requires a non-empty literal reason, emits a lint with the dropped type, and refuses user-defined `.ignore` on `#MustUse` results.

questions.text: What are the tradeoffs of option B instead of c? What is lost by going with b over c?
questions.answer: B vs C for refinements: B gives construction-checked refined values, literal checks, and flow narrowing. It does not prove arbitrary arithmetic or quantified facts. C can prove `a + b` remains PositiveInt, prove indexing is in bounds, eliminate runtime checks, and verify function postconditions over all inputs. What is lost with B: proof-preserving arithmetic, universal proofs, cross-function theorem reasoning, and check elision based on proofs. What B keeps: the most common product value, one constructor path, no solver dependency, deterministic compile times, and beginner-friendly diagnostics. Best sequencing: ship B as the surface and invariant discipline; let future C reuse those predicates if a solver/prover tier is owner-approved.

questions.text: We must ensure full expert control & auditability. We want magic out of the box for beginners but experts need to be able to see the inner workings & control as needed. Reconsider this ballot with devils advocate, make it best in the world, ensure ergonomics, magic, and full control are all considered. Tell my why your new option set is best, why you recommend your new recommendation, and how it compares to other languages
questions.answer: Updated D-WASM1. New rec: C, not pure inference. Default is inferred from effects and browser API use, but experts can pin `#Wasm`, `#Js`, and `#WasmExport`, then inspect `jet build --target web --explain-partition`. Devil’s advocate: overrides can create unsound crossings. Patch: sema checks all boundary types/effects, rejects browser handles in WASM, emits a bridge manifest, and snapshots boundary diagnostics. Compared to Next/SvelteKit: similar magic boundary inference, stronger typed bridge/audit story. Compared to Rust wasm-bindgen: less manual glue, more front-end-owned diagnostics.

questions.text: Why A not B? Is there a reason not to use B? it seems like it may be helpful to sometimes have the module level declaration
questions.answer: Reason for A over pure B: required module declarations make every beginner learn partitioning before rendering a page. But the module-level control is useful, so I folded it into A: default partitioning comes from `Browser` effect inference, and experts can add `#Target(Wasm)` / `#Target(Js)` at module level with sema validation. D-WASM1 now reflects that hybrid.

questions.text: I don’t understand what this means, dumb it down to plain language
questions.answer:
Plain version. Today your build script can look at one type at a time (to derive things). This ballot asks: may the build script also READ the finished, fully-checked program — every package, type, and function — and report its own errors?

Concrete use: your team rule is "every public function that touches the network must take a timeout". Today that rule lives on a wiki or an external linter that half-parses Jet and drifts. With B, your build entry can loop over all functions and emit a real Jet diagnostic — same format as compiler errors, and the API forces you to fill in code + what/why/fix, so quality stays I4-grade.

Hard limits that keep it safe: READ ONLY (build code cannot change your program, ever — that is rung C, still frozen); runs only from YOUR chosen build entry, never when merely importing a library (a dependency cannot run rules or code inside your build); and if you don't write one, nothing changes.

B = "the compiler will show your program to your build script and let it complain, nothing more."

questions.text: I want an exceptional and modern out of the box experience, with things like new tools that were rewritten in rust or modernized installed by default, like ripgrep, bat, eza, etc  but no "bloating". We should have the bare minimum required for this to function out of the box on the minimal install, but have a solid beginner friendly batteries included for the graphical version. Both should be baseline functional out of the box BUT ALSO have EVERYTHING fully defined in the  config.jet file so that everything is visible/auditable/modifyable. Experts need to know EXACTLY what is on their system & have COMPLETE control, allowing them to break their config by swapping low level components around if they choose, but then they are responsible for making sure it works. The beginner friendly version should be extremely easy to use, have a lot of conveniences by default, and be a fresh, modern, and fully featured experience that does not require the command line
questions.answer: Yes. Updated B-E7-BASELINE1 around this exact hybrid. Init and installer now materialize either terminal or graphical baseline directly into config.jet; no hidden baseline import, ambient default, or later silent reinsertion. Terminal stays lean but modern: full boot, storage, user, network, firewall, logging, certificate, package, and compatibility substrate plus fish, Helix, Git, OpenSSH client, curl, rsync, ripgrep, fd, bat, eza, fzf, zoxide, jq, and btop; no remote server enabled by default. Graphical adds complete GNOME Wayland/GDM, hardware enablement, JetOS Studio, browser, files, terminal, text, documents, images, media, archives, calculator, calendar, clocks, disks, screenshots, settings, and Jetpack-backed software management. Studio covers packages, settings, updates, generations, proof, and rollback without CLI use. No-bloat law: one default app per job, no second package system by default, no background service without a baseline function, and every realized package/unit must trace to a config.jet source span. Experts may remove or replace kernel, bootloader, init, networking, desktop, apps, or any other layer; JetOS reports unmet obligations and proof failures but never heals their source behind their back. Ballot recommendation remains D, rewritten as two fully materialized purpose-built baselines.
